body: **MAIN CASE** — a case the syllabus assigns (Bradwell, Zauderer).
**NOTE CASE** — the casebook discusses it in its text or notes. The casebook prints no opinions, so most cases appear this way.
**CITED ONLY** — the casebook only cites it.
**SLIDE REFERENCE** — the case appears only in the class slides.

**Cites:** MR 1.7(a)(2) is the Model Rule; MR 1.7 cmt [24] is its Comment; Ch. 22.B is the casebook chapter and section; CB 598 is the casebook's printed page. "Problem 22B-3" is a casebook problem; "(slides)" marks a point or MC question from the class slides. [[Gray italic text]] comes from outside the class materials: verify it before relying on it.
**Must / must not** is an enforceable duty, **may** is discretion, and **should** is what judgment and values counsel. Prof. Neri's problems ask all three, then the consequences.
blocks.title: How to read this outline

body: This is a statutory-analysis course: read the Rule and its Comments, and work each problem in order (all required).

items: **Question presented.** Say what the lawyer is being asked to decide.
**Rule.** Name each Rule, and note whether its language is mandatory ("shall") or discretionary ("may").
**Solutions.** Explain the possible solutions in light of the client's (or prospective client's) preferences, needs, and understanding.
**Consequences.** Name what follows from each path: discipline, civil liability (negligence, fiduciary breach, contract), disqualification, fee forfeiture, court sanctions, and informal consequences.

blocks.title: How Prof. Neri wants problems worked

body: Ask these fifteen questions in order on every fact pattern. The table below gives the Rules for each and the Part of this outline that covers them.
blocks.title: Issue-spotting checklist: run it on every fact pattern

rows: Which rules apply, and where? Is the lawyer admitted there?
Is there a client, and what kind? Current, former, prospective, organizational, government, or none? Duties to non-clients?
What is the scope? Care and candor stop at scope; loyalty and confidentiality don't.
Confidentiality? Covered at all? Exception? Minimum necessary? Privilege or work product?
Candor? To the client, the tribunal, and others.
Authority? Objective (client) or means (lawyer)? Actual, implied, apparent, ratified?
Money? Fee form and limits, fee sharing, trust accounting.
Conflicts? Personal interest, concurrent client, former or prospective client, imputed? Consentable? Consent in the right form?
A government lawyer or prosecutor? Revolving door?
Litigation conduct? Evidence, discovery, publicity, witnesses, false evidence.
Who in the firm is responsible? Managers, supervisors, subordinates; reporting up.
Dealing with non-clients? Represented, unrepresented, threats, solicitation, ads.
Decline or withdraw? Must, may, tribunal leave, exit duties.
Human factors? Authority, conformity, diffusion, dissonance, fading. When you mess up, 'fess up.

blocks.title: Sources of Law and the Model Rules

blocks.text: Reading: MR 8.1–8.5, 5.5; Chs. 1–3; Bradwell v. The State (1873). Where the rules come from, who enforces them, and which ones bind you.

items: **States regulate lawyers** (Leis v. Flynt), usually through the state's highest court. The ABA Model Rules bind no one on their own. Every state adopted a version, none verbatim, and a state's adopted rule, as its high court reads it, controls discipline there. The MPRE tests the ABA text.

**Binding vs. persuasive.** ABA and state or local bar ethics opinions (e.g., New York City, Los Angeles) and the Restatement (Third) of the Law Governing Lawyers are persuasive only. For "binding authority in New Jersey," only a New Jersey court decision counts; an ABA Formal Opinion (e.g., Op. 492) does not. A Model Rule violation as such can't be the basis for discipline; the state's version of the Rule is (Atkinson MC, slides).
**Other regimes** have their own ethics rules: federal and state judges, law clerks and court staff, bankruptcy lawyers, securities lawyers, and government lawyers (Part VII).

**History:** the first state code was Alabama's (1887); the 1908 ABA Canons were 32 aspirational precepts; the 1969 Model Code had Canons, Ethical Considerations ("should"), and Disciplinary Rules (only the DRs enforceable); the 1983 Model Rules (Rules + Comments, every Rule enforceable) followed Watergate.
**The Rules govern discipline only.** Civil liability, sanctions, and disqualification come from other law, though the Rules inform it.

body: A violation "should not itself give rise to a cause of action against a lawyer nor should it create any presumption in such a case that a legal duty has been breached," and does not necessarily warrant disqualification. The Rules are relevant evidence of the standard of care, but there is no negligence per se.
blocks.title: Preamble and Scope ¶ [20]
How the Model Rules are organized

rows: The client relationship. MR 1.0 holds the definitions; then competence and diligence, communication, fees, confidentiality, conflicts, special clients, client property, declining and withdrawing, selling a practice, prospective clients.
Counselor: advisor (MR 2.1), evaluations for third parties (MR 2.3), third-party neutral (MR 2.4).

Advocate: meritorious claims, expediting litigation, candor to the tribunal, fairness to opponents, impartiality and decorum, trial publicity, lawyer as witness, prosecutors, nonadjudicative proceedings.
Non-clients: truthfulness (MR 4.1), represented persons (MR 4.2), unrepresented persons (MR 4.3), respect for others' rights (MR 4.4).
Firms: managers and supervisors, subordinates, nonlawyer assistants, professional independence, UPL, restrictions on practice, law-related services.
Public service: pro bono, appointments, legal services and law reform organizations, limited legal services programs.
Advertising, solicitation, and political contributions to obtain work.
Integrity: bar admission (MR 8.1), statements about judges (MR 8.2), reporting misconduct (MR 8.3), the misconduct catch-all (MR 8.4), discipline and choice of law (MR 8.5).

items: **Tensions built into the Rules** (slides): they are written mainly for litigators, not deal lawyers; informed consent is hard to get when you also have to protect confidences or the client isn't sophisticated; and the advocate's role pulls against the officer-of-the-court role.

**What lawyers do and where** (Ch. 2): private firms of every size, in-house legal departments, government offices, legal aid and public defenders, and nonprofits. The organizational setting changes who the client is and who supervises you (Parts VII and IX).
**Two requirements everywhere (all required):** (1) minimum competence (bar exam and MPRE); and (2) character and fitness. The applicant bears the burden.

Inquiries must rationally relate to fitness to practice (Schware). Lawful political membership, or responsibly seeking counseling, is not a ground for denial. Rehabilitation counts: bank robbers have been admitted, but Stephen Glass (the fabricating journalist) was not.
**Candor matters most.** Bars compare your law school application with your bar application, and nondisclosure usually hurts more than the underlying fact. Fix omissions now.

blocks.name: Bradwell v. The State, 83 U.S. 130
blocks.topic: women barred from the Illinois bar
blocks.facts: Illinois refused to license Myra Bradwell, a qualified applicant who edited a leading legal newspaper, because she was a married woman.
blocks.held: The Supreme Court upheld the refusal: admission to a state's bar is not a privilege or immunity of national citizenship protected by the Fourteenth Amendment, so each state controls it. Justice Bradley's concurrence said "the paramount destiny and mission of woman are to fulfil the noble and benign offices of wife and mother."
blocks.why: States control admission, and the profession's gatekeeping has long carried bias. It is the historical counterpoint to the modern rule that admission criteria must rationally relate to fitness, and to MR 8.4(g) (Part XII).

blocks.text: The test is honesty, trustworthiness, and fitness, and candor about an item usually matters more than the item.

rows: Not automatic bars, but can show financial irresponsibility or dishonesty. Bars ask whether the applicant dealt with them responsibly.
Responsibly seeking treatment is not a ground for denial. The question is current fitness. Disclose honestly when asked.
Minor, though a pattern can suggest disregard for the law.
Dishonesty, so it weighs heavily. The more recent and mature the applicant (middle school, high school, college, law school), the worse.
Serious, but rehabilitation can overcome it.

body: In connection with a bar application or a disciplinary matter, a lawyer or applicant shall not (a) knowingly make a false statement of material fact; or (b) fail to disclose a fact necessary to correct a misapprehension known to have arisen, or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand for information from an admissions or disciplinary authority. But MR 8.1 does not require disclosing information protected by MR 1.6: you may decline to reveal a confidence; you may not lie.
blocks.title: MR 8.1 — bar applicants and lawyers in disciplinary matters

items: **Lexa MC (slides):** an old lie to the press, then "No" to "Have you ever made a public false statement?" The most likely ground for denial is the knowing false statement of material fact on the application (MR 8.1(a)), not the original lie.

body: Ignoring a bar grievance because the complaint is frivolous is itself a violation (MR 8.1(b)), even if the grievance is later dismissed. The Fifth Amendment must be asserted properly; it doesn't license silence.
blocks.title: Ignoring the grievance letter

body: (a) violate or attempt to violate the Rules, knowingly assist or induce another to do so, or do so through the acts of another (e.g., sending an investigator to contact a represented party you couldn't contact yourself, MR 4.2);
(b) commit a criminal act that reflects adversely on honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness as a lawyer (no charge or conviction needed);
(c) engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation;
(d) engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice;
(e) state or imply an ability to influence improperly a government agency or official, or to achieve results by means that violate the Rules or other law (the statement alone is enough);
(f) knowingly assist a judge or judicial officer in conduct that violates the rules of judicial conduct; or
(g) engage in harassment or discrimination in conduct related to the practice of law (Part XII). Delaware's MR 8.4 has no paragraph (g) (slides).
blocks.title: MR 8.4 — it is professional misconduct to (any one suffices):

items: **Off-duty conduct counts** (tax evasion, academic cheating). But MR 8.4(b) doesn't reach every crime: a petty civil-disobedience trespass usually doesn't reflect on fitness (MR 8.4 cmt [2]).

**Process (in order):** the complaint is privileged (no defamation suit against the complainant); then screening; investigation (cooperation required, subject to the Fifth Amendment); probable cause; and a hearing with due process (In re Ruffalo; Spevack v. Klein).

**Sanctions protect the public; they aren't punishment.** They run from private or public reprimand to suspension to disbarment, and a reprimand still follows you. Compensation comes from civil remedies.

**MR 8.2(a):** don't make a statement you know is false, or with reckless disregard for its truth, about the qualifications or integrity of a judge, adjudicatory officer, public legal officer, or candidate for judicial or legal office. Covered with advocacy in Part VIII.
**No national license.** Practicing where you aren't admitted is UPL (a misdemeanor in most states). A firm office in State B doesn't license an A-only lawyer, and colleagues' licenses don't count.

**Problem 3A-1 (slides):** a PA-only lawyer can't practice in the firm's Camden office five minutes away. **Borris MC:** an out-of-state lawyer who advises clients from a Hawaii office, files papers in Hawaii courts, and shares the firm name is engaged in UPL even if he "only" handles his home state's law.

body: (a) No practicing in a jurisdiction in violation of its regulation of the profession, or assisting another to do so. (b) A lawyer not admitted may not establish an office or other systematic and continuous presence there for practicing law, or hold out as admitted there. (c) A lawyer admitted and in good standing elsewhere may provide legal services on a temporary basis if the work (any one suffices): (1) is undertaken in association with an actively participating local lawyer; (2) is in or reasonably related to a pending or potential proceeding before a tribunal where the lawyer is, or reasonably expects to be, authorized to appear (e.g., pro hac vice); (3) is in or reasonably related to a pending or potential ADR proceeding, arising out of or reasonably related to the lawyer's home practice, that doesn't require pro hac vice admission; or (4) otherwise arises out of or is reasonably related to the lawyer's home practice. (d) In-house lawyers for their employer, and services authorized by federal or other law, are also allowed.
blocks.title: MR 5.5 — unauthorized and multijurisdictional practice

items: **Federal courts admit separately.** Each federal court sets its own bar. Most district courts admit anyone admitted in the state where the court sits; some districts, and all federal courts of appeals, admit lawyers admitted in any state (slides). After removal, a state-admitted lawyer needs admission to that district or pro hac vice ("for this occasion only").

**Problem 3A-3:** Frank and his boss kept serving discovery after removal, so they need federal admission or pro hac vice (MR 5.5(a); see MR 5.5(c)(1)–(2)). **Adam MC (slides):** a lawyer not admitted to the district court can't make even a routine "coverage" appearance, and his partner's admission doesn't help.

**McDade Amendment (28 U.S.C. § 530B):** federal government lawyers follow the ethics rules of the states where they practice. Federal employment doesn't exempt anyone from a court's contempt power. (Federal lawyers may appear in any court nationwide: Part VII.)

body: **(a) Authority.** You are subject to discipline where you are admitted (wherever the conduct occurs) and where you provide or offer services. Both states can discipline you; most states impose reciprocal discipline.

**(b) Choice of law.** (1) For conduct in connection with a matter pending before a tribunal, apply the rules of the jurisdiction where the tribunal sits, unless the tribunal's rules provide otherwise. (2) For any other conduct, apply the rules of the jurisdiction where the conduct occurred or, if its predominant effect is elsewhere, the rules of that jurisdiction. Safe harbor: no discipline if your conduct conforms to the rules of a jurisdiction where you reasonably believe the predominant effect will occur.
blocks.title: MR 8.5 — disciplinary authority and choice of law
Consequences: Civil Liability, Sanctions, and Other Law

blocks.text: "Malpractice" is just a collective term. Always name the specific duty breached and the remedy (Ch. 3).

rows: Duty, breach, actual and proximate cause, and economic damages (emotional distress almost never). A blown deadline means a case within a case: prove what you would have recovered and collected. A few states use "substantial factor" causation.

Loyalty, confidentiality, or candor. No negligence or loss required (e.g., a secret finder's fee from the other side). Remedies: disgorgement; punitive damages if intentional. **ADA Anna MC (slides):** secretly feeding the defense her research to "throw" a case her office ordered her to defend breached her duty of loyalty to her client, however just her motive; she should have withdrawn or quit.

The engagement implies all lawyer duties; damages and limitations periods differ. An express guarantee can create liability without negligence (Hawkins v. McGee). **Mr. Kent MC:** disclosing an invention despite a confidentiality clause supports breach of contract as well as fiduciary breach.
An ulterior purpose plus an improper act in using process (e.g., an unauthorized lis pendens to pressure a debtor).

A civil or criminal proceeding (all required): (1) begun (in some states, continued) against the plaintiff; (2) by, or abetted by, the defendant; (3) without probable cause; (4) primarily for a malicious purpose; (5) terminated on the merits in the plaintiff's favor; (6) causing damages. **Max-and-Chip MC:** a spiteful frivolous suit, summarily dismissed, supports malicious prosecution, not fiduciary or contract claims (Chip was never the lawyer's client).

A court order to get out or stay out. Prophylactic: the opportunity and temptation to act adversely is enough, with no harm required. **Mother and daughter on opposite sides** of one case, both staying in despite an admitted conflict: the likely remedy is disqualification of one or both (MR 1.7(a)(2)), not recusal or discipline (slides).

Setoff, reduction to actual value, or, for a serious fiduciary breach, forfeiture plus disgorgement of fees already paid. Typical fights: inefficiency, overstaffing, unnecessary tasks, or tasks the client said not to do.

An improperly obtained benefit can be disgorged as unjust enrichment even without provable loss. Emotional distress becomes recoverable in some states if the breach was intentional; punitive damages almost always require intentional (in a few states, reckless) wrongdoing.

items: **FRCP 11(b)–(c):** certification after reasonable inquiry; monetary or nonmonetary sanctions on a party's motion or the court's own; the firm is jointly responsible absent exceptional circumstances. It reaches pro se parties too (Huey MC).

**FRCP 26(g), 37:** discovery certification and misconduct, from compensatory up to terminating sanctions. **Lee MC:** withholding a responsive, non-privileged memo brings discovery sanctions against the lawyer and violates MR 3.4(a); it isn't "malpractice" owed to the opponent.
**28 U.S.C. § 1927:** excess costs for "unreasonably and vexatiously" multiplying proceedings.

**Inherent power:** a civil fee sanction must be compensatory, limited to fees the misconduct caused; punitive contempt requires criminal procedure; FRCrP 42(b) allows summary contempt in the court's presence.

blocks.name: Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. v. Haeger, 581 U.S. 101
blocks.facts: In a tire-failure suit, Goodyear and its lawyers withheld internal test results for years; after the case settled the plaintiffs learned of it and sought sanctions.
blocks.held: A sanction under the court's inherent power to pay the other side's fees must be compensatory, covering only the fees the misconduct caused (a but-for test); anything more is punitive and requires criminal-type procedure.
blocks.why: The limit on civil sanctions in the taxonomy below: compensation through civil process, punishment through contempt.

items: **Other law** applies to you too, and a license narrows your freedom. Some states require you to report sanctions to the bar. Informal consequences (lost clients, partnership, reputation) can be worst of all; many referrals come from former opposing counsel.

blocks.text: Keep this handy for every "what happens now?" question (slides).

rows: Prosecutor, often urged on by a victim
Bar prosecutor, after a complaint or referral
A violation of a Rule of Professional Conduct
Client or prospective client; sometimes non-clients owed duties
Duty, breach, causation, pecuniary harm; or abuse of process or malicious prosecution
Damages; punitive damages for intentional wrongs
Usually a client or former client
A loyalty or confidentiality breach that creates a conflict; no injury needed
An order out of the engagement
A breach that offsets or devalues fees
Reduction, forfeiture, return of fees paid
The adversary, or the court on its own
FRCP 11, 26(g), or 37; § 1927; a court order; inherent power
Money to the adversary or court; fines and jail for criminal contempt

blocks.name: Hawkins v. McGee, 84 N.H. 114
blocks.facts: A doctor promised a "hundred percent perfect hand" and the graft left the patient's hand hairy.
blocks.held: An express promise of a result is enforceable in contract without proof of negligence.
blocks.why: Never promise results. Silence in the face of unrealistic expectations may be read as a guarantee, so correct them and use a no-guarantee clause.

blocks.title: Why Smart People Do Stupid Things (Ch. 4)

blocks.text: Good people do bad things, and orders don't excuse them.

rows: Everyone assumes someone else will speak up, so no one does.
Colleagues "rounding up" hours; assuming other associates already reported a partner's racist comments (slides MC)
Subjects doubted their own eyes to match the group. One dissenter breaks the spell.
63% gave the maximum "XXX" shock when told "the experiment requires that you continue," though all predicted they'd refuse.
A good person who did something bad adopts a good-sounding justification, and the next time comes easier.
Perkins; Gellene; padding that starts as "borrowing"; "I do excellent work" to justify an affair with a client (slides MC)
Recasting a choice so the ethics drop out.
The Nevada lawyer with a gun at a deposition "forgot" he was a lawyer (6-month suspension); "Don't you want to win?" to justify coaching a witness to "bend the truth" (slides MC)

items: **Zeal is no excuse.** MR 1.3 cmt [1]: diligence doesn't require offensive tactics or preclude "courtesy and respect." Weasel words ("borrowing," "technically") mean you're too close to the line. MR 4.4(a) forbids means with no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, delay, or burden (Part XI), and courts are increasingly impatient with incivility (Lasalle v. Vogel, Cal. Ct. App. 2019: "an insidious decline in the standards of the profession").

**Billing is where the biases bite** (slides). Record time contemporaneously, in tenths. A mentor who says "firm practice is to round 10 hours up to 15" is asking you to misrepresent your time; you are personally responsible (MR 5.2(a), 8.4(c), 1.5(a)), whoever suggests it.

blocks.name: Berkey Photo, Inc. v. Eastman Kodak Co.
blocks.facts: Kodak's lead partner, Mahlon Perkins, withheld an expert's documents and then swore they had been destroyed. Associate Joseph Fortenberry knew the documents existed, whispered a warning, and did nothing further.
blocks.held: Perkins resigned, served a month in prison, and lost his license.
blocks.why: MR 5.2(a): orders don't excuse you. Fortenberry gets no MR 5.2(b) safe harbor, because withholding documents and a perjured affidavit is not an "arguable question" Perkins "resolved." A note left on a chair isn't enough: raise it directly, then go up the chain (another partner, the firm's ethics partner or general counsel) until the documents are produced and the false statements corrected (MR 3.3, 3.4(a)) (Problem 4A-1, slides).

blocks.title: The responsibility rules (first look; full treatment in Part IX)

items: **MR 5.2(a):** a lawyer is bound by the Rules even when acting at another's direction. **MR 5.2(b):** the narrow safe harbor covers only a subordinate acting on a supervisor's reasonable resolution of an arguable question of professional duty. It never covers a clear violation such as destroying evidence or lying.

**MR 5.1, 5.3:** partners, managers, and supervisors must make reasonable efforts to ensure compliance by lawyers and nonlawyers, and answer for violations they order, ratify, or fail to mitigate (Part IX).
**MR 1.16(a)(2):** a lawyer whose physical or mental condition materially impairs the representation must decline or withdraw.

**Civil:** you are personally liable for your own torts, even at a supervisor's direction; supervisors are liable for torts they directed or reasonably could have prevented; the firm is vicariously liable.

body: (a) A lawyer who knows that another lawyer has committed a violation of the Rules that raises a substantial question as to that lawyer's honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness as a lawyer in other respects shall inform the appropriate professional authority. (b) The same duty applies to a judge's violation of the judicial conduct rules that raises a substantial question as to fitness for office. (c) The duty does not require disclosing (1) information otherwise protected by MR 1.6, or (2) information gained while participating in an approved lawyers assistance program.
blocks.title: MR 8.3 — the duty to report

items: Only about half the states have adopted MR 8.3, but the MPRE tests it. Theft and forgery qualify; a one-time cured calendaring slip doesn't. Telling the wrongdoer's supervisor isn't "the appropriate professional authority." "Knows" includes willful blindness. Your client telling you the prior lawyer stole from her is MR 1.6 information, so no duty to report without her consent. The details are in Part XI (Ch. 16).

blocks.text: Partner Ted is distracted, irritable, and returning from lunch unsteady and smelling of liquor. Partner Sarah gives him a new matter "to help his hours" and assigns associate Maya to help.

items: **Ted:** must decline if his condition materially impairs him (MR 1.16(a)(2)); he risks MR 1.1 and 1.3 violations.

**Sarah:** as a partner and the assigning lawyer, she risks MR 5.1(a)–(b) (no reasonable measures or supervision), and MR 5.1(c)(2) if she knows of a violation in time to fix it and doesn't. She also risks civil liability and fee consequences for the firm. She should reassign or closely supervise the matter and steer Ted to help (a LAP or EAP).

**Maya:** bound by MR 5.2(a); she can't let the client's matter suffer because Ted is the lead. She should raise concerns with Sarah or the firm's ethics partner. MR 8.3 applies only if she knows of a violation raising a substantial question about fitness, and LAP information is exempt (MR 8.3(c)).

Error festers in darkness, and concealment almost always turns out worse. **Confess in this order (all required):** (1) your supervisor; (2) the firm's ethics partner or committee; (3) the malpractice insurer (many policies require notice before you admit error to the client); and (4) outside counsel retained for advice, so the conversation is privileged. Then the client must be told of any material error (MR 1.4; Part IV).

**Places to go for help** (slides): your supervising lawyer (unless she's the one leading you astray), your firm's "ethics czar," the bar's or your insurer's ethics hotline, or your own lawyer. MR 1.6(b)(4) lets you reveal what's reasonably necessary to get advice about your own compliance.
**Why confess early:** the mistake may have no consequences, may not be a mistake, or can be fixed. Clients trust a lawyer who comes clean, explains the fix, and doesn't charge for fixing it.
Practice stress mirrors law school stress: more stress means less sleep, and less sleep means fuzzy thinking and worse ethical judgment.

**Warning signs** of depression and anxiety: changes in sleep or eating, trouble making decisions, withdrawal. Flashbacks of a traumatic event point to PTSD, so it's the "not a common sign" answer (slides MC).

**Get help:** student services, EAPs, and Lawyer Assistance Programs. LAP help is confidential and generally isn't reported to the disciplinary authority while the lawyer complies with treatment (Linda MC); MR 8.3(c) exempts LAP information from the reporting duty.
Responsibly seeking treatment isn't a ground for denying admission, and impairment that materially affects the work triggers MR 1.16(a)(2).

blocks.title: Forming, Defining, and Ending the Relationship

blocks.text: Reading: MR 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.14, 1.16; Chs. 7, 9. The defined terms decide most close questions, so learn them exactly.

rows: **Actual knowledge**, which may be inferred from circumstances, including willful blindness. "Should have known" is not knowledge.
What a lawyer of reasonable prudence and competence would ascertain.
The lawyer actually believes it, and the belief is reasonable (subjective plus objective).

Agreement after the lawyer communicates adequate information and explanation about the **material risks** of and **reasonably available alternatives** to the proposed course. Consent usually requires an affirmative response; silence is not consent (MR 1.0 cmt [7]).
Informed consent given in writing, or a writing the lawyer promptly sends confirming oral consent. If not feasible at the time, within a reasonable time after.
Includes email and other electronic records; an electronic signature counts.
Any law partnership, professional corporation, sole proprietorship, or association, plus lawyers in a legal services organization or a corporate or other legal department.
Fraudulent under the applicable substantive or procedural law **and** with a purpose to deceive (not mere negligent misstatement).
Timely isolation of a lawyer from any participation in a matter, by procedures reasonably adequate to protect the information (Part VI).
A material matter of clear and weighty importance.
A court, a binding arbitrator, or a legislative body or agency acting in an adjudicative capacity (a neutral official renders a binding legal judgment after evidence or argument).

blocks.text: Ch. 7. Be the lawyer you'd want to hire. Competence and diligence are disciplinary duties, and no harm is required. Care is the civil duty, and causation of monetary harm is required. Criminal defense adds the Sixth Amendment.

body: "Competent representation requires the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation."
blocks.title: MR 1.1

items: **You can become competent** (cmts [2], [4]): "A newly admitted lawyer can be as competent as a practitioner with long experience." You may accept a matter if competence can be achieved by reasonable preparation, or by associating with a lawyer of established competence. Neither client consent nor pro bono status waives the duty.

**Cmt [1] factors (weighed together):** (1) the relative complexity and specialized nature of the matter; (2) the lawyer's general experience; (3) the lawyer's training and experience in the field; (4) the preparation and study the lawyer is able to give the matter; and (5) whether it is feasible to refer the matter to, or associate or consult with, a lawyer of established competence. "In many instances, the required proficiency is that of a general practitioner."

**Cmt [2]:** analysis of precedent, evaluation of evidence, and drafting are required in every matter, and "perhaps the most fundamental legal skill" is determining what kind of legal problems a situation involves. **Cmt [5] (all required):** (1) inquiry into and analysis of the facts and law; (2) methods meeting the standards of competent practitioners; and (3) preparation proportional to what is at stake. A MR 1.2(c) scope limit can narrow what you're responsible for.
**Emergency (cmt [3]):** when referral or consultation is impractical, you may give advice beyond your experience, limited to what's reasonably necessary.
**The "duty to be supervised":** ask, insist, or find help elsewhere. "I asked and asked" is no defense (MR 5.2(a)). A looming deadline requires protective action, not letting it lapse.
**Learning time vs. fees:** becoming competent doesn't justify billing an unreasonable amount of learning time. Competence (MR 1.1) and fee reasonableness (MR 1.5(a)) are separate questions.

**Forms ("go-bys") (all required):** (1) make sure it's a good example and fits; (2) never leave in, or simply delete, language you don't understand, and ask what's missing; (3) read any statute or case it relies on; and (4) customize it and check that the law hasn't changed. Thoughtless form use is a textbook competence and care failure.

**Technology (cmt [8]):** keep up with "changes in the law and its practice, including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology." Scrub metadata (hidden comments can reveal settlement authority: MR 1.1 and 1.6(c)), secure data, and use real passwords. ABA Op. 512 (2024) is the first opinion on generative AI; Op. 18-483 covers data breaches (reasonable security, monitoring, client notice); Op. 477R covers reasonably secure email. Oklahoma v. Oliver: a lawyer suspended partly for technological incompetence. **Alan MC (slides):** a solo who sends a draft with unscrubbed client comments violates MR 1.1 even with no monetary harm.

**Problem 7A-1 (Maya and sales tax):** she may expand the engagement if she becomes competent through reasonable study (without billing all of it) or by associating with or consulting a tax lawyer, and should amend the engagement letter for the new scope. **Liam MC:** a trusts lawyer who takes a USPS slip-and-fall violated MR 1.1 by not learning that the FTCA requires an administrative claim first; telling the client it was his first tort case didn't lower the standard.

blocks.name: Mata v. Avianca, Inc., 678 F. Supp. 3d 443
blocks.facts: Lawyers filed a brief citing six cases that ChatGPT had invented, then stood by them when the court and opposing counsel could not find them.
blocks.held: The lawyers and their firm were sanctioned under Rule 11 for submitting the fake cases and for doubling down instead of correcting the record.
blocks.why: Technology competence (MR 1.1 cmt [8]), candor (MR 3.3(a)(1)), and supervision of tools (MR 5.3). A vendor's guarantee isn't a defense; check every cite.

items: "Reasonable diligence and promptness." Neglect and abandonment are among the most common sources of discipline. Cmt [3]: "Perhaps no professional shortcoming is more widely resented than procrastination." Ignoring calls for months violates MR 1.3 and 1.4 even if the client isn't harmed.

Use ticklers, calendars, and staff. **Cmt [2]:** "A lawyer's work load must be controlled so that each matter can be handled competently." **Cmt [4]:** when it's unclear whether the relationship continues, clarify, "preferably in writing."

**Leanne MC (slides):** the judge orally moved deadlines, she never told her assistant, and she missed the reply. That violates MR 1.3 even though the court allowed a late filing and she won. Delegating calendaring doesn't delegate responsibility.

**Problem 7B-3 (Willie's unfunded living trust):** he never retitled the assets, and the husband died eight months later. That breaches diligence (MR 1.3, so discipline) and care (damages for probate costs, delay, and taxes); the partner is personally liable and the firm vicariously so. "Busy practice" is exactly what cmt [2] forbids.

**Problem 7B-2 (Stanley Sloppy):** he let the limitations period run on a whiplash claim and ignored the client's calls: care, MR 1.3, and MR 1.4. To recover, Wanda must prove the case within a case (all required): (1) the claim would have won; (2) for how much; and (3) the judgment would have been collectible.

blocks.title: The Civil Duty of Care and Effective Assistance

items: **Standard:** the skill, diligence, care, and knowledge of a reasonably careful and prudent lawyer in similar circumstances; a reasonable specialist's standard if you hold yourself out as one or were hired as one.

**Losing isn't negligence.** The standard guarantees no result and is only the minimum. **Louise MC:** a reasoned strategic choice not to impeach, discussed with the client beforehand, doesn't establish malpractice; the client must prove both breach and causation.
**Never promise results** (Hawkins v. McGee, Part I). Correct unrealistic expectations promptly and put a no-guarantee clause in the engagement letter.
**Causation:** a case within a case. A worthless underlying claim means no damages, but discipline remains possible.

The right attaches at the start of formal adversary proceedings (formal charge, preliminary hearing, indictment, information, or arraignment) and applies in and out of court through trial, sentencing, and the first appeal ("all of the above," slides).

**Strickland mantra:** the Constitution requires only a minimally competent defense, one that survives unless no reasonable lawyer would have provided it, plus a showing that the result would have differed. First identify which result might differ: the verdict, the sentence, or the plea.

blocks.name: Strickland v. Washington, 466 U.S. 668
blocks.topic: the two-part test for ineffective assistance
blocks.facts: At a capital sentencing, counsel skipped a psychiatric examination and character witnesses to avoid opening the door to rebuttal. Washington was sentenced to death and was executed.
blocks.held: A defendant must show (all required): (1) deficiency, meaning performance below an objective standard of reasonableness, judged with a strong presumption of competence and "wide latitude" for tactics; and (2) prejudice, meaning a "reasonable probability" of a different result. Counsel here was not deficient.
blocks.why: Most claims fail on prejudice. A Rule violation ordinarily shows deficiency, not prejudice (sleeping or drunk counsel, yet convictions affirmed on strong evidence).

blocks.name: United States v. Cronic, 466 U.S. 648
blocks.facts: A young real estate lawyer was appointed to defend a complex check-kiting case and given 25 days to prepare.
blocks.held: Not ineffective per se; remanded for a Strickland analysis. Prejudice is presumed only when the circumstances amount to no counsel at all (any one suffices): (1) counsel is absent at a critical stage; or (2) counsel fails entirely to subject the prosecution's case to meaningful adversarial testing.
blocks.why: Rare. A hard assignment or an isolated error isn't Cronic. Problem 7C-3 (counsel asleep during openings, absent during his client's cross, conceding guilt in closing, absent at the verdict) adds up to absence at critical stages and no adversarial testing. Missing a sentencing is absence at a critical stage (Danny MC). An appointed lawyer who thinks his client is dangerous, skips the alibi witness, and puts on no case fails adversarial testing and has a personal-interest conflict (Larry MC).

blocks.name: Roe v. Flores-Ortega, 528 U.S. 470
blocks.facts: Counsel failed to file a notice of appeal.
blocks.held: Ignoring a client's instruction to file a notice of appeal is deficient, and prejudice is presumed if the client would otherwise have appealed. No need to show the appeal would have won.
blocks.why: The appeal decision is the client's (MR 1.2(a)), and losing it entirely is treated like having no lawyer for that stage.

blocks.name: Missouri v. Frye, 566 U.S. 134; Lafler v. Cooper, 566 U.S. 156
blocks.facts: In Frye, counsel never told the client about a formal plea offer before it lapsed. In Lafler, counsel's bad legal advice led the client to reject a favorable offer and go to trial.
blocks.held: The right to effective assistance extends to plea bargaining. Failing to convey a formal offer is deficient (Frye), and prejudice is a reasonable probability that the plea would have been accepted and the result less severe (Lafler).
blocks.why: Identify which result might differ: here, the plea. Conveying plea offers is also an MR 1.4(a)(1) duty.

items: **Client choices aren't deficiency:** a fully informed defendant who insists on testifying and is impeached has no claim (MR 1.2(a)). **Problem 7C-1(b):** if Steve advised testifying on an inexplicable guess that the jury would believe a three-time armed robber, the advice is arguably deficient, but she must still show a reasonable probability of acquittal had she stayed off the stand, and the choice was hers.

**Consequences:** the remedy is reversal and a new trial. Most states require actual innocence for criminal malpractice (Coscia v. McKenna & Cuneo; Dombrowski v. Bulson), so Steve's missed appeal deadline (Problem 7C-2(b)) supports damages only if the client was innocent and would more likely than not have been acquitted. Once accused of ineffectiveness, defense counsel's interests shift toward the prosecutor's, which creates a conflict.

blocks.title: Forming the Relationship and Identifying the Client

blocks.text: Ch. 9.A–B. Who is your client, and what do you owe people who aren't? The Bobby Boilermaker problem: Charlie Comp's letter said "worker compensation matter," Bobby reasonably understood "all my compensation," and his products-liability claim expired. Scope is judged from the client's point of view; forming a relationship instantly imposes all four duties (loyalty, care, confidentiality, candor), and the lawyer bears the risk of uncertainty.

items: You may decline for almost any reason (e.g., disliking an abrasive client), absent a court appointment or an unlawful reason such as invidious discrimination.

**Intake red flags** (intake mistakes are among the most common): unfamiliar law; revenge or "making a point"; unmanageable expectations; serial lawyer-changers; rudeness to staff; "I don't care what it costs"; Internet experts; shifting stories.
**Court appointments:** MR 6.2 allows seeking to avoid an appointment only for good cause (Part X). Distaste alone isn't enough.
**Must decline** under MR 1.16(a) (below), including the 2023 duty to inquire into and assess the facts of each representation.

body: A client-lawyer relationship arises when (any one suffices): (1) a person manifests to a lawyer the person's intent that the lawyer provide legal services, and either (a) the lawyer manifests consent, or (b) the lawyer fails to manifest lack of consent and knows or reasonably should know that the person reasonably relies on the lawyer to provide the services; or (2) a tribunal with power to do so appoints the lawyer.
blocks.title: Forming the relationship — Restatement § 14

items: **Objective test with a subjective element:** the client must actually and reasonably believe a relationship exists. Silence can be consent ("please handle my eviction," no reply, the hearing approaching).
**Not required:** fees, a conflict check, or an engagement letter, unless you told the person there's no relationship until those are done. "Use your words."
**Status is matter by matter.** One person can be a current, former, and prospective client at once (last year's PI client who now asks about estate planning is a former and a prospective client).

**Appointment creates the relationship without any signed agreement:** Abed, appointed to defend Troy, can't skip the arraignment because Troy hasn't signed a retainer (slides). **Logan MC:** Logan took the facts, never sent the retainer or ran conflicts, and Connor did nothing further; there's a relationship (and malpractice exposure) if an objective observer would find Connor reasonably relied on Logan.

**Accidental client at a party (Problems 9A-1, 8A-5).** Risk rises at each step: small talk (none); he describes his divorce (a possible prospective client, with confidentiality); he asks whether his lawyer is doing a good job (a request for advice); Maya comments on each piece of advice (legal advice he may rely on: Togstad care, maybe a relationship under § 14); handing over her card when he wants to switch lawyers suggests future representation. Fix: "I can't advise you, and I'm not a family lawyer. Please raise this with your lawyer or get a formal second opinion."
**Open-ended engagements** (occasional consulting) are never "completed." Recent contact, bills, and no disengagement letter mean a current client, so a new adverse matter needs consent (MR 1.7).

**Who qualifies (MR 1.18(a), cmt [2]):** a person who consults a lawyer about the possibility of forming a relationship, with an actual and reasonable belief that the talk was about possible representation. Likely yes: the lawyer specifically invites information without clear warnings. Likely no: unilateral communications prompted by general advertising, and "cookie-licking" (consulting every lawyer in town to conflict them out), which fails the subjective test (ABA Op. 492). Don't infer bad faith just because someone interviewed several firms.

**MR 1.18(b):** even when no relationship follows, you may not use or reveal information learned from the prospective client (only that information, not what you find independently), except as MR 1.9 would permit for a former client. Cmt [1]: prospective clients get "some but not all" of a client's protection.
**Shola MC (slides):** a prospective client who decides not to hire you is still owed confidentiality for what she told you; threatening to publicize it violates MR 1.18(b).

**Avoid accidental prospective clients:** "I'm not a family lawyer." Invite a real consultation only after a conflict check, and limit intake to what you need to decide (that limit is what lets the firm screen under MR 1.18(d): Part VI).

**MR 1.13(a):** the lawyer for an organization represents the entity, acting through its constituents, who aren't automatically clients. **MR 1.13(f):** when the entity's interests are adverse to a constituent's, explain who the client is (an employee says "glad you're my lawyer too"; a founder asks whether the equity split is fair to him). Full treatment in Part IX.

**MR 4.3 unrepresented persons (all required):** (1) don't state or imply you're disinterested; (2) correct a misunderstanding about your role that you know or reasonably should know of; and (3) if their interests conflict or may conflict with your client's, give no legal advice except to get a lawyer. Negotiating and explaining your client's position are fine (Part XI).

**Problem 9A-2 (three founders):** the VC (a firm client) expects the firm to represent him, but Maya drafts papers reflecting all three founders' deal and forms the corporation. Who is the client depends on what each founder reasonably believed. If the firm represents only the VC, Maya must make clear to the inventor and the sales lead that she isn't their lawyer and give them no advice (MR 4.3). Representing all three, or the new company too, requires MR 1.7 analysis and consent; once formed, the corporation is a distinct client (MR 1.13(a)). Identify the client before the meeting.

blocks.title: Scope of the Engagement and Duties to Non-Clients

blocks.text: Ch. 9.B–C.

rows: Limited to scope, but covers everything within scope, asked for or not (e.g., deadlines).
Broader: no adversity to a current client in any matter.
Broader: anything obtained in connection with the representation, and it survives the engagement.

body: A lawyer may limit the scope of the representation if (all required): (1) the limitation is reasonable under the circumstances; and (2) the client gives informed consent.
blocks.title: MR 1.2(c) — limiting scope

items: No writing is required, but use one. Unbundling (drafting papers the client files and argues, trial-only work, ghostwriting) is generally allowed. Cmt [6]: limits may track insurance coverage, the client's objectives, or tactics the lawyer finds repugnant or imprudent.

**A label isn't informed consent.** "Workers' comp only" without explaining the risks and alternatives isn't informed consent (Nichols v. Keller). Scope is what the client actually and reasonably believes, judged from the client's point of view, knowledge, and experience.

**Lani MC (slides):** a $15K flat fee "to represent you in a slip and fall case" reasonably covers the case through final judgment; the lawyer should have excluded appeals in writing. A written engagement letter's main benefit is clarifying scope; it doesn't bar malpractice claims or discipline.

**Elias MC:** the client signed a "breach of contract only" agreement, but Elias never mentioned the treble-damages fraud claim, so her consent wasn't informed and the limit is ineffective. **Problem 9C-1:** "trial court only, no appeals or enforcement" and "draft the complaint only (ghostwriting)" are both reasonable limits if the client understands what's excluded, the deadlines (e.g., the notice-of-appeal clock), and what to do next.

**Three scope traps to address in every engagement letter:** (1) post-trial work (appeals and enforcement); (2) tax; and (3) insurance coverage. Charlie Comp's fix, in plain terms: "Comp only. A separate suit may be worth more. The deadline is running. See a litigator now."

blocks.name: Nichols v. Keller, 15 Cal. App. 4th 1672
blocks.topic: limiting scope without explaining what's left out
blocks.facts: A workers' compensation lawyer handled only the comp claim and never told the injured client he might also have a third-party suit, which then became time-barred.
blocks.held: The lawyer could be liable: even when the engagement is limited, a lawyer must alert the client to reasonably apparent related legal problems outside the scope.
blocks.why: MR 1.2(c) requires informed consent to a limit, and MR 1.0(e) requires explaining material risks and alternatives. The Charlie Comp problem.

body: A lawyer shall not (1) make an agreement prospectively limiting the lawyer's malpractice liability unless the client is independently represented in making the agreement; or (2) settle a claim or potential claim for such liability with an unrepresented client or former client unless that person is advised in writing of the desirability of seeking, and given a reasonable opportunity to seek, independent counsel.
blocks.title: MR 1.8(h) — limiting malpractice liability

items: Written advice to get a lawyer isn't enough under (h)(1); the client must actually be represented. Timothy's standard "waive all future malpractice claims or I won't take you" clause is valid only if the client is independently represented in agreeing to it (slides). States disfavor these waivers substantively too.

blocks.text: You can assume one duty without assuming them all. The most common are confidentiality and care.

rows: (1) A prospective-client consultation (MR 1.18); (2) a promise, e.g., anonymity to a witness (it can bind you and your client and conflict with candor, so check with the client first); (3) a client's confidentiality obligations to others, e.g., insurers. Disqualification can follow even without a client relationship (Westinghouse v. Kerr-McGee, Part VI).

(1) Advice given while declining (Togstad); (2) intended beneficiaries (Restatement § 51(3); Lucas v. Hamm); (3) work that third parties are invited to rely on, e.g., opinion letters to a lender (MR 2.3; Restatement § 51(2)).

blocks.name: Togstad v. Vesely, Otto, Miller & Keefe, 291 N.W.2d 686
blocks.facts: Mrs. Togstad consulted a lawyer about a possible medical malpractice claim over her husband's paralysis. He told her "I don't think you have a case," charged nothing, and said nothing about the limitations period. She relied on him, consulted no one else, and the claim expired.
blocks.held: A jury could find an attorney-client relationship (or negligent advice she relied on), and the verdict for the Togstads exceeded $600,000.
blocks.why: The duty came from how he declined. The Togstad-safe non-engagement letter (all required): (1) say you won't provide services; (2) give no advice or evaluation of the claim; (3) encourage them to seek other counsel promptly; (4) warn that limitations periods and deadlines apply; and (5) put it in writing.

blocks.name: Lucas v. Hamm, 56 Cal. 2d 583
blocks.facts: A lawyer drafted a will whose trust provision violated the rule against perpetuities, and the intended beneficiaries lost their share.
blocks.held: Intended beneficiaries of a will may sue the drafting lawyer for negligence despite the lack of privity. But the court found no negligence, because the rule against perpetuities was so confusing that a reasonable lawyer could err; no other jurisdiction follows that part.
blocks.why: Care can run to non-clients the client intended to benefit (Restatement § 51(3)). Problem 9B-3: the unborn descendant is an intended beneficiary; "Ted was my only client" isn't a defense, and the engagement letter doesn't bind the non-client.

items: **Limits on third-party reliance:** liability usually runs only to those specifically to or for whom the statement was made (Bily v. Arthur Young & Co.), and reliance must be reasonable (Goodman v. Kennedy).

**Slide applications.** 9B-1 (Wendy Waitress): Frank was right to clear the anonymity promise with the client first, because it binds the client too; they can still report the busboy's theft to the police but can't identify Wendy as the source. 9B-2 (doctor conflict): suing a current client is a MR 1.7(a)(1) conflict; if the firm won't seek the doctor's consent, it must decline, Togstad-safe (no view of the merits, flag the limitations period, recommend other counsel), and should just say "a conflict," because the doctor's identity as a client is confidential. 9B-4 (nephew's defense): the nephew is the client and Ted is a third-party payor (MR 1.8(f)); the opioid information is the nephew's confidence, so Frank and Willie can't tell Ted without the nephew's informed consent.

**Hareem MC:** a lawyer who declines and suggests another lawyer may have exercised reasonable care; the risk lies in not flagging the FTCA administrative-claim deadline. The answer is "maybe," not "no duty to a non-client." **Duty-of-care MCs:** a QDRO drafted for Keyan: duty to Keyan only, because an adversary in the divorce isn't an intended beneficiary. Owen's exposure assessment that the client said would go to the buyer: duty to both the hospital and the purchaser. A negligent opinion letter relied on by its addressee: professional negligence.

body: A lawyer may accept compensation from someone other than the client only if (all required): (1) the client gives informed consent; (2) there is no interference with the lawyer's independence of professional judgment or with the client-lawyer relationship; and (3) information relating to the representation is protected as MR 1.6 requires. MR 5.4(c): whoever recommends, employs, or pays the lawyer may not direct or regulate the lawyer's professional judgment (an employer can't veto witness interviews).
blocks.title: Third-party payors — MR 1.8(f) and 5.4(c)

items: The payor relationship is arm's-length: no privilege with the payor (sharing may waive it) and no disclosure to the payor without the client's consent.

blocks.text: The casebook doesn't treat MR 1.14; this section follows the Rule and its Comments as amended (the Rule now speaks of "decision-making limitations," not "diminished capacity").

body: **(a)** As far as reasonably possible, maintain an ordinary client-lawyer relationship with a client with decision-making limitations. A person has decision-making limitations if the person has substantial difficulty receiving and understanding information, evaluating information, or making or communicating decisions, even with appropriate supports or accommodations.

**(b)** When the lawyer reasonably believes that the client (all required): (1) has decision-making limitations; (2) is at risk of substantial physical, financial, or other harm unless action is taken; and (3) cannot adequately act in the client's own interest to address the risk, the lawyer may take reasonably necessary protective action to address the risk.

**(c)** Information relating to the representation is protected by MR 1.6, but when taking protective action under (b), the lawyer may reveal information to the extent reasonably necessary to protect the client's interests.
blocks.title: MR 1.14

items: **An ordinary relationship comes first** (cmts [1]–[4]): limitations can be situational and vary by issue and over time. The client still decides objectives, is kept informed, and is treated with attention and respect. Try supports and accommodations first.

**Family members and agents** (cmts [5]–[7]): get the client's informed consent before others sit in (MR 1.6(a)). When a relative brings the client, identify who the client is. Even with an agent under a power of attorney, take direction from the client to the extent feasible.

**Assessing limitations (cmt [13], weighed together):** (1) the client's ability to articulate reasoning leading to a decision; (2) variability of state of mind and ability to understand consequences; (3) appreciation of the substantive fairness of a decision; (4) consistency of the decision with the client's known long-term commitments and values; and (5) whether supports or accommodations could alleviate the limitations. Focus on functional abilities rather than a diagnosis alone; no court or doctor needs to have made a finding (cmt [14]).

**Protective action** (cmts [12], [15]–[17]): start with the least intrusive measures, such as consulting family members, a reconsideration period, voluntary tools like a durable power of attorney, or support groups, healthcare professionals, or adult-protective agencies; consider a guardian or conservator only when necessary. Be guided by the client's wishes and values, best interests, and the goal of minimizing intrusion on autonomy. You may not advocate for a guardianship or conservatorship the client opposes, and as the respondent's lawyer you must advocate the client's objectives (cmt [16]). You must tell the client of protective action you take; it doesn't by itself require withdrawal, but check MR 1.16(a) and 1.7 (cmt [17]).

**Disclosure is risky** (cmt [18]): raising capacity can trigger involuntary civil commitment, so reveal only what's reasonably necessary, and first ask whether the person you consult is likely to act adversely to the client.

**Criminal clients and minors** (cmts [8]–[9]): competence may require seeking a competency evaluation; a minor's lawyer maintains an ordinary relationship as far as reasonably possible. A guardian ad litem advocates best interest, which may diverge from the person's objectives (cmt [10]).

**Emergencies** (cmts [19]–[20]): when a person's health, safety, or finances face imminent and irreparable harm, a lawyer may act even though no relationship can be formed, keeping the person's confidences as if dealing with a client.

blocks.text: Ch. 9.D. Getting out properly, and what you still owe on the way out.

items: **Ending the relationship.** It ends by completion on its terms or by termination; open-ended engagements never complete. Send a disengagement letter: it confirms the end (and can start the tolled malpractice limitations period), lists tasks you won't handle, and addresses the file (MR 1.3 cmt [4]). Ending an open-ended relationship turns a current client into a former one, which helps with conflicts (Problem 9D-1, Leo Landlord: billed twice within nine months and never disengaged, so still a current client). **Gabrielle MC:** a transactional lawyer leaving for a federal agency needs no court permission when no tribunal is involved, but should still withdraw carefully and in writing.

**The client may discharge you anytime**, with or without cause (cmt [4]), and still owes fees earned. **Ruth MC:** she needs no cause to fire Jeff, though with trial weeks away the court must allow substitution. Appointed counsel is the exception: the court controls substitution (cmt [5]).

body: A lawyer **shall inquire into and assess** the facts and circumstances of each representation to determine whether to accept or continue it (2023). Except as stated in (c), a lawyer shall not represent a client, or shall withdraw, if (any one suffices): (1) the representation will result in violation of the Rules or other law (e.g., a nonconsentable conflict); (2) the lawyer's physical or mental condition materially impairs the lawyer's ability to represent the client; (3) the lawyer is discharged; or (4) the client or prospective client seeks to use or persists in using the lawyer's services to commit or further a crime or fraud, despite the lawyer's MR 1.2(d) and 1.4(a)(5) discussion of the limits on the lawyer's help (2023).
blocks.title: MR 1.16(a) — must decline or withdraw

items: **The 2023 duty to inquire:** ABA Op. 513 calls for a risk-based, proportional inquiry at intake, repeated when circumstances change. The "must withdraw" threshold sits somewhere between naked suspicion and actual knowledge. No state had adopted these amendments as of the casebook, but the MPRE tests them.

body: Except as stated in (c), a lawyer may withdraw if (any one suffices): (1) withdrawal can be accomplished without material adverse effect on the client's interests (the ordinary cost of switching doesn't count; a looming deadline does); (2) the client persists in a course of action involving the lawyer's services that the lawyer reasonably believes is criminal or fraudulent; (3) the client has used the lawyer's services to perpetrate a crime or fraud; (4) the client insists on action the lawyer considers repugnant or fundamentally disagrees with (in a firm, ask to be reassigned); (5) the client fails substantially to fulfill an obligation to the lawyer (e.g., payment) after reasonable warning that the lawyer will withdraw (so build a long runway); (6) the representation will result in an unreasonable financial burden on the lawyer or has been rendered unreasonably difficult by the client; or (7) other good cause exists.
blocks.title: MR 1.16(b) — may withdraw

body: "A lawyer must comply with applicable law requiring notice to or permission of a tribunal when terminating a representation. When ordered to do so by a tribunal, a lawyer shall continue representation notwithstanding good cause for terminating the representation."
blocks.title: MR 1.16(c)

items: **Why courts keep you in:** to protect the calendar and prevent opportunism (firing lawyer after lawyer on the eve of trial). Until relieved, every duty continues, even if the client is at fault. Leave is most often denied close to trial or when the motion looks opportunistic.

**Two routes out:** substitution of counsel (almost always approved; look before you leap if you're the one coming in), or a motion to withdraw. Your reasons are confidential, so say only that "professional considerations require termination" (cmt [3]). If ordered to say more, MR 1.6(b)(6) permits it; ask for sealing or in camera review.

**Nonpayment disclosures:** ABA Op. 476 (2016) suggests you may disclose the fact of nonpayment under MR 1.6(b)(5) when withdrawing, but the case law is mixed, so avoid it unless the court presses. "Your lack of planning is not my emergency": courts deny last-minute motions.
**Never threaten to skip trial to get paid.** That's abandonment and violates MR 1.16(c), 1.1, and 1.3, with sanctions and liability to follow. Warn the client and move to withdraw instead.

**9D-2:** the client is behind, trial is two weeks out, and the deposit request is unanswered. The firm should have warned early and moved to withdraw early (MR 1.16(b)(5)–(6)) instead of letting arrears pile up. Now a motion will likely be denied, so prepare for trial. An email threatening not to appear is the wrong tool: not appearing brings sanctions, an order to show cause, and liability.

**9D-3:** the response to the order to show cause shouldn't volunteer the confidential fee details; "professional considerations" plus the procedural history is the frame. There's no excuse for the non-appearance itself.

**9D-4:** fired by email two weeks before trial: you've appeared, so you still need leave (MR 1.16(c)); until relieved, keep preparing; then comply with MR 1.16(d). A fee suit is allowed, but MR 1.6(b)(5) limits what you reveal, and filing it before protecting the client looks terrible.

**9D-6:** withdrawal sought a week before trial after a threatening email, with the client disputing fees and wanting the trial date kept: the court will likely deny leave (too close to trial, looks like game-playing, and the notice problem was the firm's own doing).

**Marta MC:** leave was denied, so she had to represent Ashton at trial; skipping it is disciplinable. **Max MC:** as successor counsel he owned every deadline once substitution was approved, including the expert report due the next day: "look before you leap."

rows: (a) A solo buried in millions of documents in a price-fixing class action

He must stay competent (MR 1.1, 1.3): associate co-counsel or vendors, or seek leave to withdraw for unreasonable financial burden (MR 1.16(b)(6)). If he can't competently continue, he must withdraw (MR 1.16(a)(1)).
(b) An associate whose parents died of smoking-related disease, assigned to defend Big Tobacco
Personal repugnance (MR 1.16(b)(4)) or a personal-interest conflict. In a firm, ask to be reassigned; the firm can keep the matter.
(c) The client no-shows her own deposition three times
May withdraw: the client made it unreasonably difficult (MR 1.16(b)(6)) or failed an obligation after warning (MR 1.16(b)(5)). Warn her in writing first, and get leave.
(d) The client keeps using misleading private-placement documents you drafted
Must withdraw (MR 1.16(a)(1), (a)(4)). May disaffirm the documents (noisy withdrawal), may disclose under MR 1.6(b)(2)–(3), and must disclose if needed to avoid assisting the fraud (MR 4.1(b)).

blocks.text: When a client used your work product (an opinion letter or offering documents) for fraud (all apply): (1) you must withdraw (MR 1.16(a)(4)); (2) you may give notice and disaffirm the opinion or document (MR 1.2 cmt [10]); (3) any disclosure beyond that needs a MR 1.6 exception, usually (b)(2)–(3); and (4) MR 4.1(b) makes disclosure mandatory if it's needed to avoid assisting the fraud. For in-house counsel, mandatory withdrawal can mean quitting your job; employment never excuses assisting fraud, and the company is the client.

body: On termination, take steps to the extent reasonably practicable to protect the client's interests, such as (all that apply): (1) giving reasonable notice; (2) allowing time to employ other counsel; (3) surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled; and (4) refunding any advance payment of fee or expense not earned or incurred. You may retain papers only to the extent other law permits. Cmt [9]: these duties apply even if you were unfairly discharged.
blocks.title: MR 1.16(d)

items: **Files are the client's.** In all but a few states (Illinois and Georgia are exceptions), you can't hold the file for unpaid fees. "Papers to which the client is entitled" means at least everything reasonably necessary to protect the client's rights, paid for or not (an unpaid expert report). Turn over embarrassing items too: they're discoverable, and withholding them looks like a cover-up. You may withhold your own privileged consultations with properly designated firm counsel.

**Never destroy or "lose" file material to hide an error.** That violates MR 3.4(a), risks obstruction charges, and turns negligence into an intentional tort. Handing over the whole file is usually the least bad option.

**Also:** return unearned funds and hold disputed amounts in trust (no self-help); give the client all dates and deadlines in writing; flag limitations periods; forward papers that arrive later; and help successor counsel within reason, "especially when the client doesn't deserve it." A detailed file index isn't required.

blocks.title: Problems 9D-7 to 9D-9: what goes to the client on exit?

rows: Expert report the lawyer paid for but the client hasn't reimbursed, disclosure deadline approaching
**Must** turn over: reasonably necessary to protect the client, and nonpayment is no excuse (MR 1.16(d), cmt [9]).
Notes of an interview with a witness the team decided not to call
**Should**, and in "entire file" states **must**: strategy can change.
Notes of the lead lawyer's talk with the managing partner about an expected fee dispute
Ordinarily turn over; **may** withhold if it was a privileged consultation with designated firm counsel (where the state protects that).
A to-do list with an uncompleted task marked with a red asterisk
**Must**: withholding embarrassing material looks like a cover-up.
An associate's email calling the client a "whiny pain"
**Must** (part of the file). A lesson in what to put in writing.
Reminding the client of the trial date and deadlines already emailed
**Should**, arguably **must** under MR 1.16(d): restate them in writing on exit.
Warning of a limitations period on a claim not yet pleaded
**Must**: squarely within protecting the client's interests.
A detailed index of every document produced
An afternoon with successor counsel answering questions

blocks.text: Reading: MR 1.6; Ch. 8; the Buffalo Law Review handout (1975). Three questions in order (all required): (1) to whom is the duty owed; (2) what information does it cover; and (3) what does it require? Only then look for an exception.

rows: Survives termination. Time, truth, and a memoir aren't exceptions.
Only information learned from the prospective client (Part II).

body: "A lawyer shall not reveal information relating to the representation of a client unless the client gives informed consent, the disclosure is impliedly authorized in order to carry out the representation or the disclosure is permitted by paragraph (b)."
blocks.title: MR 1.6(a)

items: **Incredibly broad:** information from any source (witnesses, documents, your own research); the client's identity and the fact of representation; even public records. Filings at the clerk's office aren't "generally known," so you can't confirm them to a reporter. Say "I can't discuss client matters," and don't lie.

**Limits on what counts at all (limits, not exceptions):** (1) for prospective clients, only what they told you (MR 1.18(b)); (2) "relating to" means "obtained in connection with": what Ron learned from Petrified is Petrified's, even though it's relevant to Mojo, and loyalty to one client never licenses breaching duties to another; and (3) generally known information (MR 1.9(c)(1); ABA Op. 479): "widely recognized by members of the public in the relevant geographic area" or the client's industry, which is much more than one disclosure or a public record. Information that takes more than minimal effort to find isn't generally known: a front-page headline in a major paper is; something buried in a 90-page land-records filing isn't (slides).

body: MR 1.9(c)(1) lets you **use** generally known information to a former client's disadvantage. MR 1.9(c)(2) still bars **revealing** it except as the Rules permit. "Generally known" isn't a general disclosure license (some states, e.g., New York, exclude generally known information from the duty entirely).
blocks.title: Use vs. reveal for former clients

items: **No voluntary disclosure**, except to the client or its agent, or to people in your firm who need to know. "Voluntary" is the key word: confidentiality yields to legal compulsion (subpoenas, discovery), but privilege and work product must be asserted in good faith. Appeal where warranted; you need not defy a final order.

**No use to the client's disadvantage** (MR 1.8(b), 1.9(c)(1), 1.18(b)). Wrongful profit that doesn't hurt the client (insider trading on a deal) isn't a confidentiality-Rule violation, but brings disgorgement and criminal liability. General knowledge, research, and forms may be reused (MR 1.8 cmt [5]); client-specific facts may not.

**Reasonable safeguards (MR 1.6(c)):** reasonable efforts to prevent inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, client information. Cmt [18] factors (weighed together): (1) the sensitivity of the information; (2) the likelihood of disclosure without more safeguards; (3) the cost of more safeguards; (4) the difficulty of implementing them; and (5) the extent to which they would hurt the lawyer's ability to represent clients. Reasonableness, not perfection: being mugged while carrying a locked briefcase isn't a violation. Cmt [19] (transmission): reasonable precautions against unintended recipients; special security isn't required if the method carries a reasonable expectation of privacy, but sensitive matters may warrant more.

**In practice:** no talk in elevators, lobbies, rideshares, or restaurants; no valet with files in the car; lock up market-moving material; a screen guard where others can see your laptop; electronic safeguards scaled to sensitivity (Op. 477R).

**8A-8 (Frank finds proof the wife cheated):** (a) tell supervising partner Sally: yes, she needs to know; (b) tell an associate not on the case: no, no need to know; (c) use it as settlement leverage with opposing counsel: no, not without the client's informed consent, and gratuitous use of irrelevant embarrassing facts risks MR 4.4(a); (d) produce it in response to the wife's document request: yes, compelled disclosure; (f) discuss with classmates at a bar: only as a hypothetical with no reasonable likelihood the listener could identify the client or situation (MR 1.6 cmt [4]).

**8A-10:** tipping a friend that the property is for sale breaches MR 1.6. Reusing the partner's rejection-and-counteroffer form, customized, is fine (general knowledge). Making his own offer on the client's preferred terms uses the client's information to its disadvantage (MR 1.8(b)) and is a MR 1.8(a) business deal.

**8A-11:** files locked in the trunk during a quick stop are reasonable; left visible on the passenger seat, riskier. A stolen laptop isn't a violation if safeguards were reasonable (encryption, password). Market-moving IPO drafts left on a desk overnight aren't reasonable (5D-3: the partner isn't being a neat freak). A cross outline on a desk inside a secure DA's office is closer to reasonable.

**5D-2 (gossip at the reunion):** the classmate breached MR 1.6 by sharing a client's STD story, even without a name if the client is identifiable. Danielle should speak up; MR 8.3 applies only if she knows of a violation raising a substantial question about fitness.

**When the duty ends (any one suffices):** (1) the client's informed waiver; (2) the information becomes generally known (for use, and in some states for disclosure); or (3) death, in about half the states, at least in part (mostly for disputes among heirs). The federal privilege survives death (Swidler & Berlin v. United States).

rows: Everything obtained in connection with the representation, unless generally known
Communications in confidence between lawyer and client for legal advice
Documents and things prepared in anticipation of litigation by or for a party or its representative
Bars voluntary disclosure and use; yields to compulsion
Qualified: yields to substantial need plus undue hardship. Mental impressions are almost never discoverable. A witness can always get her own statement.
One authorized disclosure generally waives it for all purposes
The lawyer holds it; the client can require waiver

items: **Privilege elements (all required):** (1) an attorney-client relationship existed at the time; (2) the communication was confidential and not shared with third parties; and (3) it was made to obtain or give legal advice. Even a minor voluntary disclosure ends privilege for all purposes. The joint-defense (common-interest) doctrine lets co-defendants share privileged information without waiver. Work product applies whether or not shared with the client, and necessity can overcome it.

**Consulting firm counsel:** some courts deny privilege to internal consultations (Bank Brussels Lambert v. Credit Lyonnais). Newer state supreme court decisions protect consultations with designated firm counsel (RFF Family P'ship v. Burns & Levinson; St. Simons Waterfront v. Hunter Maclean).

blocks.name: Swidler & Berlin v. United States, 524 U.S. 399
blocks.facts: The independent counsel subpoenaed a lawyer's notes of a meeting with deputy White House counsel Vince Foster shortly before Foster's suicide.
blocks.held: The attorney-client privilege survives the client's death, even in a criminal investigation.
blocks.why: Contrast the duty of confidentiality, which about half the states end, at least in part, at death.

blocks.title: Problem 8A-12: confidential, privileged, or work product?

rows: (a) Press clippings on public reaction to the client's project
Only if gathered in anticipation of litigation
(b) Prosecutor's notes of a witness interview
(c) DA investigator's notes of the interview
Yes, but the witness can get her own statement
(e) Defense lawyer saw the client arrive with a bloody shirt
(g) The same email sent to Frank for advice on suing
The transmittal request may be; the pre-existing email isn't
(h) Maya's research memo for the partner on a deal clause
(i) The memo sent to the client

body: A lawyer's observations (the bloody shirt) are confidential but not privileged. A pre-existing document sent to counsel doesn't become privileged, though the cover request for advice may be. Interview notes with a non-client witness are confidential and work product, not privileged. A deal research memo is confidential and arguably privileged, but not work product.
blocks.title: Classification traps

items: **Break information into its smallest units.** Check whether each unit is confidential at all before hunting for an exception. "Not confidential" means only "may," not "should."

**Every MR 1.6(b) exception is permissive, covers disclosure only (not use), and applies only "to the extent the lawyer reasonably believes necessary"** (all required): (1) the minimum information; (2) to the minimum people; (3) for the specific purpose. Exceeding any of the three is a violation. "Reasonably believes" is a subjective belief that is also objectively reasonable.

**Consent and implied authorization.** Express informed consent needs no particular form (confirm significant consents in writing). Implied authorization covers need-to-know sharing with the firm team and facts in a filed complaint (cmt [5]), but it doesn't override an express client restriction. **Problem 8B-1:** briefing a firm colleague helping review documents is implied; revealing where the bodies are, after explaining the goodwill and the incriminating effect and getting the client's agreement, is informed consent; previewing the client's anticipated testimony in an opening statement is implied (though it's wise to walk the client through it).
**Exceptions also live outside MR 1.6:** MR 1.13(c), 1.14(c), 3.3(c), and 4.1(b). States vary on MR 1.6(b) more than on any other provision.

body: (1) to prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm;

(2) to prevent the client from committing a crime or fraud reasonably certain to cause substantial injury to another's financial interests or property, in furtherance of which the client has used or is using the lawyer's services;

(3) to prevent, mitigate, or rectify substantial financial injury that is reasonably certain to result or has resulted from the client's commission of such a crime or fraud, in furtherance of which the client has used the lawyer's services;
(4) to secure legal advice about the lawyer's compliance with the Rules;

(5) to establish a claim or defense for the lawyer in a controversy with the client; to defend against a criminal charge or civil claim against the lawyer based on conduct involving the client; or to respond to allegations in any proceeding concerning the lawyer's representation of the client;
(6) to comply with other law or a court order; or

(7) to detect and resolve conflicts arising from the lawyer's change of employment or changes in a firm's composition or ownership, but only if the disclosure would not compromise privilege or otherwise prejudice the client.
blocks.title: MR 1.6(b) — a lawyer may reveal information to the extent the lawyer reasonably believes necessary (any one suffices):

rows: "Reasonably certain" means imminent, or a present and substantial threat (cmt [6]). Not limited to client crimes (e.g., a victim who will die without aid).
