Venting ("I'll wring her neck") doesn't qualify; a gun plus a threat does. Try to dissuade the client first if that's safe. No Model Rule duty to warn, though some states impose one. It doesn't apply once the harm is complete. **8B-2:** "I choked her... she wasn't moving" lets you call 911, since aid may still prevent death; a visibly drunk client about to drive 45 minutes after you tried to dissuade him lets you call the troopers; for lead in a city's water causing neurological harm to children, (b)(1) can apply, but a newspaper reporter isn't the minimum audience. In-house counsel should report up (MR 1.13(b)), then out to health regulators (MR 1.13(c)) to the extent necessary.
The client has used or is using the lawyer's services in furtherance; the lawyer needn't have knowingly assisted.

Reaches completed frauds, but still requires use of your services. Pre-retention crimes, or crimes committed without your services, never qualify (an old embezzlement), and defending the past crime isn't "use."

To keep it privileged, retain the adviser as your counsel. You must be the client, asking on your own behalf. Hallway chats, a retired aunt, or an uninvolved partner likely aren't privileged; a no-names hypothetical avoids disclosure altogether. **8B-4 (Gina Grayhair):** a retired, inactive-status aunt likely isn't privileged; an office suite-mate with her own practice probably isn't either; a short email confirming she'll act as your lawyer for this limited purpose (paying her rate helps) makes it privileged; the senior partner on the case is part of the team (implied authorization); for the uninvolved litigation chair, disclosure within the firm is permitted, but privilege depends on the state's firm-counsel rule.

Minimum relevant information only (the negotiation file yes; an irrelevant ten-year-old fraud judgment no). Cmt [10]: you may respond to an assertion of complicity before any proceeding is filed. Not for online reviews (ABA Op. 496): give a neutral, non-disclosing reply. **8B-5 (Bonnie Badmouth):** in fee arbitration, emails showing she approved the tasks are OK; trust records and emails sent to the bar's disciplinary inquiry are OK; answering Dan's fraud accusation with Bonnie's documents that formed the basis for your statements is OK, but her ten-year-old fraud judgment is not; telling Carla at church about Bonnie's dementia is not OK (no proceeding, gratuitous); "I can't discuss Bonnie's affairs, but what she said isn't true" is risky, since even a denial reveals something; "I can't discuss client matters" is the safe line.

Assert privilege, seek review, then comply with a binding order; seek sealing or in camera review. "Other law" includes discovery (FRCP 26–37), mandatory disclosures, and subpoenas. **8B-6:** assets aren't privileged communications, so labeling secret offshore money in your trust account "privileged" on a court-mandated asset form was improper; once ordered, you must comply even over the client's objection (MR 1.6(b)(6), 3.3, 3.4(c)) and consider withdrawal. Filing the trade-secret description after seeking (but not getting) a stay is proper.
Limited information only (identities and the general nature of matters). Not if it would compromise privilege or prejudice the client, e.g., an unannounced takeover (cmt [13]).

blocks.title: When Disclosure Becomes Mandatory; Hard Cases

items: **MR 4.1(b):** you must disclose a material fact when necessary to avoid assisting a client's crime or fraud, unless MR 1.6 prohibits it. This turns a MR 1.6(b)(2)–(3) permission into a duty (Part XI). See noisy withdrawal (Part II).

**MR 1.13(b) report up:** an organization's lawyer who knows of a constituent's violation likely to cause the organization substantial injury must act in its best interest, ordinarily reporting to higher authority up to the board. **MR 1.13(c) report out:** if the highest authority fails to address a clear violation reasonably certain to cause substantial injury, the lawyer may reveal information even if MR 1.6 wouldn't permit it, to the extent necessary. Unlike MR 1.6(b)(2), this doesn't require use of the lawyer's services; MR 1.13(d) excludes lawyers hired to investigate or defend the violation (Part IX).

**MR 3.3:** no false statements to a tribunal, disclosure of directly adverse controlling authority, and remedial measures for false evidence, even if compliance requires disclosing MR 1.6 information (MR 3.3(c); Part VIII).
**MR 8.1 and 8.3 don't require revealing confidences.**

**Honesty and confidentiality together:** when asked about a confidential plan ("Will you move to dismiss?"), decline to answer, and don't lie (MR 4.1(a), 8.4(c); In re Pressly). "I can't discuss that" satisfies both duties.

blocks.title: Disclosure map: may, must, or must not?

rows: Anything relating to the representation, from any source, including identity and public records, unless consent, implied authorization, or an exception applies.
MR 1.6(b)(1)–(7); MR 1.13(c) (report out); MR 1.14(c) (protective action). Always to the minimum extent necessary.

MR 4.1(b) (to avoid assisting a crime or fraud, when MR 1.6 permits it); MR 3.3 (false evidence or statements to a tribunal, even over MR 1.6); MR 1.13(b) (report up, inside the entity); complying with a final court order.
MR 8.1 and 8.3 reports that would reveal MR 1.6 information; MR 8.3 reports of LAP information.

items: **8C-1, miscarriage of justice:** another man is imprisoned for the client's crime. Imprisonment isn't death or bodily harm, and there's no wrongful-conviction exception, so urge the client to come forward. Things that can change the answer: the client's death (in some states) or an approaching execution (arguably "reasonably certain death").
**8C-2, kidnapped children:** if they may be alive, MR 1.6(b)(1) permits disclosing the location, limited to what's necessary (McClure v. Thompson).

**The Buried Bodies Case (Lake Pleasant, N.Y., 1970s; the Week 3 handout):** defense lawyers who knew where two missing girls' bodies were stayed silent even when the families begged them. They were ostracized locally and lionized by the defense bar. Contrast Problem 8B-1(b), where the client consented to disclosure. [[A criminal charge against lawyer Frank Belge for failing to report the bodies was dismissed on privilege grounds (People v. Belge, N.Y. 1975).]]

blocks.name: McClure v. Thompson, 323 F.3d 1233
blocks.facts: A defense lawyer, believing two missing children might still be alive, revealed to police where his client said the bodies could be found; they were dead. The client later claimed ineffective assistance.
blocks.held: The disclosure was permissible if the lawyer reasonably believed it was necessary to prevent death or serious bodily harm, judged by what he knew then, after reasonable inquiry.
blocks.why: MR 1.6(b)(1) looks forward to preventing harm and requires a reasonable belief and the minimum disclosure; it does not apply once the harm is complete.

blocks.text: Reading: MR 1.4; Chs. 5–6. "Not honesty alone, but the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive" (Meinhard v. Salmon).

items: **By status:** lawyers (always, to clients, everywhere), agents, trustees, guardians, directors, general partners, doctors, clergy.

**By circumstance:** someone reposes special trust and the fiduciary accepts it (a neighbor given signature authority over an elderly friend's accounts; some states call this a "confidential relationship," sometimes treated as less than a full fiduciary relationship). It arises when the beneficiary offers, and the fiduciary accepts, trust because of (any one suffices): (1) the special nature of the relationship; (2) the fiduciary's special skills; or (3) the beneficiary's entrusting of secret or confidential information.
**Scope** is limited by beneficiary (identified persons) and subject matter (the engagement).

**Self-dealing claims:** in many states the burden shifts to the fiduciary to prove fairness, and enhanced remedies (disgorgement, punitive damages) are available. Expect a higher standard even when you "weren't acting as a lawyer."

blocks.name: Meinhard v. Salmon, 249 N.Y. 458
blocks.facts: Salmon managed a hotel lease in a joint venture with Meinhard. Near the end of the lease, the landlord offered Salmon alone a much larger redevelopment deal, which he took without telling Meinhard.
blocks.held: Salmon breached his fiduciary duty by appropriating an opportunity that arose from the venture; Meinhard got a share (Cardozo, C.J.).
blocks.why: The classic statement of the fiduciary's duty of loyalty, which lawyers owe clients (and firms, Part IX). A fiduciary may not take an opportunity that belongs to the beneficiary.

items: **Obligation.** What is the obligation, and to whom?
**Breach.** Was it breached?
**Harm.** What harm did, or could, the breach cause, and to whom?
**Consequences.** What follows (the "Very Bad Thing")?

body: **Nora Neighbor (Problem 5B-1):** a situational fiduciary who invested Dale's savings in her spouse's start-up is self-dealing, so expect the burden to shift to her, with disgorgement and punitive damages possible, and discipline under MR 8.4(c) even though she was never Dale's lawyer.
blocks.title: The four-question fiduciary analysis (slides)
The four duties (analyze each separately, in this order)

rows: Treat clients at least as well as you'd treat yourself. No adversity in any matter (beyond scope). No self-benefit beyond reasonable compensation.
Disqualification, disgorgement; discipline only via a specific Rule (MR 1.7–1.10)

The reasonably careful and prudent lawyer (Part II). Some cases demand "all the skill, care and diligence at [the fiduciary's] disposal" (FDIC v. Stahl); others treat care as non-fiduciary (Tante v. Herring). Use your state's formulation.
Don't disclose, don't use to the client's disadvantage, protect it. It survives the engagement (Part III).

body: A conflict of interest is the opportunity and temptation to be disloyal. It has consequences (mainly disqualification) even if you never act on it. There's no general loyalty Rule: due process requires discipline to rest on a specific Rule (MR 1.7, 1.8, 1.9). Civil claims and disqualification need no such Rule. Competent work never excuses a secret conflicting interest. Conflicts in full: Part VI.
blocks.title: Conflicts need no harm

items: **No sexual relations with a client** unless a consensual sexual relationship existed when the client-lawyer relationship began (e.g., a spouse). The client's consent or a signed waiver doesn't cure it, and it isn't imputed to the firm (MR 1.8(k)).
**Why:** confiding breeds vulnerability, dependence, and undue influence, so the party with clear judgment carries the constraint (Ch. 5.C). It is most common in family law.

body: **(a)** A lawyer shall (all required): (1) promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance requiring the client's informed consent (so settlement offers and plea offers must be conveyed unless the client has already said how to handle them); (2) reasonably consult with the client about the means of pursuing the client's objectives; (3) keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter; (4) promptly comply with reasonable requests for information; and (5) consult with the client about any relevant limitation on the lawyer's conduct when the lawyer knows the client expects help the Rules or other law don't permit (e.g., backdating a document).
**(b)** Explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions.
blocks.title: MR 1.4 — communication

items: **Materiality:** what this client, or a reasonable client, would find significant to the engagement. Candor is limited to scope: private facts unrelated to the work (a lawyer's marriage, sexual orientation) aren't material. The client's reaction is a business risk, not a candor duty.

**Your own mistakes (ABA Op. 18-481):** disclose if material, meaning "reasonably likely to harm or prejudice a client" or of a nature that "would reasonably cause a client to consider terminating the representation even in the absence of harm." Disclose promptly, before any harm occurs. You may consult firm counsel and the insurer first, but don't let that delay the disclosure.
**The don't-wanna test:** the more you don't want to disclose it, the more likely it's material.

**Delaying bad news (cmt [7]):** you may delay transmitting information when the client is likely to react imprudently to immediate disclosure (e.g., a psychiatric diagnosis). You may never withhold to serve your own or another's interest. That's the frame for Problem 8A-8(e), Frank's worry that news of the wife's affair would devastate the husband; the affair is also irrelevant to the divorce, so it may not be within the scope of candor at all.

**Disclose more than the minimum:** "we do the minimum the law requires" isn't a slogan for your website. Agree early on what this client wants to hear and how often; use ticklers for periodic updates even when little is happening; consider "N/C" (no charge) for short status messages.

**Consequences of silence:** discipline, damages for avoidable losses, and a "cover-up" theory that turns an innocent mistake into punitive damages. "Conversations that begin 'Why didn't you tell me...' rarely end well."

**Problem 5D-5 (deBilder's missing acceleration clause):** an errant keystroke deleted the clause from a $2.4M installment note. That's material (reasonably likely to harm the client if the buyer defaults), so it must be disclosed promptly, however crusty the client. First tell your boss, who may need to notify firm management and the malpractice carrier; then tell the client, with a proposed fix (e.g., negotiating an amendment) and no charge for the fix.

**Problem 7B-1 (Dan Distraught):** candor includes realistic expectations. Explain, with compassion, that a civil lawyer can't put the boy in prison or on a sex-offender registry (the prosecutor's call), and what a civil claim can do. "Make it right" with friends from work calls for a MR 1.2(d)/1.4(a)(5) conversation; if a threat becomes reasonably certain bodily harm, MR 1.6(b)(1) is available.

**MR 2.1 (advisor):** exercise independent judgment and give candid advice; you may refer to moral, economic, social, and political factors, not just law. The client still decides objectives (Part VIII).

blocks.title: The Lawyer as Agent: Authority (Ch. 6; MR 1.2(a))

blocks.text: Fiduciary law governs lawyer and client. Agency adds the lawyer's power to change the client's legal relations with third parties.

items: **Formation:** the principal manifests assent that the agent act on the principal's behalf and subject to its control, and the agent consents (Restatement (Third) of Agency § 1.01). If you're someone's lawyer, you're their agent: authorized contracts bind the client, and for the agent's torts both principal and agent can be liable.

**The Homeowners:** "Honest Abe" did nothing, and they lost the foreclosure despite winning defenses. Careless decisions about means bind the client, so there's no automatic do-over; the remedy is against the lawyer. Otherwise third parties couldn't rely on agents, and debtors would hire lawyers to fail on purpose.

**The book's three questions (all required):** (1) What kind of authority (actual, implied, apparent, ratification), from what facts? (2) What is its scope? (3) If exceeded, what are the consequences, and who bears them?

rows: The agent reasonably believes, "in accordance with the principal's manifestations to the agent," that the principal wants it done.

"Not less than $25K" authorizes $30K, and buyer's remorse doesn't undo the deal. An uncommunicated change of mind doesn't revoke authority; a communicated revocation (a voicemail heard before acting) ends it.
What is "necessary, usual, and proper" to accomplish an express grant.
A form of actual authority, and the source of control over means (filing, scheduling extensions, recording the deed).
A third party reasonably believes the actor has authority, and the belief is traceable to the principal's manifestations.

Hiring a lawyer alone creates no apparent authority to settle. The lawyer's own claims never count ("I'm her lawyer, aren't I?"). The client telling opposing counsel "whatever my lawyer agrees to is fine" does create it, even against a private floor.
Affirmance after the fact, by words or by conduct (keeping the benefits, e.g., depositing the check).
You must ratify the whole act (§ 4.07) and before the third party withdraws (§ 4.05). Never plan on it: you've already violated MR 1.2(a), and ratification doesn't erase the ethics violation.

items: **Equal dignities (Agency § 3.02):** if the law requires a signed writing for the act (e.g., certain land conveyances), oral authority to sign as agent isn't enough. Don't extend this to ordinary instructions.

**The 13 words in § 2.01** (slides): "in accordance with the principal's manifestations to the agent." Problem 6A-2(c): Payne's change of heart, told only to her spouse and minister, doesn't revoke Frank's authority, so the $25K deal binds her. 6A-2(d): her call to Frank the night before does revoke it. 6A-2(a): Frank's firm earning more, for less work, on a quick contingent settlement creates no authority to accept against her instructions, and that incentive is itself a personal-interest pressure.

**The 3Cs for ambiguous authority** ("I guess you could take $150K. Maybe."): (1) check with the client; (2) clarify the implications (finality, no day in court, the net after fees); and (3) confirm in writing, and consider a signature, to avoid a swearing contest.
**Discipline** under MR 1.2(a) (failing to abide by the client's decision). A false claim of authority also violates MR 4.1(a) and 8.4(c).
**Undoing the act:** rescission, quiet title, reinstatement (FRCP 60), usually after litigating authority.
**Liability to the client:** an unreasonable belief in authority breaches care, and the client recovers the cost of cleanup.

**Liability to the opponent:** signing implies a warranty of authority; claiming authority you know you lack is fraud, and the firm is liable by respondeat superior. Misrepresentation (tort) and breach of warranty of authority (contract) carry different damages measures.

**What the opponent does next:** walk away (which doesn't excuse your ethics violation), or try to enforce the deal, often by motion in the pending case (Kokkonen v. Guardian Life). Either way, expect your client to sue you, fire you, and dispute your fees. The relationship can be saved only with informed consent, preferably in writing, and that's unlikely. Opposing counsel may have to report you (MR 8.3).

**Ratification outcomes (Problem 6A-4):** (a) she grumbles "have it your way," signs, then fires Frank: ratified and bound; (b) she refuses, the defense withdraws, then she wants the deal: too late (§ 4.05); (c) she X's out the agreement but deposits the check as a "down payment": conduct ratifies, and she can't take the benefit while rejecting the rest (§ 4.07), so the settlement is likely enforceable.
**Negotiating safely: the "non-offer offer."** "My own view is X. My client wants more, but I'd recommend X if your side would." Report it to the client, who decides.

body: A lawyer "shall abide by a client's decisions concerning the objectives of representation and, as required by Rule 1.4, shall consult with the client as to the means by which they are to be pursued," and may take action impliedly authorized to carry out the representation. The client decides (all reserved to the client): (1) whether to settle; and, in a criminal case, (2) the plea to be entered; (3) whether to waive a jury trial; and (4) whether to testify.
blocks.title: MR 1.2(a)

rows: Settle or not, and material settlement terms (gag or confidentiality clauses); binding arbitration (it waives trial: Blanton v. Womancare); high-low agreements (they set the outcome); the plea; jury waiver; testifying; whether to appeal. The four listed decisions are examples: anything that is a fundamental right or the end result the client hired you for.

Claims and theories to plead; discovery; which witnesses; the defense theory at trial; nonbinding mediation (but consult); professional courtesies such as a harmless extension ("you needn't be a mad dog"). Consultation is required only for material means. In practice clients have strong input, since they can fire you.

items: **No end-runs:** an advance blanket grant of settlement authority ("settle for any amount the lawyer considers reasonable") is void, but specific advance authority ("accept anything over $70K") is fine, subject to revocation and changed circumstances (cmt [3]).

**Fee terms that penalize the client's decision are void or unconscionable:** hourly fees that kick in if the client rejects a recommended settlement, or retroactive conversion to hourly. Ordinary deposits for real next steps are fine, but coercive timing is suspect.

**Appointed criminal counsel** may make means decisions over objection and needn't present a baseless theory. The client's right to discharge appointed counsel is limited (MR 1.16 cmt [5]). The client still controls the plea, jury, and testimony.

**MR 1.2(b):** representation, including by appointment, is not an endorsement of the client's views. **MR 1.2(d):** don't counsel or assist conduct you know is criminal or fraudulent, but you may discuss the legal consequences and help the client determine what the law requires (Part XI).

blocks.name: Blanton v. Womancare, Inc., 38 Cal. 3d 396
blocks.topic: binding arbitration is the client's call
blocks.facts: Without the client's consent, and against her instructions, her lawyer stipulated to binding arbitration of her medical malpractice claim.
blocks.held: The stipulation did not bind her: agreeing to binding arbitration surrenders the right to trial, a substantial right that requires the client's authority.
blocks.why: An objectives decision (MR 1.2(a)). A lawyer's authority over procedure doesn't reach choices that waive a client's fundamental rights.

blocks.text: Reading: MR 1.5, 1.15; Chs. 20–21; Delaware Rule 1.15. Fee agreements are contracts with special overlays, and trust money is sacred.

items: **Fees vs. expenses:** fees pay for professional services. Expenses are out-of-pocket costs specific to this matter, never rent or general salaries. In-house charges (copying, research) must reflect actual cost or a reasonable amount agreed in advance; a markup disclosed only on the invoice doesn't count (MR 1.5 cmt [1]).

body: The scope of the representation and the basis or rate of the fee and expenses for which the client will be responsible "shall be communicated to the client, preferably in writing, before or within a reasonable time after commencing the representation, except when the lawyer will charge a regularly represented client on the same basis or rate." Any change in the basis or rate must also be communicated (a long-time client's rate increase too). Best practice: a writing signed by the client (cmt [2]).
blocks.title: MR 1.5(b) — communicating the fee

body: A contingent fee agreement must be in a writing signed by the client and state (all required): (1) the method of determining the fee, including the percentage or percentages that accrue to the lawyer in the event of settlement, trial, or appeal; (2) the litigation and other expenses to be deducted from the recovery; (3) whether those expenses are deducted before or after the contingent fee is calculated; and (4) any expenses for which the client will be liable whether or not the client is the prevailing party. At the end, the lawyer must give a written closing statement stating the outcome, the remittance to the client, and how it was calculated.
blocks.title: MR 1.5(c) — contingent fees

items: A signature doesn't cure missing terms, and the lawyer's own email plus the client's "sounds good" isn't a writing signed by the client. Any contingent component of a hybrid fee (a success bonus, reverse contingency, or shares payable on sale) needs the client's signed writing.

header: What it is and what to cover
rows: A sum certain for defined tasks. Say when, and which portions, are earned if the engagement ends early (cmt [4]). Rewards efficiency, but risks curtailed effort when the money runs out (MR 1.1, 1.3).

Hours times each timekeeper's rate, billed in tenths. Scalable as a matter grows or shrinks, but rewards inefficiency. Losing doesn't erase a reasonable hourly fee. Billing work not done is fraud (mail or wire fraud federally).
A percentage of the recovery, in a signed writing. Can pit lawyer against client when a trial would cost the firm more than it gains.
Any mix within MR 1.5's limits. Contingent parts need a signed writing.
Associates and in-house lawyers draw a salary; owners share fee revenue less overhead and reserves.

items: **MR 1.5 cmt [5]:** no terms that might induce the lawyer to curtail services or act against the client. Don't cap services at a stated amount when more work is foreseeable unless you explain the situation (otherwise the client must bargain mid-matter). Defining services by the client's ability to pay is fine. Don't run up hourly fees with wasteful procedures.

**MR 1.5 cmt [4]:** you may require advance payment but must return any unearned part (MR 1.16(d)). You may take property as a fee (e.g., an ownership interest), but not a proprietary interest in the litigation's subject (MR 1.8(i)), and it may trigger MR 1.8(a) (Part VI).

body: $1M recovery, $100K costs, 30% fee. **Costs first** (more common, client-favorable): $900K x 30% = $270K fee, so the client nets $630K. **Fee first:** $300K fee, then $700K minus $100K costs, so the client nets $600K. After a loss, the client owes whatever costs the agreement says are owed regardless of outcome, plus possibly the opponent's taxable costs. "No fee unless we win" can mislead (MR 7.1) if clients still owe costs; MR 1.8(e)(1) lets lawyers make repayment of costs contingent on the outcome.
blocks.title: Contingent-fee math: costs first vs. fee first
Limits on Fees, Retainers, and Fee Sharing (MR 1.5(a), (d), (e); 5.4; 7.2(b))

body: A lawyer shall not make an agreement for, charge, or collect an unreasonable fee or an unreasonable amount for expenses; the violation is complete on agreeing or charging, even without collecting. **Factors (weighed together; none alone decides):** (1) the time and labor required, the novelty and difficulty of the questions, and the skill requisite; (2) the likelihood, if apparent to the client, that the engagement will preclude other work; (3) the fee customarily charged in the locality; (4) the amount involved and the results obtained; (5) time limitations imposed by the client or the circumstances; (6) the nature and length of the professional relationship; (7) the experience, reputation, and ability of the lawyer; and (8) whether the fee is fixed or contingent. The client's ability to pay is not a factor.
blocks.title: MR 1.5(a) — no unreasonable fee

items: **Judge fees as of the agreement**, accounting for the risk assumed. A quick $150K settlement a week after a 33% agreement doesn't make the fee unreasonable. Rush premiums agreed in advance are fine (factors 2 and 5), and different rates for different work are fine.

**Statutory caps bind** (workers' comp, med-mal, Social Security, probate, the FTCA's 25%). Goldfarb v. Virginia State Bar: bar minimum-fee schedules violated antitrust law, which is different from lawful statutory caps.

body: No contingent fee (any one is barred): (1) in a domestic relations matter, contingent on securing a divorce or on the amount of alimony, support, or a property settlement in lieu thereof; or (2) for representing a defendant in a criminal case. Signatures and reasonableness don't cure either.
blocks.title: MR 1.5(d) — prohibited contingent fees

items: The book calls both anachronisms, but they're still the law. Civil plaintiff contingencies are fine. **Cmt [6]:** a contingent fee to collect post-judgment arrears of support, alimony, or other financial orders is allowed. Rationales: the domestic ban avoids discouraging reconciliation (McCarthy v. Santangelo: "The state does not favor divorces"); the criminal ban guards against corrupting justice (Peyton v. Margiotti).
**Prohibited fee:** voidable, a defense to collection, and disgorgement. Lying about services rendered is fraud or theft (mail fraud in federal cases).

**Formal defect (no signed writing):** the agreed fee is unenforceable, leaving quantum meruit at most (usually a lodestar at a reasonable rate, often far below the contract; contingent fees usually eliminated). Some states allow nothing.

**Discharged lawyers:** the client may fire you anytime but owes for services, usually quantum meruit capped at the contract price; for a contingent fee, payable only if the contingency occurs. Fee terms that unduly burden discharge are void.

rows: Operating account. Rare; some states ban it (ABA Op. 505)
Future fees and costs (evergreen or wasting)

items: **Labels don't control.** Calling an advance for future work "nonrefundable" doesn't make it earned on receipt. States that allow true retainers often require a writing signed by the client stating with particularity what is being paid for, when it's earned, and whether it's refundable. With an evergreen deposit, the client tops it back up after each draw.

blocks.title: Sharing fees and paying for referrals

items: **"Sharing"** means payment measured by fees a client paid (or the profit on them). Paying rent or a loan from fee revenue isn't sharing. Within a firm, share on any terms, without telling the client (unless a lawyer is screened).

body: Allowed only if (all required): (1) the division is in proportion to the services each lawyer performs, or each lawyer assumes joint responsibility for the representation; (2) the client agrees to the arrangement, including the share each lawyer will receive, and the agreement is confirmed in writing; and (3) the total fee is reasonable.
blocks.title: MR 1.5(e) — dividing a fee between lawyers not in the same firm

items: This authorizes co-counseling, not pure referral fees (a few states allow pure referral fees; most don't). Joint responsibility (cmt [7]) means financial and ethical responsibility as if the lawyers were partners, an unconditional guarantee usually without insurance coverage.

body: Don't give anything of value to anyone for recommending your services, except (any one suffices): (1) the reasonable costs of permitted advertising; (2) the usual charges of a legal service plan or a not-for-profit or qualified lawyer referral service; (3) paying for a law practice under MR 1.17; (4) a reciprocal referral agreement with another lawyer or a nonlawyer professional, if (i) it is not exclusive and (ii) the client is informed of its existence and nature; or (5) nominal gifts as thanks, neither intended nor reasonably expected as compensation (Part XI).
blocks.title: MR 7.2(b) — no paying for recommendations

body: **(a)** No sharing legal fees with a nonlawyer, except (any one suffices): (1) payments over time after a lawyer's death to the lawyer's estate or designated persons; (2) the purchase price of a deceased, disabled, or disappeared lawyer's practice (MR 1.17); (3) nonlawyer employees in a compensation or retirement plan, even one based on profit-sharing; or (4) court-awarded fees shared with a nonprofit that employed, retained, or recommended the lawyer in the matter. **(b)** No partnership with a nonlawyer if any of its activities are the practice of law. **(c)** No letting whoever recommends, employs, or pays the lawyer direct or regulate the lawyer's judgment. **(d)** No practicing in a for-profit professional corporation or association if (any one bars it): (1) a nonlawyer owns any interest (except a lawyer's estate representative briefly); (2) a nonlawyer is a director or officer; or (3) a nonlawyer has the right to direct or control a lawyer's professional judgment.
blocks.title: MR 5.4 — professional independence

items: Client consent doesn't change MR 5.4. Why: independent judgment, though the book calls the rule hard to justify apart from guild protection; D.C. and others are experimenting with nonlawyer ownership.

body: A case-specific bonus to a paralegal (10% of the fee, or even a flat $5K) for bringing in a client violates both MR 5.4(a) and 7.2(b). A general profit-sharing retirement plan is fine. A lawyer who refers a case, does no work, and takes no joint responsibility can't be paid a share, even with the client's oral consent.
blocks.title: Paralegal bonuses and referral fees

blocks.text: Ch. 21. "Property" includes money (the client's, unearned fees, or a third party's), documents, and physical evidence. The fiduciary standard is being "more than ordinarily careful." Green money (operating, yours) you can spend; red money (trust, theirs) you must safeguard. A segregation failure is a disciplinary violation by itself, but civil liability usually requires a monetary loss.

items: **Three duties (all required):** (1) safeguard; (2) segregate; and (3) account. "Substantial compliance" is hardly ever enough. The duties are nondelegable: you may use staff but keep full disciplinary and financial responsibility, even for a trusted bookkeeper's unforeseeable theft. "Delegate; don't abdicate. Trust, but verify."
**Two kinds of accounts:** the operating account (the lawyer's money) and the client trust account (everyone else's).

body: **(a)** Hold others' property separate from your own. Funds go in a separate account in the state where your office is (elsewhere only with consent). Other property must be identified and safeguarded "with the care required of a professional fiduciary" (cmt [1]); bearer bonds are cash and belong in a safe or safe-deposit box. Keep complete records for five years after the representation ends. **(b)** Your own funds may go in trust only to pay bank charges. **(c)** Advance fees and expenses go in trust, withdrawn "only as fees are earned or expenses incurred." **(d)** Promptly notify anyone with an interest when you receive funds, promptly deliver what they're entitled to, and on request promptly render a full accounting. **(e)** Keep disputed property separate until the dispute is resolved, and promptly distribute the undisputed part.
blocks.title: MR 1.15 — safekeeping property

rows: A violation by itself, even if temporary, quickly fixed, and every dollar is there. No loss is required. An advance deposited in operating "for convenience" is commingling.
Several clients' funds together is fine, with separate ledgers. Only mixing your money with theirs is barred.
Only enough for bank charges. "Top off the tank, don't overfill it." No overdraft cushions.
Move them promptly to operating. Too early is misappropriation; too late is commingling. Define "earned" in the agreement. "We'll put it back" never cures an early withdrawal.
Deposit in trust, wait until it clears, then promptly move your share and pay the client. Never deposit it in operating.

Provisional credit can be charged back. The retainer scam: a fake cashier's check, then an urgent "refund" wire funded with other clients' money. Disburse only against good funds (cash, a cleared check, a cashier's check confirmed with the bank).
Pay a client's expenses from that client's funds only. Never pay your own bills (bar dues) from trust.

Hold only the disputed amount and distribute the rest. No self-help, and no holding undisputed money to coerce payment or a release (cmt [3]). Suggest arbitration. A client-vs-third-party dispute (a medical lien) may call for interpleader (cmt [4]).
"Promptly notify" anyone with a colorable claim, not just the undisputed owner. An accounting on request covers the required records, but don't reveal other clients' information in it.

Nominal or short-term pooled funds go to the state IOLTA program, which funds legal services for the poor or a client-protection fund. Large or long-term deposits go in a separate account earning interest for the client.

DE Rule 1.15(a): the account is designated solely for funds held in connection with the practice of law in Delaware; the lawyer's own funds for bank charges may not exceed $2,000 and must be separately accounted for; records are kept five years after the events they record.
Client ledgers, journals, and monthly reconciliation. Imperfect records are a violation even if every dollar is present (the "Al Capone problem"). Trust overdrafts are reported to the bar.

body: **Class example:** 30% contingency, costs "off the top," $100K settlement, $10K costs. The lawyer's share is $10K costs plus 30% of $90K ($27K fee), so $37K; the client gets $63K. Deposit the whole check in trust, send the closing statement (giving a chance to object), then move the $37K to operating.
**Dispute on exit:** $10K in trust; you bill $4K; the client disputes $1K and fires you. Take $3K, hold $1K, refund $6K now.

**Integrated version:** 25% after costs, $100K settlement, $4K costs, so the fee base is $96K and the fee $24K. If the client disputes $6K of the fee: $18K fee plus $4K costs to operating, $6K held in trust, $72K to the client now, with a closing statement.
blocks.title: Worked allocations
Formality ladder: what each consent must look like

rows: Disclosing confidences (MR 1.6(a)); scope limits (MR 1.2(c)); third-party payment (MR 1.8(f)); evaluations that may hurt the client (MR 2.3(b)). Confirm significant ones in writing anyway.
Fee scope and basis or rate (MR 1.5(b)).

Fee division between firms (MR 1.5(e)); concurrent-conflict waivers (MR 1.7(b)(4)); former-client waivers (MR 1.9(a), (b)); prospective-client consents (MR 1.18(d)(1)); government-agency consents (MR 1.11(a), (d)); former-neutral consents (MR 1.12(a)). A writing from the lawyer confirming oral consent is enough.

To the prospective client when screening (MR 1.18(d)(2)(ii)); to the former client (MR 1.10(a)(2)(ii)); to the government agency (MR 1.11(b)(2)); to the parties and tribunal (MR 1.12(c)(2)); to clients when selling a practice (MR 1.17(c)).
Settling a malpractice claim with an unrepresented client (MR 1.8(h)(2)); part of MR 1.8(a)(2).
Contingent fees, including any contingent component (MR 1.5(c)); business deals with clients (MR 1.8(a)(3)); aggregate settlements (MR 1.8(g)). Some states: true retainers.

Same-litigation claims between clients (MR 1.7(b)(3)); sex with a client (MR 1.8(j)); MR 1.5(d) fees; nonlawyer ownership (MR 5.4); blanket settlement authority; a proprietary interest in the litigation beyond a lien or civil contingent fee (MR 1.8(i)); literary rights during the engagement (MR 1.8(d)); financial assistance outside MR 1.8(e)'s exceptions.

blocks.text: Reading: MR 1.7, 1.8, 1.18; Ch. 22.A–B. Ch. 22 is "several chapters in one." The recurring hypothetical: Ron Rainmaker's firm represents Mojo, and Petrified Petroleum comes calling.

items: **(1) Personal interest:** the lawyer's own interests against a client's (MR 1.8; 1.7(a)(2)).
**(2) Whom you know (loyalty):** ongoing relationships with clients that tempt you to favor one over another, governed by the "concurrent client rule" (MR 1.7(a)).

**(3) What you know (confidentiality):** confidential information you might share with, or use for, another client to the original client's disadvantage, governed by the "successive client" or "former client rule" (MR 1.9, 1.18(c)).
**Class quiz 22.A Q1:** a "client's duty to the lawyer vs. the legal system" is not one of the categories.

body: **A continuum (CB 559):** conflicting interests run from hardly any conflict to zero-sum opposition. Many are mild enough to need nothing beyond decency and common sense.

**No harm required (CB 561):** a serious conflict breaches the duty by its mere existence and potential to harm. The most common consequence is **disqualification**, an order to get out and stay out before harm occurs (class quiz 22.A Q2). Conflicts can also bring discipline (no harm needed), **fee forfeiture** and disgorgement of fees paid during the conflict, and damages for actual harm.

**Two kinds of rules (CB 560):** bright-line rules that forbid arrangements or require formal steps (most of MR 1.8), and general standards with a fuzzier threshold (MR 1.7(a)(2)'s "significant risk" of "material limitation").
blocks.title: Two observations to keep throughout Ch. 22
Financial assistance to litigation clients: MR 1.8(e)

body: A lawyer shall not provide financial assistance to a client in connection with pending or contemplated litigation, except that a lawyer may (any one suffices): (1) advance court costs and expenses of litigation, repayment of which may be contingent on the outcome; (2) pay court costs and expenses of litigation for an indigent client; or (3) when representing an indigent client pro bono (through the lawyer's firm, a nonprofit legal services or public interest organization, or a law school clinical or pro bono program), give modest gifts for food, rent, transportation, medicine, and other basic living expenses, if the lawyer (all required): (i) doesn't promise, assure, or imply them before retention or as an inducement to continue; (ii) doesn't seek or accept reimbursement from the client, a relative, or anyone affiliated with the client; and (iii) doesn't publicize or advertise a willingness to give them to prospective clients.
blocks.title: MR 1.8(e)

items: The ban reaches almost any assistance: a loan, guarantee, or gift (CB 563).

**Implicit exceptions (CB 566; any one suffices):** (1) delaying or discounting your fee, or working pro bono; (2) a contingent fee; and (3) assistance to non-litigation clients or non-clients (the Rule covers only "pending or contemplated litigation").
**Class quiz 22.A Q5:** lending a litigation client money for living expenses is prohibited, whatever the collateral (a lien on the client's car doesn't help).

A lawyer shall not (either is barred): (1) solicit any substantial gift from a client, including a testamentary gift; or (2) prepare an instrument giving the lawyer or a person related to the lawyer a substantial gift, unless the lawyer or other recipient is related to the client. "Related" means a spouse, child, grandchild, parent, grandparent, or other relative or individual with whom the lawyer or client maintains a close familial relationship (CB 569).

Another lawyer must draft it. Accepting a modest unsolicited gift (a $100 bottle of wine) is fine. **Class quiz 22.A Q7:** drafting a will leaving the lawyer expensive paintings is "maybe": it depends on whether lawyer and client are closely enough related.

Before the representation ends, a lawyer shall not make or negotiate an agreement giving the lawyer literary or media rights to a portrayal or account based in substantial part on information relating to the representation (CB 572). **Class quiz 22.A Q3:** taking all media and literary rights to the litigation violates MR 1.8(d); a discounted fee, a contingent fee, or the client's own bank loan doesn't.

blocks.title: Proprietary interests in the litigation: MR 1.8(i)

items: A lawyer shall not acquire a proprietary interest in the cause of action or subject matter of litigation the lawyer is conducting for a client, except (any one suffices): (1) a lien authorized by law to secure the lawyer's fee or expenses; or (2) a reasonable contingent fee in a civil case (CB 572). Example: no ownership stake in the disputed parcel you're litigating over.

body: A lawyer shall not enter into a business transaction with a client or knowingly acquire an ownership, possessory, security, or other pecuniary interest adverse to a client unless (all required): (1) the transaction and terms are fair and reasonable to the client and are fully disclosed and transmitted in writing in a manner that can be reasonably understood by the client; (2) the client is advised in writing of the desirability of seeking, and is given a reasonable opportunity to seek, the advice of independent legal counsel on the transaction; and (3) the client gives informed consent, in a writing signed by the client, to the essential terms of the transaction and the lawyer's role in it, including whether the lawyer is representing the client in the transaction.
blocks.title: MR 1.8(a)

items: **Scope is sweeping (CB 573):** any business transaction with a client, or any acquisition of an interest adverse to a client (a lien on the client's property is the classic example). Loans, investing in the client's restaurant, taking stock as a fee.

**Three recognized exclusions (any one suffices):** (1) an ordinary fee agreement paid in money (MR 1.5 governs instead); (2) an attorney's lien or security interest in the litigation claim or its proceeds, which many states exempt (some exempt it only to secure a contingent fee, and require MR 1.8(a) to secure an hourly or flat fee); and (3) standard commercial transactions for products or services the client generally markets to others (cmt [1]; class quiz 22.A Q8).

**Class quiz 22.A Q6:** a contractual lien on the client's home (property other than the recovery) to secure the fee is a business transaction under MR 1.8(a) (cmt [16]): allowed only if fair and reasonable, with written advice to seek counsel and informed consent in a signed writing.
**Fairness alone is never enough.** Miss any formal requirement and you face discipline, and the transaction is subject to rescission and restitution, even if it was completely fair (CB 580).
**Class quiz 22.A Q4:** a lawyer who takes the client's business opportunity for herself breaches her fiduciary duty and forfeits her fees (Meinhard v. Salmon, Part IV).

rows: No using information relating to a current client's representation to the client's disadvantage without informed consent (Part III).
Third-party payors: client's informed consent, no interference with judgment, confidentiality protected (Part II).

**Aggregate settlements** of claims of two or more clients (or aggregated pleas in a criminal case) require each client's informed consent, in a writing signed by the client, after disclosure of the existence and nature of all claims or pleas and of each person's participation. Majority approval doesn't count.
Prospective malpractice limits require independent representation; settling a malpractice claim with an unrepresented client requires written advice to seek counsel (Part II).
No sexual relations with a client unless a consensual relationship predated the representation (Part IV).
Prohibitions (a) through (i) are **imputed** to every lawyer in the firm; (j) is personal and not imputed.

items: **The test is predictive (CB 582):** a "significant risk" that the representation will be "materially limited" by a personal interest of the lawyer, judged before anything bad happens and even if nothing ever does. Consent cures it if consentable (MR 1.7(b)).

**Relationships with opposing counsel or parties (ABA Op. 494; CB 582):** (1) intimate and close family relationships almost always create a conflict; (2) friendships may, depending on their nature and strength; and (3) acquaintances are unlikely to. Even when no conflict arises, the connection may matter enough to disclose under MR 1.4; err on the side of disclosure and consent (CB 583).
**Lawyers related by blood or marriage** on opposite sides (MR 1.7 cmt [11]): each needs the client's informed consent, and the conflict isn't imputed to their firms.

**Other personal interests:** a lawyer negotiating for a job with the opponent's firm (cmt [10]); a defense lawyer angling for a prosecutor job or running for DA who calls his client a "monster"; a lawyer's own exposure for the conduct at issue.

**Class quiz 22.A Q9 and Q10:** a mere acquaintance with the opposing party "generally require[s] no action," so accept without disclosing. An ex-spouse on the other side is a close personal relationship, a MR 1.7(a)(2) conflict: notify the client and proceed only with its informed consent, confirmed in writing (the ex-spouse isn't the one who consents).
**Imputation:** personal-interest conflicts under MR 1.7(a)(2) generally aren't imputed unless other firm lawyers are similarly affected (CB 583; MR 1.10(a)(1)).

blocks.title: Concurrent Clients: The Concurrent Client Rule (MR 1.7)

body: **(a)** A lawyer shall not represent a client if the representation involves a concurrent conflict of interest, which exists if (any one suffices): (1) the representation of one client will be **directly adverse** to another client; or (2) there is a **significant risk** that the representation of one or more clients will be **materially limited** by the lawyer's responsibilities to another client, a former client, or a third person, or by a personal interest of the lawyer.

**(b)** Notwithstanding a concurrent conflict, a lawyer may represent a client if (all required): (1) the lawyer reasonably believes that the lawyer will be able to provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client; (2) the representation is not prohibited by law; (3) the representation does not involve the assertion of a claim by one client against another client represented by the lawyer in the same litigation or other proceeding before a tribunal; and (4) each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.
blocks.title: MR 1.7 — conflict of interest: current clients

items: **The classic example:** representing one current client in litigation or negotiation against another current client represented by other counsel. Forbidden without both clients' informed consent, confirmed in writing (CB 598).

**Unrelated matters still count (CB 600).** Because the rule rests on loyalty, the adversity need not be in the same or a related matter, and no confidential information need be at risk. Suing a current closing client in a tort case is a conflict.

**"Directly adverse" means head-on, nose-to-nose** adversity in the same litigation or transaction (CB 603). It also covers cross-examining a current client as an adverse witness and serving a third-party subpoena on a current client (class quiz 22.B Q4, Q6). **Economic competitors** aren't directly adverse (cmt [6]): representing Bullseye and Wal-Mark, each sued by its own employees, is fine (class quiz 22.B Q5).

**Prospective clients:** before taking a new matter, ask whether the new client would be directly adverse to a current client; if so, decline unless both properly consent (CB 599; class quiz 22.B Q1: decline the engagement unless both Opal and Nona waive).
**Discovered midstream:** if a concurrent conflict arises after both engagements are underway, withdraw as soon as possible, probably from both (CB 599).

blocks.title: Current or former client? The hot-potato rule

items: **The line matters (CB 600):** you may never be adverse to a current client, but you may be adverse to a former client in any matter where you can't use its confidential information against it. When an engagement's endpoint is unclear, the client may still be current (Part II).

**The hot-potato rule (CB 601):** you may not drop a current client "like a hot potato" to turn it into a former client so you can take a matter against it for a client you like better. Violating it isn't a MR 1.7 violation, so no discipline; the consequence is disqualification from the new engagement (class quiz 22.B Q1–Q2).

blocks.text: Two rough categories, treated the same (CB 605):

items: **(1) Currently indirect conflicts (CB 606):** adversity isn't nose-to-nose in the same matter but is serious now. Weigh how the indirectly affected client will be affected and how adverse the effects are likely to be. **Positional conflicts** (inconsistent positions on an issue of law or fact for two clients in different cases) usually need no consent, unless there is "a significant risk that a lawyer's action on behalf of one client will materially limit the lawyer's effectiveness in representing another client in a different case; for example, when a decision favoring one client will create a precedent likely to seriously weaken the position taken on behalf of the other client" (MR 1.7 cmt [24]). Opposite positions on the same ordinance in the same court qualify (class quiz 22.B Q3, Q8). Even a positional conflict that needs no consent can hurt client relations.

**(2) Possible future conflicts (CB 607):** adversity is insignificant now, but there is a reasonable possibility it will become serious or direct later. If so, you must not proceed unless you inform all affected clients and get their informed consent, confirmed in writing, up front, or else represent only one.

**The most common possible-future conflict (CB 608):** joint clients' interests can almost always diverge, which requires disclosure and every joint client's informed consent, confirmed in writing, at the outset. If the conflict becomes actual later, more steps are needed (below).

**Driver and passenger** (class quiz 22.B Q11): the classic conflict is the passenger's possible claim against the driver; there could be a conflict if the evidence leads the passenger to want a cross-claim. **Co-defendants** (class quiz 22.B Q9): once the facts give one defendant reason to blame the other, the clients are actually adverse, and the lawyer should withdraw from both (MR 1.9 then bars staying on for either against the other). In criminal cases, ordinarily decline to represent more than one co-defendant (cmt [23]).

**Forming a business** for several clients is permitted with each client's informed consent, confirmed in writing, about the conflicts and the lawyer's inability to advocate for any one of them (cmt [28]; class quiz 22.B Q10). **Scriveners** (documenting a deal the clients already struck) and **aggregate settlements** (MR 1.8(g); class quiz 22.B Q7) raise their own issues (CB 610–611).
**Divorcing spouses** in a contested proceeding: representing both is a nonconsentable direct conflict (MR 1.7(b)(3); class quiz 22.B Q12). The clients' satisfaction is irrelevant.

blocks.title: Once you have a concurrent conflict (CB 614)

items: **(1)** You must either abstain or withdraw, or obtain all affected clients' informed consent, confirmed in writing (better, signed by each), if the conflict is consentable and the clients agree.
**(2)** Otherwise, discipline and disqualification can follow. The conflict exists as soon as interests conflict or a significant risk arises; no actual harm is required.
**(3)** If the conflict caused actual harm, tort damages are available.
**(4)** Many jurisdictions treat fees incurred under a serious unwaived conflict as unearned and forfeited.

blocks.title: Former and Prospective Clients: The Successive Client Rule (MR 1.9, 1.18(c))

blocks.text: Reading: MR 1.9; Ch. 22.C.

body: **(a)** A lawyer who has formerly represented a client in a matter shall not thereafter represent another person (all elements bar the representation): (1) in the same or a substantially related matter; (2) in which that person's interests are materially adverse to the interests of the former client; (3) unless the former client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.

**(b)** A lawyer shall not knowingly represent a person in the same or a substantially related matter in which a firm with which the lawyer formerly was associated had previously represented a client (1) whose interests are materially adverse to that person, and (2) about whom the lawyer had acquired information protected by MR 1.6 and 1.9(c) that is material to the matter, unless the former client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.

**(c)** A lawyer who has formerly represented a client, or whose present or former firm has, shall not thereafter (1) use information relating to the representation to the former client's disadvantage except as the Rules permit or when the information has become generally known; or (2) reveal information relating to the representation except as the Rules permit.
blocks.title: MR 1.9 — duties to former clients

items: **The point (CB 637):** the old engagement and the new one must not involve the same dispute or deal, or a substantively similar one, where the new client's interests are materially adverse to the former client's. Unrelated later matters are fine.

**Prospective clients (MR 1.18(c); CB 629):** similar language, but the bar applies only if the information received "could be significantly harmful" to the prospective client in the matter, which makes the protection a little narrower than for former clients.
**Current clients (CB 629):** the concurrent client rule already forbids adversity in any respect, so current clients' confidences get broader protection.

body: When a lawyer owes a duty of confidentiality to anyone (a prospective, current, or former client, or someone else), the lawyer must not take on or continue an engagement in which the lawyer might reasonably be able to use that confidential information against the person to whom the duty is owed.
blocks.title: A practical paraphrase of the successive client rule (CB 630)

items: **Where it's used:** mostly in discipline and civil disqualification proceedings (CB 631).

**Two methods, often mixed (any one suffices):** (1) the person seeking protection describes in general terms the confidential information actually confided, or discloses specific confidences under seal or in camera (CB 632); or (2) without revealing anything, it describes the earlier engagement from the outside, and the court infers what confidential information was likely imparted, compares it with what is likely to matter in the new engagement (also viewed from the outside), and asks whether the two are substantially related (CB 633). Don't confuse a substantial relationship between *matters* with how "substantial" the lawyer-client relationship was.

**Playbook information (CB 635):** general information about how a client operates (its "plays") is confidential, but ordinarily isn't enough to create a substantial relationship unless it is so voluminous, detailed, or specifically applicable that it creates a substantial unfair advantage.

blocks.title: Consequences of violating the successive client rule (CB 637)

items: **(1) Discipline** under MR 1.9(a) or 1.18, limited to information received from a former or prospective client.

**(2) Disqualification** reaches more broadly in most states: it is also available when a lawyer holds substantially related confidential information from anyone to whom the lawyer assumed a duty of confidentiality outside an actual or prospective client relationship. Morrison Knudsen v. Hancock Rothert & Bunshoft (Cal. Ct. App. 1999): disqualified lawyers had acquired a duty to a third party because their client in the old engagement had assumed one.
**(3) Fee forfeiture** for a substantial, serious conflict, with possible disgorgement of fees paid.

**(4) Damages or restitution** only if the conflict actually caused compensable harm or an ill-gotten gain (e.g., insider trading on the former client's information). No use or harm is required for disqualification.

blocks.name: Westinghouse Elec. Corp. v. Kerr-McGee Corp., 580 F.2d 1311
blocks.facts: A law firm representing a petroleum industry trade association gathered confidential information from member oil companies, promising to keep it confidential, while another office of the firm represented Westinghouse in an antitrust suit against some of those same companies.
blocks.held: The firm was disqualified: by promising confidentiality, it had assumed a duty to the member companies, which the court described as an implied attorney-client relationship.
blocks.why: A duty of confidentiality, and the disqualification that protects it, can arise without a full client relationship. The casebook agrees with the result but not the "implied representation" reasoning: only one duty was assumed (CB 256, 637).

blocks.text: Reading: MR 1.10; Ch. 22.D.

body: **(a)** While lawyers are associated in a firm, none of them shall knowingly represent a client when any one of them practicing alone would be prohibited by MR 1.7 or 1.9, unless (any one suffices): (1) the prohibition is based on a personal interest of the disqualified lawyer and does not present a significant risk of materially limiting the representation by the remaining lawyers; or (2) the prohibition is based on MR 1.9(a) or (b), arises out of the disqualified lawyer's association with a prior firm, and (all required): (i) the disqualified lawyer is timely screened from any participation in the matter and is apportioned no part of the fee; (ii) written notice is promptly given to any affected former client, describing the screening procedures, stating the firm's and the screened lawyer's compliance, stating that review may be available before a tribunal, and agreeing to respond promptly to written inquiries or objections; and (iii) certifications of compliance are provided by the screened lawyer and a partner, at reasonable intervals on the former client's written request and when the screening ends.

**(b)** When a lawyer has left a firm, the firm may represent a person materially adverse to a client the departed lawyer represented and the firm no longer represents, unless (both required for the bar): (1) the matter is the same or substantially related; and (2) a lawyer remaining in the firm has material information protected by MR 1.6 and 1.9(c).
**(c)** An imputed disqualification may be waived by the affected client under the conditions of MR 1.7. **(d)** Government lawyers' firms are governed by MR 1.11 (Part VII).
blocks.title: MR 1.10 — imputation of conflicts: general rule

items: **The general rule (CB 647):** if any lawyer in a practice organization has a conflict (or a relationship or knowledge that could create one), every lawyer and the organization itself is deemed to have it. In most situations the presumption is **conclusive** (CB 649). It applies across offices and states: Keisha, Chrissy, Victor in Garden, and Abigail in Keystone are all conflicted (class quiz 22.D Q1).

**Rebuttable presumptions (CB 650):** in seven defined situations, the firm may rebut imputation, and other lawyers may proceed without any client consent as long as the personally disqualified lawyer stays out. Most states apply the same exceptions to disqualification.

rows: Narrower than it sounds (CB 652): most personal-interest conflicts are conclusively imputed by MR 1.8(k). The ones that aren't are sex with a client (MR 1.8(j)) and MR 1.7(a)(2) personal-interest conflicts. **Class quiz 22.D Q2:** Amir's religious objection to suing the church isn't imputed if he does no work on the matter and his beliefs create no significant risk of limiting Leona's representation (MR 1.10 cmt [3]).

A lawyer who changes jobs brings to, and imputes within, the new firm only confidential information the lawyer personally knew (CB 654). It has no effect on concurrent conflicts. **Class quiz 22.D Q3:** Lulu, whose conflict was purely imputed at her old firm and who acquired no material information about the adverse party, needs no screen (MR 1.9(b), cmt [5]).
Every lawyer exposed to the client's information must have left, and no trace of it (paper or digital) may remain (CB 658). It applies only to successive conflicts, never concurrent ones.

blocks.title: Rebutting imputation with an ethical screen

items: **What a screen is (MR 1.0(k); CB 660):** prophylactic measures restricting confidential information to a lawyer or small group and keeping it from everyone else in the firm, through the timely imposition of procedures reasonably adequate to protect the information. Most conflicts can't be cured by a screen, and a screen never cures a concurrent conflict.

**Common features (MR 1.0 cmts [8]–[10]; all expected):** (1) the screened lawyer's written undertaking not to communicate about the matter or touch its files; (2) written notice and instructions to all other firm personnel forbidding communication with the screened lawyer about it; (3) denial of access to files and information, paper and electronic; (4) periodic reminders to everyone; (5) no share of the fee where a Rule requires it (MR 1.10(a)(2), 1.11, 1.12, 1.18(d)); and (6) timeliness: in place as soon as practical once the firm knows or reasonably should know a screen is needed (cmt [10]).

**Only four successive-conflict situations can be cured by a screen alone (CB 663–667; any one suffices):** (1) nonlawyer staff exposed to confidential information (MR 1.10 cmt [4]); (2) a lawyer exposed to the information before becoming a lawyer, e.g., as a paralegal or law clerk (MR 1.10 cmt [4]); (3) a lateral lawyer's actual knowledge from a prior firm (MR 1.10(a)(2), with notice and certifications); and (4) a prospective client's information, if the lawyer took reasonable measures to avoid more exposure than needed to decide whether to take the matter, is timely screened with no part of the fee, and written notice is promptly given to the prospective client (MR 1.18(d)(2)).
Government lawyers (MR 1.11) and former judges and neutrals (MR 1.12) have their own screening rules (Part VII).

blocks.title: Addressing Conflicts: Abstention, Consent, and Conflict Checks

blocks.text: Reading: Ch. 22.E–F.

items: **Abstaining:** "No conflict; no consequences." But you can abstain only from an engagement you never took on. Once the prospective client reasonably believes you're his lawyer, you are, and a conflicted engagement then requires withdrawal, likely from every engagement creating the conflict, unless all affected clients give informed consent, confirmed in writing, to which engagements continue and on what terms.

**Two ways to proceed (CB 680; any one suffices):** (1) rebut imputation and staff the matter with lawyers who aren't personally disqualified (MR 1.10); or (2) if the conflict is consentable, obtain all affected clients' informed consent in the required form and substance.

body: A conflict can't be cured by consent when (any one suffices): (1) the representation is prohibited by law (MR 1.7(b)(2)); (2) it is one of the personal-interest conflicts MR 1.8 forbids outright; (3) it involves the assertion of a claim by one client against another client the lawyer represents in the same proceeding before a tribunal (MR 1.7(b)(3)); or (4) the lawyer doesn't reasonably believe the lawyer can provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client (MR 1.7(b)(1)). The belief must be subjectively held and objectively reasonable; if no reasonable client would consent, the conflict is nonconsentable.
blocks.title: The four nonconsentable conflicts

items: **Class quiz 22.E–F Q1:** co-defendants Maru and Neo blame each other and have incompatible defenses, so Oscar can't reasonably represent both (MR 1.7(b)(1), cmt [23]). **Q2:** a braking discrepancy and different injuries between two clients from one accident need evaluation but don't automatically bar Shiva from representing both; with informed consent, confirmed in writing, and MR 1.7(b) satisfied, she may (cmts [18], [23]).

**An enforceable waiver should, and arguably must, disclose (all required):** (1) "the facts and circumstances giving rise to the situation" (MR 1.0 cmt [6]); (2) "the material risks of" the proposed course (MR 1.0(e)); (3) the "reasonably available alternatives," including the client's absolute right to refuse consent (MR 1.0(e)); and (4) the client's right to seek independent advice and take the time needed (MR 1.0 cmt [6]; the casebook recommends always advising independent counsel).

**Joint representation disclosures (CB 686–687):** jointly represented clients have no privilege against one another and, in most states, no confidentiality against one another. Say so up front, and say what happens if interests diverge (the lawyer may have to withdraw from both). **Class quiz 22.E–F Q4:** Amity can't give informed consent to a joint estate plan without learning of Buzz's child; Chuck must first get Buzz's authorization to disclose (MR 1.6(a)), and if Buzz insists on secrecy, withdraw from both rather than finish the wills while withholding material information (MR 1.7 cmts [18], [19], [31]).

**Advance waivers (MR 1.7 cmt [22]; CB 691):** "The effectiveness of such waivers is generally determined by the extent to which the client reasonably understands the material risks that the waiver entails." That usually requires describing the kind of conflict that later materializes. A specific, explained waiver is more likely to work than an open-ended one, and no advance waiver can authorize a future nonconsentable conflict (class quiz 22.E–F Q7).

**When interests later diverge:** the initial consent doesn't cover new antagonism. Continuing for one of two doctors requires both doctors' informed consent, confirmed in writing, plus compliance with duties to the departing client (MR 1.7 cmt [29]; MR 1.9; class quiz 22.E–F Q6). Cleo, representing her own client's litigation opponent on conflicting positions about the same trade dress, should withdraw from both (class quiz 22.E–F Q3).

**Every affected client consents.** Nicole may represent Orin against current firm client Morris, even in an unrelated transaction, only if both Morris and Orin consent, confirmed in writing (MR 1.7(a)(1), cmt [7]; MR 1.10(a); class quiz 22.E–F Q5).
Most states require informed consent **confirmed in writing**; a few require a writing signed by the client, which is the better practice everywhere.

**Silence is not consent:** "Obtaining informed consent will usually require an affirmative response... In general, a lawyer may not assume consent from a client's or other person's silence" (MR 1.0 cmt [7]).
**Disclosure comes first.** Consent given before the disclosure and explanation "is no consent at all."

blocks.name: Sheppard Mullin v. J-M Manufacturing Co., 6 Cal. 5th 59
blocks.facts: Sheppard, Mullin, Richter & Hampton took on J-M in a qui tam suit under an engagement letter with a broad advance waiver, without telling J-M that the firm was then also representing one of the public entities suing J-M, in unrelated matters.
blocks.held: The advance waiver didn't cover a known, existing conflict the firm failed to disclose, so J-M's consent wasn't informed and the engagement agreement was unenforceable; the firm could at most seek quantum meruit fees, depending on the seriousness of the violation.
blocks.why: Informed consent requires disclosing conflicts you know about; boilerplate can't waive what wasn't explained (MR 1.7 cmt [22]). The casebook notes the amicus brief arguing that big firms demand such waivers on a take-it-or-leave-it basis.

items: Practice organizations must maintain policies, procedures, and systems to recognize and respond to conflicts **before** agreeing to a new engagement.

A conflicts database tracks every interaction that may have created duties to anyone: clients, prospective clients, adverse parties, co-parties, and people to whom confidentiality was promised. Check each potential engagement, and everyone involved, against it.

Run the check before receiving more than the minimum information (MR 1.18(d)(2)), and update it when parties are added, firms merge, or lawyers join (MR 1.6(b)(7)). MR 5.1(a) makes partners responsible for having such a system (Part IX).
**Identify every person to whom duties are owed:** current, former, and prospective clients, and non-clients promised confidentiality.
**Classify the conflict:** personal interest (MR 1.8, 1.7(a)(2)); concurrent (MR 1.7(a)(1)–(2)); successive (MR 1.9, 1.18(c)).
**Impute it** across the firm (MR 1.10(a), 1.8(k)), then ask whether imputation can be rebutted by situational facts or a screen.
**Ask whether it is consentable** (MR 1.7(b)(1)–(3); MR 1.8's outright bans).
**Get informed consent from every affected client in the required form**, or abstain or withdraw (MR 1.16(a)(1)).
**Name the consequences:** disqualification, discipline, fee forfeiture, damages.

blocks.title: The Government Lawyer's Client, Conflicts, and Extra Duties

blocks.text: Reading: MR 1.11, 1.12, 3.8; Ch. 25. Week 10 also brought the 15-question multiple-choice exam (Oct. 26).

items: **Same rules, with a few twists (CB 816):** government lawyers follow the same Rules as everyone else, plus (1) obligations outside the Rules that apply because they are government employees; (2) recurring situations that make the general Rules hard to apply; and (3) two Rules that apply only to them: MR 1.11 (conflicts for current and former government lawyers) and MR 3.8 (prosecutors).

**Where they may practice (CB 817):** state and local government lawyers need a license where they practice, like anyone else. The federal government requires a license in at least one state or D.C., and by statute (28 U.S.C. § 517) a federal lawyer may appear in any state or federal court nationwide (class quiz Ch. 25 Q5). Federal lawyers still follow the conduct rules of the jurisdiction or court where they appear (the McDade Amendment, 28 U.S.C. § 530B); with no tribunal involved, the rules of the licensing jurisdiction generally govern.

**Often clear:** a specific state, county, city, or agency. Sometimes the lawyer represents an interest or function of government, nominally represents the agency head while really representing the agency, or personally represents an employee, but only to protect the employer's interests too.

**The law that creates the entity defines it** (CB 818): constitutions, statutes, and regulations identify the client and the official empowered to direct counsel and speak for it. The Rules won't tell you who calls the shots.

**Prosecutors represent the sovereign:** the State or "the People," not the DA personally, the victim, or the investigating officer, who are witnesses (class quiz Ch. 25 Q2, Q6). The victim's own private lawyer represents the victim (Q7).

**Defending government actors (CB 822):** governments act only through people, so suits often name employees. In an **official-capacity** suit the true client is the agency, and the named official is its procedural representative (Q3, Q8). When a government lawyer represents an employee **personally** (e.g., a Bivens damages claim against a federal officer), the employee is a full client owed every duty, yet the lawyer represents her only to serve the government's interests, so the agency's interests always count too. Conflicts can develop midstream, so disclose and get informed consents from everyone at the outset (CB 827).

**Are two agencies one client?** Sometimes substantive law says whether agencies are distinct enough to be different "clients," so one government law office can represent one against the other. Sometimes officials agree which lawyers handle each side; written informed consents resolve any lingering concern.

**Absent agreement, infer the client from reasonable expectations, considering (weighed together):** (1) how the government client is legally defined and funded; (2) whether it has independent legal authority over the matter; and (3) the extent to which the matter has broader implications for the government. Resolve doubt in favor of detailed written disclosures and consents all around.
Even when two entities aren't the same client, MR 1.7(a)(2) still bars a significant risk of material limitation.

Leaders of government law offices and courts often expect a "higher standard" of government lawyers. Specific laws apply that don't bind private lawyers: conflict-of-interest statutes, "ethics in government" laws, codes of conduct, personnel rules, and gift rules that often bar even shared meals from people with business before the agency.
**Class quiz Ch. 25 Q1:** may Patty accept Derrick's offer? "Maybe": besides the Rules, she must check the gift laws and other government ethics rules.
MR 1.11 covers service as any "public officer or employee," not only as a practicing lawyer (CB 831).

**Concurrent conflicts are not imputed in government (CB 832).** An individual government lawyer may not take part in a matter adverse to her own current client, but others in her office may. MR 1.10 doesn't apply (MR 1.10(d)); MR 1.11 does.

body: **(a)** A lawyer who formerly served as a public officer or employee (1) is subject to MR 1.9(c); and (2) shall not otherwise represent a client in connection with a matter in which the lawyer participated personally and substantially as a public officer or employee, unless the appropriate government agency gives its informed consent, confirmed in writing.

**(b)** When a lawyer is disqualified under (a), no lawyer in the lawyer's firm may knowingly undertake or continue the matter unless (all required): (1) the disqualified lawyer is timely screened from any participation and is apportioned no part of the fee; and (2) written notice is promptly given to the appropriate government agency to enable it to ascertain compliance.

**(c)** A lawyer having information the lawyer knows is **confidential government information** about a person, acquired as a public officer or employee, may not represent a private client whose interests are adverse to that person in a matter in which the information could be used to the person's material disadvantage. The firm may proceed only if the disqualified lawyer is timely screened and apportioned no part of the fee.

**(e)** "Matter" includes (1) any judicial or other proceeding, application, request for a ruling or other determination, contract, claim, controversy, investigation, charge, accusation, arrest, or other **particular matter involving a specific party or parties**; and (2) any other matter covered by the agency's conflict rules.
blocks.title: MR 1.11(a)–(c) — former government lawyers
Four levels of prior government involvement (CB 833–837)

rows: (1) Participated personally and substantially in the same "matter"

The narrow MR 1.11(e) "matter": a particular matter involving specific parties (not rulemaking). The bar applies even if the private client's interests aren't adverse to the government: it forbids switching sides, and more.

The former government lawyer is personally out unless the agency gives informed consent, confirmed in writing (MR 1.11(a)(2)). The firm may proceed with a timely screen, no fee share, and prompt written notice to the agency (MR 1.11(b)); more measures are probably needed to make the screen effective.
(2) No personal and substantial participation, but has "confidential government information" about a third party

Information obtained under governmental authority that the government is prohibited by law from disclosing or has a privilege not to disclose, and that isn't otherwise public (e.g., that someone was secretly investigated, or a sealed indictment). It must concern a third party adverse to the new client and be usable to that party's material disadvantage.
Personally disqualified; the firm may proceed with a timely screen and no fee share (MR 1.11(c)). No notice requirement.
(3) Participated only in something that isn't a "matter" (e.g., rulemaking), or knows ordinary confidential information that isn't confidential government information
A major departure from the private-sector rules.

No one is disqualified and no screen is required (some firms screen anyway). The lawyer may not use the information to the former government client's disadvantage or disclose it (MR 1.9(c)); if she can't work on the matter without doing so, she must stay out.
(4) No involvement and no confidential information
