items: **No cooling-off period.** The Model Rules turn on personal and substantial participation, not time (class quiz Ch. 25 Q9: the former prosecutor is disqualified only if she participated personally and substantially in the prosecution).

**Class quiz Ch. 25 Q10:** Adina, personally disqualified under MR 1.11(a)(2), must be screened, with no share of the fee and written notice to the Department of Labor, before her new firm can keep the wage-and-hour case. **Q11:** Praveen's nonpublic Medicare data about Dr. Hildenbrant is confidential government information under MR 1.11(c); he should have been disqualified and screened, and he certainly couldn't use or share it.

body: A lawyer currently serving as a public officer or employee (1) is subject to MR 1.7 and 1.9; and (2) shall not (either is barred): (i) participate in a matter in which the lawyer participated personally and substantially while in private practice or nongovernmental employment, unless the agency gives informed consent, confirmed in writing; or (ii) negotiate for private employment with any person who is involved as a party or as lawyer for a party in a matter in which the lawyer is participating personally and substantially, except that a law clerk to a judge, adjudicative officer, or arbitrator may negotiate as MR 1.12(b) allows.
blocks.title: MR 1.11(d) — current government lawyers

items: **Why (d)(2)(i) bars even helping the former client (CB 839):** MR 1.9(a) bars only adversity to a former client, but MR 1.11(d)(2)(i) bars participation altogether, to guard against using government power for the special benefit of the former client.
**Why "revolving door" (CB 841):** many lawyers cycle in and out of government, some more than once.

body: **(a)** Except as stated in (d), a lawyer shall not represent anyone in connection with a matter in which the lawyer participated personally and substantially as a judge or other adjudicative officer, a law clerk to one, or an arbitrator, mediator, or other third-party neutral, unless all parties to the proceeding give informed consent, confirmed in writing.

**(b)** A judge, adjudicative officer, arbitrator, mediator, or other neutral shall not negotiate for employment with any party or lawyer for a party in a matter in which the lawyer is participating personally and substantially. A **law clerk** may, but only after notifying the judge or other adjudicative officer.

**(c)** If a lawyer is disqualified by (a), the firm may proceed only if (all required): (1) the disqualified lawyer is timely screened and apportioned no part of the fee; and (2) written notice is promptly given to the parties and any appropriate tribunal.
**(d)** A partisan arbitrator on a multimember panel may later represent that party.
blocks.title: MR 1.12 — former judges, arbitrators, mediators, other neutrals, and law clerks

blocks.text: Each paragraph of MR 3.8 marks a point in the criminal process where a prosecutor must favor justice over merely winning (CB 843). A prosecutor "may strike hard blows, [but] is not at liberty to strike foul ones" (Berger v. United States).

body: (a) refrain from prosecuting a charge that the prosecutor knows is not supported by probable cause;
(b) make reasonable efforts to assure that the accused has been advised of the right to, and the procedure for obtaining, counsel and has been given reasonable opportunity to obtain counsel;
(c) not seek to obtain from an unrepresented accused a waiver of important pretrial rights, such as the right to a preliminary hearing;

(d) make timely disclosure to the defense of all evidence or information known to the prosecutor that tends to negate the guilt of the accused or mitigates the offense, and, in connection with sentencing, disclose to the defense and to the tribunal all unprivileged mitigating information known to the prosecutor, unless relieved by a protective order of the tribunal;

(e) not subpoena a lawyer in a grand jury or other criminal proceeding to present evidence about a past or present client unless the prosecutor reasonably believes (all required): (1) the information sought is not protected from disclosure by any applicable privilege; (2) the evidence sought is essential to the successful completion of an ongoing investigation or prosecution; and (3) there is no other feasible alternative to obtain the information;

(f) except for statements necessary to inform the public of the nature and extent of the prosecutor's action that serve a legitimate law enforcement purpose, refrain from extrajudicial comments that have a substantial likelihood of heightening public condemnation of the accused, and exercise reasonable care to prevent investigators, police, and others assisting the prosecutor from making statements the prosecutor couldn't make under MR 3.6 or this Rule;

(g) when the prosecutor knows of new, credible, and material evidence creating a reasonable likelihood that a convicted defendant did not commit an offense of which the defendant was convicted: (1) promptly disclose it to an appropriate court or authority; and (2) if the conviction was obtained in the prosecutor's jurisdiction, (i) promptly disclose it to the defendant unless a court authorizes delay, and (ii) undertake further investigation, or make reasonable efforts to cause an investigation, to determine whether the defendant was convicted of an offense the defendant did not commit; and

(h) when the prosecutor knows of clear and convincing evidence establishing that a defendant in the prosecutor's jurisdiction was convicted of an offense the defendant did not commit, seek to remedy the conviction.
blocks.title: MR 3.8 — the prosecutor in a criminal case shall:

items: **(a) Probable cause (CB 844):** a floor, not a target; the Rule is violated only when the prosecutor knows probable cause is lacking.

**(b)–(c) Pretrial rights (CB 846):** the prosecutor can't sit idly by if the court fails to advise the accused of the right to counsel. **Class quiz Ch. 25 Q4:** gently remind the judge that the defendant wasn't advised of the right to counsel and that her finances should be assessed for appointed counsel. MR 3.8(c) helps ensure that waivers of rights like a preliminary hearing are knowing and voluntary. It doesn't apply to an accused appearing pro se with the tribunal's approval, or forbid lawful questioning of an uncharged suspect who has knowingly waived counsel and silence (cmt [2]).

**(d) Disclosure (CB 847):** broader than the constitutional rule. Brady v. Maryland and Giglio v. United States require disclosing material exculpatory and impeachment evidence as due process, but the Constitution requires less for impeachment evidence before a plea (United States v. Ruiz) and limits mandated disclosure of impeachment material (Strickler v. Greene). MR 3.8(d) has no materiality limit: everything that tends to negate guilt or mitigate, timely.
**(e) Subpoenas to lawyers (CB 849):** the testimony must be (1) unprivileged, (2) essential, and (3) the only feasible source.
**(f) Publicity (CB 850):** on top of MR 3.6 (Part VIII); no "perp walk" commentary that heightens condemnation.

**(g)–(h) Wrongful convictions (CB 851).** "Credible" means a reasonable factfinder could believe it; "material" means it creates a reasonable likelihood the defendant didn't commit the offense, so it must bear on guilt (impeachment or mitigation evidence is covered by MR 3.8(d) instead, except impeachment so devastating that it meets the standard).

rows: New, credible, material evidence (reasonable likelihood of innocence)
MR 3.8(g)(1)–(2): disclose to an appropriate court or authority; disclose to the defendant (unless a court authorizes delay); investigate or cause an investigation
MR 3.8(g)(1): disclose to an appropriate court or authority
Clear and convincing evidence of innocence
MR 3.8(h): seek to remedy the conviction (and (g) duties)

items: **Class quiz Ch. 25 Q12–Q13:** evidence that is new, credible, and material but not clear and convincing, in his own jurisdiction, triggers MR 3.8(g)(2): disclose to Norman and investigate (and (g)(1) disclosure to a court or authority too). The duty to seek to remedy the conviction requires clear and convincing evidence of wrongful conviction in the prosecutor's jurisdiction (MR 3.8(h)).
**Truthfulness binds prosecutors too:** police may use some deception in interrogation (Frazier v. Cupp), but prosecutors may not lie to a suspect about the evidence (MR 4.1(a), 8.4(c); Part VIII).

blocks.name: Brady v. Maryland, 373 U.S. 83
blocks.facts: The prosecution withheld a co-defendant's statement admitting that he, not Brady, did the actual killing.
blocks.held: Suppressing evidence favorable to an accused that is material to guilt or punishment violates due process, whatever the prosecutor's good or bad faith.
blocks.why: The constitutional floor that MR 3.8(d) builds on. Giglio v. United States (1972) extends it to impeachment evidence (a promise of leniency to a key witness), and United States v. Bagley (1985) defines materiality as a reasonable probability of a different result. MR 3.8(d) has no materiality limit.

blocks.name: Berger v. United States, 295 U.S. 78
blocks.facts: A federal prosecutor misstated facts, put words in witnesses' mouths, and made improper insinuations in a counterfeiting trial.
blocks.held: The misconduct required a new trial. The prosecutor represents a sovereign "whose interest... in a criminal prosecution is not that it shall win a case, but that justice shall be done"; he "may strike hard blows, [but] is not at liberty to strike foul ones."
blocks.why: The source of the "higher standard" courts expect of government lawyers (CB 829) and the theme of MR 3.8.

blocks.title: The Lawyer as Counselor and Neutral (MR 2.1, 2.3, 2.4, 3.9)

body: In representing a client, a lawyer shall exercise independent professional judgment and render candid advice. In rendering advice, a lawyer may refer not only to law but to other considerations such as moral, economic, social, and political factors that may be relevant to the client's situation.
blocks.title: MR 2.1 — advisor

items: Don't soften advice because the client won't like it (cmt [1]); purely technical legal advice can be inadequate (cmt [2]). When a client proposes something unlawful, MR 2.1 is the license for extra-legal advice about whether it's wise (Part XI). The client still decides objectives (MR 1.2(a)).

body: **(a)** A lawyer may evaluate a matter affecting a client for someone other than the client if the lawyer reasonably believes the evaluation is compatible with other aspects of the relationship. **(b)** When the lawyer knows or reasonably should know the evaluation is likely to affect the client's interests materially and adversely, the lawyer shall not provide it unless the client gives informed consent. **(c)** Except as disclosure is authorized in connection with the report, information relating to the evaluation is otherwise protected by MR 1.6.
blocks.title: MR 2.3 — evaluation for use by third persons

items: Examples: a title opinion for a purchaser, an opinion letter for a lender, an audit-response letter (cmts [1], [6]). Whether the lawyer owes the third person a legal duty is a question of other law (cmt [3]); the casebook treats such reliance as one way to assume a duty of care to a non-client (Part II). Distinguish an evaluation from investigating a non-client, e.g., the vendor's title for the purchaser (cmt [2]).

body: **(a)** A lawyer is a third-party neutral when helping two or more non-clients resolve a dispute or other matter (arbitrator, mediator, or similar). **(b)** The neutral shall inform unrepresented parties that the lawyer is not representing them, and when the lawyer knows or reasonably should know a party doesn't understand the role, shall explain the difference between a neutral and a lawyer who represents a client.
blocks.title: MR 2.4 — lawyer serving as third-party neutral

items: Later representing a party in the same matter is governed by MR 1.12 (Part VII). Lawyers representing clients in ADR follow the Rules: candor under MR 3.3 in binding arbitration (a "tribunal," MR 1.0(m)); otherwise MR 4.1 (cmt [5]).

body: A lawyer representing a client before a legislative body or administrative agency in a nonadjudicative proceeding (lobbying, rulemaking, hearings) shall (all required): (1) disclose that the appearance is in a representative capacity; and (2) conform to MR 3.3(a)–(c), 3.4(a)–(c), and 3.5.
blocks.title: MR 3.9 — advocate in nonadjudicative proceedings

items: It applies to official hearings or meetings where the lawyer presents evidence or argument, not to bilateral negotiations with the government (cmt [3]).

blocks.title: The officer of the court (Ch. 24.A; CB 744)

blocks.text: Being "an officer of the court" brings three ideas into play (all three): (1) advocacy may draw extra scrutiny beyond other lawyer conduct; (2) courts expect behavior beyond the minimum demands of the Rules and procedure; and (3) the advocate's loyalty to the client is constrained by enforceable duties owed to the court and the legal system.

items: **MR 4.4(a):** in representing a client, a lawyer shall not use methods of obtaining evidence that violate the legal rights of a third person (trespass, wiretapping, intrusion into seclusion).

**Class quiz Ch. 24 A–B Q1:** an investigator videotaping the "housebound" plaintiff from a public street probably doesn't violate MR 4.4(a), unless local law forbids that surveillance. The lawyer answers for an investigator's unlawful methods (MR 5.3, 8.4(a)).

**Q2:** prosecutors may not lie to a suspect about the evidence ("the video shows you in the bank" when it's impossible to tell). Police may use some deception in interrogation (Frazier v. Cupp), but lawyers, including prosecutors, are bound by MR 4.1(a) and 8.4(c) (CB 746 n.4).
**Q4:** a prosecutor threatening to circulate humiliating photographs of a minor to coerce cooperation uses means with no substantial purpose other than to embarrass (MR 4.4(a)).

body: A lawyer shall not (c) knowingly disobey an obligation under the rules of a tribunal, except for an **open refusal** based on an assertion that no valid obligation exists; or (d) in pretrial procedure, make a frivolous discovery request or fail to make reasonably diligent effort to comply with a legally proper discovery request by an opposing party.
blocks.title: MR 3.4(c)–(d)

items: Discovery misconduct is a disciplinary violation as well as sanctionable (FRCP 26(g), 37; Part I). **Q5:** openly refusing to produce the secret soda formula on the ground that no valid obligation exists isn't a MR 3.4(c) violation (though contempt or sanctions may follow so the issue can be reviewed). **Ch. 24.C Q6:** citing an unpublished opinion in violation of the court's rule violates MR 3.4(c), even though the brief candidly called it unpublished.

body: A lawyer shall not (a) **unlawfully** obstruct another party's access to evidence, or **unlawfully** alter, destroy, or conceal a document or other material having **potential** evidentiary value, or counsel or assist another to do so; (b) falsify evidence, counsel or assist a witness to testify falsely, or offer an inducement to a witness prohibited by law; or (f) request a person other than a client to refrain from voluntarily giving relevant information to another party, unless (both required) (1) the person is a relative, employee, or other agent of the client, and (2) the lawyer reasonably believes the person's interests won't be adversely affected.
blocks.title: MR 3.4(a)–(b), (f)

items: **"Unlawfully" matters (CB 748):** lawyers lawfully withhold all the time: proper discovery objections, instructions not to answer privileged questions, advising a client not to talk to police.

**"Potential" matters (CB 749):** the material needn't be admissible or requested; it need only be relevant to or potentially useful in a pending or reasonably foreseeable proceeding. Most jurisdictions forbid **spoliation**, and electronically stored information has intensified the focus.

**Consequences for the client (CB 750):** monetary sanctions, then evidentiary or terminating sanctions after an order compelling discovery; for lost material that should have been preserved, remedial measures even without bad faith (e.g., failing to halt automatic deletion).

**Counsel's own duty (CB 750):** many courts impose personal obligations on lawyers for their clients' preservation and production. Become actively involved immediately on retention, and circulate a **litigation hold** (document preservation memo) to everyone who may have relevant material (Zubulake).

**Evidence handed to you (CB 752):** your possession can put you in a legal and ethical bind. You may not conceal, destroy, or alter it, or counsel anyone else to (MR 3.4(a)). **Class quiz Q7:** driving the client's bloody knife to another town and throwing it in a dumpster is unlawful concealment and destruction, a clear MR 3.4(a) violation and likely obstruction; no proceeding need be pending. [[Many courts hold that a lawyer who takes possession of physical evidence of a crime may keep it a reasonable time for examination but must then turn it over to the authorities.]]

**MR 3.4(f) (CB 364):** you may ask your own client, or the client's relatives, employees, or agents, not to talk voluntarily to the other side, but only if you reasonably believe they won't be hurt by it (Part XI).

blocks.name: Zubulake v. UBS Warburg LLC, 229 F.R.D. 422
blocks.topic: litigation holds and counsel's duty to preserve
blocks.facts: In an employment discrimination suit, UBS employees deleted relevant emails and failed to produce others despite counsel's instructions to preserve them.
blocks.held: Counsel must issue a litigation hold, communicate with key players, and monitor compliance, and the court gave an adverse-inference instruction for the lost emails (Scheindlin, J.).
blocks.why: Preservation is not the client's job alone. The source of the duty to send and police a litigation hold (CB 750).

body: A lawyer who receives a document or electronically stored information relating to the representation of the lawyer's client and knows or reasonably should know that it was inadvertently sent shall promptly notify the sender.
blocks.title: MR 4.4(b)

items: **That's the whole Model Rule duty.** Whether to return it, stop reading, or delete it is left to other law and professional judgment (cmts [2]–[3]). Metadata is covered (cmt [2]; class quiz Q3: track-changes comments in produced files trigger only the duty to notify).

**FRCP 26(b)(5)(B)** adds duties in federal civil cases: once notified of a privilege claim, the receiving party must promptly return, sequester, or destroy the material, not use or disclose it until the claim is resolved, and may present it to the court under seal (class quiz Q8: both may apply).

**The ABA's views have evolved** (from "return it unread" to "just notify"), and states vary widely; some stricter states disqualify counsel who exploit privileged material, and evidentiary sanctions may also be available (CB 755–757).
**Q6:** opposing counsel's email to his client, sent to you by mistake ("Dear Cynthia"): promptly notify the sender, and don't contact his represented client (MR 4.2).
**Protect your own documents:** know what metadata your software embeds, and scrub documents before they leave the firm unless there's a good reason not to (CB 754 n.9; MR 1.1, 1.6(c)).

body: A lawyer shall not (any one is a violation): (a) seek to influence a judge, juror, prospective juror, or other official by means prohibited by law; (b) communicate ex parte with such a person during the proceeding unless authorized by law or court order; (c) communicate with a juror or prospective juror after discharge of the jury if (any one bars it) (1) the communication is prohibited by law or court order, (2) the juror has made known a desire not to communicate, or (3) the communication involves misrepresentation, coercion, duress, or harassment; or (d) engage in conduct intended to disrupt a tribunal.
blocks.title: MR 3.5

items: **Officials include court reporters:** offering a reporter $1,000 to "fix" the deposition transcript violates MR 3.5(a) even though she refused (class quiz Ch. 24.C Q1).
**Post-trial juror contact:** a juror who said on the record she didn't want to talk can't be asked for feedback, even in a chance coffee-shop meeting (MR 3.5(c)(2); Q2).
**Disruption includes depositions** (cmt [5]): baseless objections to every question and improper instructions not to answer violate MR 3.5(d), and MR 3.1 and 3.4(c)–(d) too (Q3).
**Abusive judges:** "A lawyer may stand firm against abuse by a judge but should avoid reciprocation" (cmt [4]). Finish professionally, then report the judge (MR 8.3(b); Q4).

A lawyer shall not make a statement the lawyer **knows to be false or makes with reckless disregard** as to its truth or falsity concerning the qualifications or integrity of a judge, adjudicatory officer, public legal officer, or candidate for judicial or legal office. **MR 8.2(b):** a lawyer running for judicial office must follow the Code of Judicial Conduct.

The standard borrows from New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, and opinions based on disclosed facts are generally protected (Standing Committee v. Yagman, 9th Cir. 1995); courts tend to read the protection narrowly (CB 766–767; Ch. 14.C).

blocks.title: Meritorious claims and expediting litigation: MR 3.1, 3.2 (CB 767)

body: A lawyer shall not bring or defend a proceeding, or assert or controvert an issue in it, unless there is a basis in law and fact for doing so that is not frivolous, which includes a good-faith argument for an extension, modification, or reversal of existing law. A lawyer for a criminal defendant, or a respondent in a proceeding that could result in incarceration, may nevertheless defend so as to require that every element of the case be established.
blocks.title: MR 3.1

items: **Say so** when you argue for a change in the law. **Class quiz Q5:** with no binding authority on point (only district court and out-of-circuit decisions), Kalina is arguing an open question, not seeking a reversal, and need not disclose the non-controlling cases. **Q9:** the one defense always allowed: a criminal defendant may put the state to its proof on every element, however overwhelming the evidence.

**MR 3.2:** make reasonable efforts to expedite litigation consistent with the client's interests. Delay for its own sake, for financial gain, or to frustrate an opponent isn't a legitimate interest (cmt [1]). Compare FRCP 11, § 1927, and MR 4.4(a).

**MR 3.3(a)(1):** don't knowingly make a false statement of law to a tribunal. Discipline requires actual knowledge, not carelessness, but sloppy or misleading argument costs credibility long after the case.

**MR 3.3(a)(2):** disclose legal authority in the **controlling jurisdiction** known to be **directly adverse** to the client's position and not disclosed by opposing counsel. A factually identical case from another jurisdiction need not be disclosed (Q8); controlling adverse authority must be, even if a partner reviewed the brief (Q25: Renaldo can't bury United States v. Smith without a parenthetical, and MR 5.2(b) doesn't help on a clear duty).

body: **(a)** A lawyer who is participating or has participated in the investigation or litigation of a matter shall not make an **extrajudicial** statement that the lawyer knows or reasonably should know will be publicly disseminated and will have a **substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing** an adjudicative proceeding in the matter.

**(b) Safe harbors (any one suffices):** a lawyer may state (1) the claim, offense, or defense involved and, except when prohibited by law, the identity of the persons involved; (2) information in a public record; (3) that an investigation is in progress; (4) the scheduling or result of any step in litigation; (5) a request for assistance in obtaining evidence; (6) a warning of danger concerning a person's behavior when there's reason to believe there is a likelihood of substantial harm; and (7) in a criminal case, also (i) the accused's identity, residence, occupation, and family status; (ii) information necessary to aid in apprehending an accused at large; (iii) the fact, time, and place of arrest; and (iv) the identity of the investigating and arresting officers or agencies and the length of the investigation.

**(c) Right of reply:** a statement a reasonable lawyer would believe is required to protect a client from the substantial undue prejudicial effect of recent publicity not initiated by the lawyer or client, limited to what's necessary to mitigate it.
**(d)** No lawyer in the same firm or government agency may make a statement prohibited by (a).
blocks.title: MR 3.6

items: **Presumptively prejudicial subjects (cmt [5]; any one raises the risk):** (1) the character, credibility, reputation, or criminal record of a party, suspect, or witness, or the expected testimony of a party or witness; (2) in a criminal case, the possibility of a guilty plea, or the existence or contents of a confession, admission, or statement, or a refusal to make one; (3) the performance or results of any examination or test, or a refusal to submit to one; (4) any opinion as to the guilt or innocence of a defendant or suspect; (5) information the lawyer knows or reasonably should know is likely to be inadmissible and would create a substantial risk of prejudicing an impartial trial; and (6) the fact that a defendant has been charged with a crime, unless accompanied by a statement that the charge is merely an accusation.
**Who's covered:** only lawyers participating (or who participated) in the matter and their firm or agency colleagues. A blogging lawyer who isn't involved isn't covered (Q12).

**Only extrajudicial statements:** a closing argument in a packed courtroom isn't one (Q13). Telling a reporter when you'll finish calling witnesses is a safe harbor (MR 3.6(b)(4); Q14). An opinion on guilt is not a safe harbor (cmt [5](4); Q15). A sealed indictment isn't a public record (Q16). Revealing breathalyzer results on the eve of trial is presumptively prejudicial (cmt [5](3); Q17). Prosecutors have the extra limits of MR 3.8(f) (Part VII).
**Overcorrecting destroys the right of reply:** go only as far as reasonably necessary to mitigate (CB 772).

blocks.name: Gentile v. State Bar of Nevada, 501 U.S. 1030
blocks.topic: trial publicity and the First Amendment
blocks.facts: Hours after his client's indictment, a defense lawyer held a press conference saying the client was a scapegoat and that a police officer was the likely thief. The client was acquitted months later, and the bar disciplined the lawyer.
blocks.held: The "substantial likelihood of material prejudice" standard is constitutional for lawyers in pending cases, but Nevada's safe-harbor provision (allowing a lawyer to state "the general nature of the defense") was void for vagueness as applied, so the discipline was reversed.
blocks.why: The constitutional backdrop for MR 3.6. It explains the Rule's structure: a prejudice standard, specific safe harbors, and the right of reply in MR 3.6(c).

body: **(a)** A lawyer shall not act as advocate at a trial in which the lawyer is likely to be a **necessary witness** unless (any one suffices): (1) the testimony relates to an uncontested issue; (2) the testimony relates to the nature and value of legal services rendered in the case; or (3) disqualification would work substantial hardship on the client. **(b)** A lawyer may act as advocate at a trial in which another lawyer in the firm is likely to be called as a witness, unless MR 1.7 or 1.9 precludes it.
blocks.title: MR 3.7

items: **Not imputed** (CB 774): a colleague may try the case while you testify. Client consent, admissibility, or being called by the other side are not exceptions (Q18).

**(a)(2) means your own fees in this case:** testifying as a damages expert on what the plaintiff-lawyer would have earned isn't covered (Q19); testifying in your own pro se fee suit is (Q22). MR 3.7 applies to bench trials too, though the confusion risk is lower.

body: In trial, a lawyer shall not (any one is a violation): (1) allude to any matter the lawyer doesn't reasonably believe is relevant or that won't be supported by admissible evidence; (2) assert personal knowledge of facts in issue except when testifying as a witness; or (3) state a personal opinion as to the justness of a cause, the credibility of a witness, the culpability of a civil litigant, or the guilt or innocence of an accused.
blocks.title: MR 3.4(e)

items: **Class quiz:** referring in closing to a conviction the judge excluded violates (1), even with a certified copy in hand (Q10). Asking "Aren't you a wife-beating, pill-popping alcoholic?" with no factual basis violates (1); "Withdrawn," a curative instruction, or acquittal doesn't cure it (Q11). Reciting an unadmitted hearsay statement in closing violates (1), though it supplied a good-faith basis to ask on cross (Q23). "Thank you for your honest testimony" in front of the jury vouches for credibility, violating (3) (Q24).

**Trickery:** secretly seating a look-alike at counsel table to bait a misidentification misleads the tribunal (MR 3.3, 3.4, 3.5(d), 8.4(c)–(d); United States v. Thoreen; Q20). Ordinary cross and argument about weak identification are fine.

body: **(a)** A lawyer shall not knowingly: (1) make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal, or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the tribunal by the lawyer; (2) fail to disclose legal authority in the controlling jurisdiction known to be directly adverse to the client's position and not disclosed by opposing counsel; or (3) offer evidence that the lawyer knows to be false. If a lawyer, the lawyer's client, or a witness called by the lawyer has offered material evidence and the lawyer comes to know of its falsity, the lawyer shall take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the tribunal. A lawyer may refuse to offer evidence, **other than the testimony of a defendant in a criminal matter**, that the lawyer reasonably believes is false.

**(b)** A lawyer representing a client in an adjudicative proceeding who knows that **a person** intends to engage, is engaging, or has engaged in criminal or fraudulent conduct related to the proceeding shall take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the tribunal.
**(c)** The duties in (a) and (b) continue to the **conclusion of the proceeding**, and apply even if compliance requires disclosure of information otherwise protected by MR 1.6.

**(d)** In an **ex parte** proceeding, a lawyer shall inform the tribunal of all material facts known to the lawyer that will enable the tribunal to make an informed decision, whether or not the facts are adverse.
blocks.title: MR 3.3 — candor toward the tribunal
Don't lie, and don't present false evidence (CB 778–785)

items: Lying to a tribunal or presenting false evidence is a disciplinary violation and, when knowing, a crime (perjury, subornation, obstruction) and sanctionable. MR 3.3 covers ancillary proceedings like depositions and sworn interrogatory answers (cmt [1]): Dean can't serve interrogatory answers he knows are false, and the client's verification doesn't absolve him (Q21).

**"False" evidence** includes any falsity that frustrates truth-finding: false statements, or inauthentic exhibits. A photoshopped photo is false evidence even if an unsuspecting witness authenticates it (MR 3.3(a)(3), 3.4(b); Q30). You may offer false evidence **to prove its falsity**, e.g., a forged agreement offered to prove the forgery (cmt [5]; Q29).
**MR 3.4(b) vs. MR 3.3(a)(3):** 3.4(b) bars falsifying evidence or counseling false testimony; 3.3(a)(3) bars offering evidence you know is false, whoever falsified it.

Nothing forbids properly preparing a witness, client or not, but communications with a non-client witness aren't privileged. Explaining procedure, demeanor ("speak up, make eye contact"), and privilege is fine; refreshing recollection with a document is fine if the memory is genuinely refreshed (Q26). Telling the client that truthful testimony would hurt and advising her not to testify isn't counseling perjury (Q27). Telling her to say she wore snow boots when she wore stilettos is (Problem 24C-8(g)).

**Fact witnesses** must not be paid to testify, but you may pay their expenses (travel, lodging, meals) and reasonable compensation for time lost from work testifying or preparing, or reviewing records germane to the testimony, if (all required): (1) the amount is reasonable; (2) it is clearly not for the substance or fact of the testimony and is not conditioned on it; and (3) the governing jurisdiction permits it (ABA opinion; Q28: a train ticket and hotel for the busy architect are fine).
**Experts** may be paid for their time and testimony, but almost everywhere not a contingent fee, which no witness may receive.
A MR 3.4(b) violation means some other law was broken, e.g., the federal anti-gratuity statute (18 U.S.C. § 201); the testimony may be excluded, fees awarded, or a mistrial declared.

blocks.title: Evidence you only suspect is false (CB 785–786)

header: What you may or must do
rows: You reasonably believe it's false (but don't know)
**May** refuse to offer it, even over the client's objection, or may offer it.
You reasonably believe a **criminal defendant's** own testimony is false (but don't know)

**Must** let the defendant testify: the decision is the defendant's (MR 1.2(a); Q31). Consult, advise of the risks (inconsistency, disbelief, damage to the rest of the defense), and try to persuade, but if the client insists, it's the client's call.

blocks.title: The criminal defendant who will lie (CB 786)

items: If you **know** your criminal client will testify falsely, MR 3.3(a)(3) and 1.2(d) say you must not offer it, but the defendant has a constitutional right to testify. No single solution exists; know your jurisdiction's method. The most common in the U.S. is the **"narrative" approach**: the defendant testifies in narrative form without counsel's questioning, and counsel doesn't argue the false testimony. The Model Rules note that "some jurisdictions" use it without endorsing it (MR 3.3 cmt [7]).
[[In Nix v. Whiteside (1986), the Supreme Court held that a lawyer who threatened to disclose and withdraw if the client testified falsely did not violate the Sixth Amendment.]]

**What triggers it (any one suffices):** (1) you made a false statement of material fact or law to the tribunal, knowing or not at the time (MR 3.3(a)(1)); (2) you, your client, or your witness offered material evidence you later learn is false (MR 3.3(a)(3); only "material" evidence: Q32); or (3) you know any person intends, is engaging, or has engaged in criminal or fraudulent conduct related to the proceeding, such as bribing a juror (MR 3.3(b)).
**Reasonable remedial measures, in order (cmt [10]):**
**Remonstrate.** Privately urge the person who supplied the falsehood to correct it, with your help, noting that you must report it if she won't (Q33).
**Withdraw** if the client refuses and withdrawal will cure it (MR 1.16(a)(1)); sometimes you must.

**Disclose to the tribunal** what is reasonably necessary to remedy the situation, even if it reveals MR 1.6 information (MR 3.3(c)). Your own misstatement is usually corrected by a filing, served on opposing counsel (MR 3.5(b)).
**Minimum disclosure:** only what's needed to correct the wrong.

**Duration:** until the conclusion of the proceeding, meaning when a final judgment has been affirmed on appeal or the time for review has passed (cmt [13]). Other consequences (perjury prosecutions, relief from judgment under FRCP 60(b)) have their own time limits.

With no adversary to correct the record, disclose all material facts, adverse or not (Q7). A sealed qui tam conference on extending the seal is ex parte, so the AUSA must disclose the evidence suggesting an innocent error too (Q34). The duty applies whenever opposing counsel is simply absent: telling the judge a motion is "unopposed" without mentioning your agreement giving the other side 30 days to amend violates MR 3.3 (Malmin v. Oths; Q35). Half-truths can equal misrepresentations (cmt [3]).

blocks.title: Law Firms, Supervision, and Organizational Clients

items: **Any organization offering legal services is a "law firm"** (MR 1.0(c); CB 478): partnerships, PCs, solos, legal services organizations, and corporate or government legal departments. The casebook calls them "practice organizations."

**The organization never shields you (CB 479).** Each lawyer has a nondelegable, personal duty to comply with the Rules and other law. Agents are personally liable for their own torts within the scope of the agency, and no one goes to prison for you.

body: **(a)** A lawyer is bound by the Rules notwithstanding that the lawyer acted at the direction of another person. **(b)** A subordinate lawyer does not violate the Rules by acting in accordance with a supervisory lawyer's **reasonable resolution of an arguable question of professional duty**.
blocks.title: MR 5.2 — the subordinate lawyer

items: **The exception is extremely narrow (CB 480):** it applies only when it was genuinely unclear how to comply and the supervisor's instruction was a reasonable way to comply. It excuses discipline, not necessarily tort liability. It never covers clear violations (Kodak-Berkey, Part I; Renaldo's buried adverse authority, Part VIII).

**Two kinds of oversight:** (1) **managerial** authority is indirect, general authority over the firm's professional work, or a part of it (a practice-group leader; an office's managing partner), covering both lawyers and staff; and (2) **supervisory** authority is day-to-day responsibility for specific people's work. A lawyer may have either, both, or neither.

rows: **(a)** Partners and lawyers with comparable managerial authority shall make reasonable efforts to ensure the firm has measures giving reasonable assurance that all lawyers conform to the Rules (e.g., a conflicts-check system, calendaring, trust-account controls). No harm is needed for a violation.
**(a)** The same for measures giving reasonable assurance that nonlawyers' conduct is compatible with the lawyers' professional obligations: policies so staff don't do what lawyers can't.
**(b)** A lawyer with direct supervisory authority over another lawyer shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that lawyer conforms to the Rules.

**(b)** A lawyer with direct supervisory authority over a nonlawyer shall make reasonable efforts to ensure the person's conduct is compatible with the lawyer's obligations. Includes outside vendors, investigators, outsourcing, cloud services, and AI tools: select, instruct, and oversee.

**(c)** Responsible for another lawyer's violation if (any one suffices): (1) the lawyer orders it or, with knowledge of the specific conduct, ratifies it; or (2) the lawyer is a partner, manager, or direct supervisor who knows of the conduct when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated and fails to take reasonable remedial action.
**(c)** The same, for a nonlawyer's conduct that would violate the Rules if a lawyer did it.

items: **Not respondeat superior.** Discipline requires your own failure: inadequate measures, inadequate supervision, ordering or ratifying, or failing to mitigate what you know. If reasonable measures existed and you neither ordered, ratified, nor could mitigate, you're not responsible (CB 486).

**Other consequences of failing to manage or supervise (CB 482):** civil liability (supervisors for torts they directed or reasonably could have prevented; the firm vicariously), court sanctions (FRCP 11(c)(1) holds the firm jointly responsible), and fee consequences.
**Causing a subordinate to violate a Rule** is the supervisor's own violation too (MR 8.4(a): violating the Rules through the acts of another).

Not a separate duty but a feature of competence and care: a subordinate must get the support needed to do the job competently. Ask, insist, and if necessary go elsewhere for help. "I asked and asked" is no defense; a looming deadline requires protective action (Part II).

blocks.title: Duties to the Firm, Changing Jobs, and Selling a Practice (MR 1.17, 5.7)
Loyalty to the practice organization (Ch. 19.E; CB 492)

items: Lawyers owe their firms a duty of loyalty much like the fiduciary duty owed to clients, and owe each other a duty to be forthright and honest. No exploiting your firm position for personal benefit beyond the firm's regular rewards, interfering with the firm's business, or appropriating practice opportunities that belong to the firm (Meinhard v. Salmon, Part IV).
Violations can bring discipline, civil liability, and, very likely, employment consequences.

**You keep your duties to every client you served.** If you leave current clients behind, you have all the duties of a withdrawing lawyer: notice, a smooth transition, and tribunal permission where required (MR 1.16(c)–(d)). Once you leave, every client you served there is your former client for the rest of your career (MR 1.9), however many colleagues also worked for it.

**Taking clients with you:** both the departing lawyer and the firm must tell clients of material changes, including the departure of a lawyer with substantial responsibility for their matter (MR 1.4), and clients decide who will represent them. Despite the duty of loyalty to the firm, the departing lawyer may generally tell clients of the impending departure and their right to choose counsel. Timing and content vary by jurisdiction and are complex.

**Conflicts follow the mobile lawyer** only as far as actual knowledge goes (MR 1.9(b)), and screens may protect the new firm (MR 1.10(a)(2); Part VI). MR 1.6(b)(7) permits limited disclosures to detect conflicts.
**Noncompetes** are barred by MR 5.6(a), except retirement benefits (Part XI).

body: A lawyer or firm may sell or buy a law practice, or an area of practice, including good will, if (all required): (a) the seller ceases to engage in the private practice of law, or in the area of practice sold, in the geographic area or the jurisdiction (a state chooses which) where the practice was conducted; (b) the entire practice, or the entire area of practice, is sold to one or more lawyers or firms; (c) the seller gives each client written notice of (1) the proposed sale, (2) the client's right to retain other counsel or take possession of the file, and (3) the fact that consent to the transfer of the file will be presumed if the client does not act or object within 90 days of receiving notice (a client who can't be given notice may be transferred only by court order, with in camera disclosure limited to what's necessary); and (d) the fees charged clients are not increased by reason of the sale.
blocks.title: MR 1.17 — sale of a law practice

items: **Why "entire":** so less lucrative clients aren't left stranded while the profitable matters are sold (cmt [6]). Good-faith offering of the whole practice satisfies it even if some clients choose other counsel (cmt [2]).

**Ceasing practice** doesn't bar taking a government, legal services, or in-house job (cmt [3]). The purchaser must honor existing fee and scope arrangements (cmt [10]); client autonomy, including the right to discharge, survives the sale (cmt [9]).

**Payments:** the purchase price of a deceased, disabled, or disappeared lawyer's practice may be paid to the estate (MR 5.4(a)(2)), and paying for a practice is an exception to the ban on paying for referrals (MR 7.2(b)(3)). Restrictions in a practice-sale agreement don't violate MR 5.6 (cmt [3] to MR 5.6).

body: **(a)** A lawyer is subject to the Rules when providing law-related services (any one suffices): (1) by the lawyer in circumstances not distinct from the lawyer's legal services to clients; or (2) by an entity the lawyer controls, alone or with others, if the lawyer fails to take reasonable measures to assure that a person obtaining the services knows they are not legal services and that the protections of the client-lawyer relationship do not exist. **(b)** "Law-related services" are services that might reasonably be performed in conjunction with, and in substance are related to, legal services, and that are not prohibited as UPL when provided by a nonlawyer.
blocks.title: MR 5.7 — law-related services

items: Examples: title insurance, financial planning, accounting, lobbying, tax preparation, real estate consulting. The burden is on the lawyer to show reasonable measures were taken, and sophisticated users may need less explanation (cmts [6]–[7]). Referring a client to the lawyer's own law-related business is a MR 1.8(a) transaction (cmt [5]).

blocks.text: Ch. 23. Ron Rainmaker's longtime client Ted Tech, a serial entrepreneur, illustrates how easily the lines blur between a founder and the companies he forms.

body: **(a)** A lawyer employed or retained by an organization represents the organization acting through its duly authorized constituents. **(f)** In dealing with directors, officers, employees, members, shareholders, or other constituents, a lawyer shall explain the identity of the client when the lawyer knows or reasonably should know that the organization's interests are adverse to those of the constituents. **(g)** A lawyer representing an organization may also represent any of its constituents, subject to MR 1.7. If the organization's consent is required, it must be given by an appropriate official other than the individual to be represented, or by the shareholders.
blocks.title: MR 1.13(a), (f), (g)
Knowing who the client is (Ch. 23.A; CB 706–711)

items: **Duties run exclusively to the organization**, not to any constituent (CB 706).

**Confidentiality and privilege belong to the organization** (CB 708). Communications with constituents acting for it are confidential and can be privileged, but the organization alone holds and controls the privilege. You may disclose its information to a constituent (or anyone) only as the organization, through an authorized constituent, permits (MR 1.13 cmt [2]).

**Dual representation is allowed (MR 1.13(g); CB 709)**, if you address any conflicts it creates, concurrent or successive. The organization's consent must come from an official other than the constituent being represented, or from the shareholders, so it is independent and informed (CB 711).

**Organizational formation (CB 711):** be clear, in your own mind and with everyone involved, about who your clients are and who they aren't. Founders often assume the lawyer represents them all (Problem 9A-2, Part II).

blocks.name: Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U.S. 383
blocks.topic: the corporate privilege and the "Upjohn warning"
blocks.facts: Upjohn's general counsel investigated possibly illegal payments to foreign officials by sending questionnaires to managers and interviewing employees. The IRS summoned the questionnaires and interview notes.
blocks.held: The attorney-client privilege covered communications from employees at all levels, made at the direction of superiors so counsel could advise the corporation, about matters within their duties; the Court rejected the narrow "control group" test. The notes were also protected work product.
blocks.why: The privilege belongs to the corporation, not the employee, so counsel who interviews employees must warn them that counsel represents only the company and that the company may waive the privilege and share what they say. That warning bears the case's name.

items: **MR 4.3 applies to unrepresented constituents (all required):** (1) don't state or imply that you're disinterested; (2) correct any misunderstanding of your role that you know or reasonably should know of; and (3) when their interests conflict or may conflict with the organization's, give no legal advice except to get a lawyer.
**MR 1.13(f) adds a duty to speak up** whenever you know or reasonably should know the organization's interests are adverse to the constituent's, even if the constituent shows no confusion (CB 718).

**Three typical divergences (CB 719; any one triggers concern):** the constituent (1) is harming the company for personal benefit (embezzlement, theft); (2) is causing the company to violate the law (dangerous products, environmental harm, regulatory violations, fraud, antitrust); or (3) has personal difficulties (depression, addiction, illness) that interfere with the job.

**What the warning says (CB 720):** tailored to the circumstances, but always that you represent the company only, not the constituent, plus the implications of that role that may cut against the constituent: the conversation may be privileged, but the privilege is the company's, which may waive it and share what the constituent says, including with the government.

**When (CB 721):** at the start of any conversation where you expect the constituent may be engaged in conduct contrary to the organization's interests, because you then already reasonably should know of the adversity. If a surprise comes up mid-conversation, stop and clarify your role at that moment.
**Form:** no formal requirements, so an oral warning is allowed, but in an investigation give it in writing and let the constituent review it and ask questions first.

**Consequences of a late or missing warning (CB 721):** discipline (MR 1.13(f), 4.3); an implied duty of confidentiality to the constituent that conflicts with your duties to tell the company, forcing withdrawal or disqualification (potentially of the whole in-house department); damages if you disclose; exclusion of improperly obtained information in later litigation; and undoing decisions the constituent made on your forbidden advice.

**First ask whether you have a conflict.** If you represent only the organization, competing instructions from warring factions don't create one: you have a single client. If you also represent a warring constituent (in anything), or have personal ties strong enough to create a significant risk of material limitation, you do.

Be transparent with every faction that has a colorable claim to direct the company, limit yourself to issues proper for the organization's lawyer (not business advisor or faction counsel), and keep asking whether the organization would be no worse off if you withdrew.

body: If a lawyer for an organization **knows** that an officer, employee, or other associated person is engaged in action, intends to act, or refuses to act in a matter related to the representation that is (1) a violation of a legal obligation to the organization, or a violation of law that reasonably might be imputed to it, and (2) likely to result in substantial injury to the organization, then the lawyer shall proceed as is reasonably necessary in the organization's best interest. Unless the lawyer reasonably believes it isn't necessary, the lawyer shall refer the matter to higher authority, including, if warranted, the highest authority that can act for the organization under applicable law.
blocks.title: MR 1.13(b) — reporting up

items: **Level by level (CB 726):** report to the constituent's boss, then the next level, up to the board if warranted. A rogue officer's demand for silence doesn't control.
**Failing to report up** is disciplinable and, if it harms the organization, actionable as malpractice or breach of fiduciary duty, and the damages can be substantial (CB 729).

body: **(c)** Except as provided in (d), if (all required): (1) despite the lawyer's efforts under (b), the highest authority that can act for the organization insists on or fails to address in a timely and appropriate manner an action or refusal to act that is **clearly a violation of law**; and (2) the lawyer reasonably believes the violation is **reasonably certain to result in substantial injury to the organization**, then the lawyer **may** reveal information relating to the representation, whether or not MR 1.6 permits it, but only if and to the extent the lawyer reasonably believes necessary to prevent substantial injury to the organization. **(d)** Paragraph (c) doesn't apply to information relating to the lawyer's representation of the organization (either is excluded) (1) to investigate an alleged violation of law, or (2) to defend the organization or a constituent against a claim arising out of an alleged violation of law. **(e)** A lawyer who reasonably believes she was discharged because of actions under (b) or (c), or who withdraws in circumstances requiring or permitting such action, shall proceed as reasonably necessary to assure that the highest authority is informed of the discharge or withdrawal.
blocks.title: MR 1.13(c)–(e) — reporting out

items: **Minimum disclosure (CB 732):** report out as little, to as few, as will address the problem the organization refused to fix. Overreporting destroys the exception and invites discipline and liability.
**Compared with MR 1.6(b)(2)–(3):** MR 1.13(c) doesn't require that the lawyer's services were used, but it protects only against injury to the organization, and only after reporting up all the way.
**In-house counsel** who must withdraw may have to quit (Part II); MR 1.13(e) makes sure the board hears why.

blocks.title: Pro Bono, Appointments, and Public-Service Organizations (MR 6.1–6.5)

blocks.text: Reading: MR 6.1–6.5 with their Comments. The casebook has no chapter on these Rules, so this section follows the Rules and Comments.

body: Every lawyer has a professional responsibility to provide legal services to those unable to pay, and **should aspire** to render at least **50 hours** of pro bono publico service a year. In doing so, the lawyer should: **(a)** provide a **substantial majority** of the 50 hours without fee or expectation of fee to (1) persons of limited means, or (2) charitable, religious, civic, community, governmental, and educational organizations in matters designed primarily to address the needs of persons of limited means; and **(b)** provide any additional services through (1) free or substantially reduced-fee services to individuals, groups, or organizations seeking to secure or protect civil rights, civil liberties, or public rights, or to charitable, religious, civic, community, governmental, and educational organizations in matters furthering their organizational purposes, where standard fees would significantly deplete their resources or be otherwise inappropriate; (2) substantially reduced-fee services to persons of limited means; or (3) activities improving the law, the legal system, or the legal profession. A lawyer should also voluntarily contribute financial support to organizations that provide legal services to persons of limited means.
blocks.title: MR 6.1 — voluntary pro bono publico service

items: **Aspirational, not enforceable:** "should," and the responsibility "is not intended to be enforced through disciplinary process" (cmt [12]). It's an MPRE favorite precisely because it's the one Rule with no discipline behind it.

**Intent matters (cmt [4]):** services count only if rendered without fee or expectation of fee, so an uncollected fee isn't pro bono; but an award of statutory attorney's fees in a case originally accepted pro bono doesn't disqualify it (lawyers who receive such fees are encouraged to contribute a portion to organizations serving persons of limited means).

**Who qualifies (cmt [3]):** persons eligible for Legal Services Corporation programs, and those slightly above the guidelines who still can't afford counsel. **(b)(1) examples (cmt [6]):** First Amendment claims, Title VII claims, environmental protection claims. **(b)(2) (cmt [7]):** judicare programs and court appointments paid well below the lawyer's usual rate. **(b)(3) (cmt [8]):** bar committees, legal services boards, Law Day, CLE teaching, mediation, and arbitration.

**When pro bono isn't feasible** (cmt [9]), a lawyer may discharge the responsibility by financial support; firms should enable and encourage their lawyers' pro bono work (cmt [11]). Government and public-sector lawyers who are barred from outside practice may meet it through (b) activities (cmt [5]).

body: A lawyer shall not seek to avoid appointment by a tribunal to represent a person except for good cause, such as (any one suffices): (a) representing the client is likely to result in violation of the Rules or other law; (b) representing the client is likely to result in an unreasonable financial burden on the lawyer; or (c) the client or the cause is so repugnant to the lawyer as to be likely to impair the client-lawyer relationship or the lawyer's ability to represent the client.
blocks.title: MR 6.2 — accepting appointments

items: **Good cause, not distaste (cmts [1]–[2]):** a lawyer is ordinarily free to decline a client whose character or cause is repugnant, but an appointment is different. Good cause exists if the lawyer couldn't handle the matter competently (MR 1.1), if an improper conflict would result, or if the case would be unjustly burdensome; repugnance must be strong enough to impair the representation.

**Appointed counsel owes everything retained counsel owes (cmt [3]):** loyalty, confidentiality, and the same limits (no assisting violations of the Rules). Appointment itself creates the relationship (Restatement § 14; Part II), and the court controls withdrawal and substitution (MR 1.16(c), cmt [5]).

body: A lawyer may serve as a director, officer, or member of a legal services organization, apart from the lawyer's firm, even though it serves persons with interests adverse to the lawyer's clients. The lawyer shall not knowingly participate in a decision or action of the organization (either is barred): (a) if participating would be incompatible with the lawyer's obligations to a client under MR 1.7; or (b) where the decision or action could have a material adverse effect on the representation of a client of the organization whose interests are adverse to a client of the lawyer.
blocks.title: MR 6.3 — membership in a legal services organization

items: Board service doesn't make the organization's clients the lawyer's clients (cmt [1]), but the lawyer must recuse from decisions that would hurt her own clients or the organization's clients adverse to them.

body: A lawyer may serve as a director, officer, or member of an organization involved in reform of the law or its administration even though the reform may affect a client's interests. When the lawyer knows that a client's interests may be **materially benefitted** by a decision in which the lawyer participates, the lawyer shall disclose that fact, but need not identify the client.
blocks.title: MR 6.4 — law reform activities affecting client interests

items: Lawyers in law reform organizations generally don't represent the organization (cmt [1]); otherwise an antitrust litigator might be disqualified from helping revise the antitrust rules. Compare MR 1.2(b): representing a client isn't an endorsement.

body: **(a)** A lawyer who, under the auspices of a program sponsored by a nonprofit organization or court, provides short-term limited legal services to a client without expectation by either that the lawyer will provide continuing representation in the matter: (1) is subject to MR 1.7 and 1.9(a) only if the lawyer **knows** the representation involves a conflict of interest; and (2) is subject to MR 1.10 only if the lawyer **knows** another lawyer in the lawyer's firm is disqualified by MR 1.7 or 1.9(a) in the matter. **(b)** Except as provided in (a)(2), MR 1.10 is inapplicable to a representation governed by this Rule.
blocks.title: MR 6.5 — nonprofit and court-annexed limited legal services programs

items: **Why relax conflicts (cmts [1], [3]–[4]):** hotlines, advice-only clinics, and court help desks can't run systematic conflict checks, and the limited nature of the service reduces the risk. The other Rules, including MR 1.6 and 1.9(c), still apply.

**Limited scope still needs informed consent** (MR 1.2(c); cmt [2]). If a short-term limited representation wouldn't be reasonable, the lawyer may give advice but must also advise the client of the need for further assistance.
**If the lawyer goes on to represent the client on an ongoing basis,** MR 1.7, 1.9(a), and 1.10 apply in full (cmt [5]).

body: MR 6.1 is the only Rule that is purely aspirational: "should," 50 hours, no discipline. MR 6.2 is mandatory ("shall not seek to avoid") but lists good causes. MR 6.3 and 6.4 permit board service with recusal (6.3) or disclosure without naming the client (6.4). MR 6.5 relaxes conflicts only for short-term limited services and only when the lawyer doesn't know of a conflict.
