blocks.text: Reading: MR 4.1–4.4, 7.1–7.3, 7.6; Chs. 10–14, 16–18; Zauderer v. Office of Disciplinary Counsel (1985). The Thanksgiving break fell this week (Nov. 25–29).

body: In the course of representing a client, a lawyer shall not knowingly: (a) make a false statement of material fact or law to a third person; or (b) fail to disclose a material fact when disclosure is necessary to avoid assisting a criminal or fraudulent act by a client, unless disclosure is prohibited by MR 1.6.
blocks.title: MR 4.1

items: **Scope (CB 310):** statements by a lawyer (or on a lawyer's behalf), to a third person (not a client; MR 1.4 protects clients), in the course of representing a client. Consequences beyond discipline: tort or criminal liability and rescission of any agreement the misrepresentation procured.

blocks.title: What is a "false statement of material fact" (Ch. 10.B; CB 312–316)

items: **The elements (all required):** (1) a **statement**, by any means (oral, written, by context), including adopting another's statement you know is false; (2) **material**; (3) **factual**, meaning provably true or false, not opinion or position; (4) **false**: if a reasonable recipient would be misled into understanding it as a statement of a fact the speaker knows is false, it's a misrepresentation (CB 314); and (5) made **knowingly**.

**Negotiation (CB 315; MR 4.1 cmt [2]):** by convention, some statements aren't taken as statements of fact: estimates of price or value, a party's intentions as to an acceptable settlement ("my client won't take less than $500K"), and the existence of an undisclosed principal (unless nondisclosure would be fraud). This "puffing" or "posturing" is fine; "we have another offer at $500K," if false, isn't.

**Knowledge (CB 316):** negligent ("should have known") or innocent misstatements can't support discipline under MR 4.1(a), but knowing or negligent misrepresentation can support tort liability, and even an innocent one can support rescission or a contract defense.
**Half-truths and strategic ambiguity** violate MR 4.1(a) (CB 316): once you speak, don't leave a misleading impression.

**You must disclose an undisclosed material fact in only two situations (any one suffices):** (1) you said something that makes the omission misleading (MR 4.1(a)); or (2) disclosure is necessary to avoid assisting a client's crime or fraud (MR 4.1(b)).

**The 4.1(b) twist (CB 320):** if the client won't allow the disclosure, withdraw (with leave where required), and you **must** make it unless MR 1.6 **prohibits** it. Because a permissive exception (MR 1.6(b)(2)–(3)) means MR 1.6 doesn't prohibit disclosure, MR 4.1(b) turns that "may" into a "must."

**Problem 10 setup:** Maya, assisting partner Ron Rainmaker on an acquisition, learns facts the other side doesn't know. Silence is generally fine; affirmative misstatements, misleading half-truths, and silence that assists the client's fraud are not.

body: In representing a client, a lawyer shall not communicate about the subject of the representation with a person the lawyer **knows** to be represented by another lawyer **in the matter**, unless the lawyer has the consent of the other lawyer or is authorized to do so by law or a court order.
blocks.title: MR 4.2

items: **Know which world you're in (CB 327):** represented (MR 4.2) or unrepresented (MR 4.3).

**Who must follow it (CB 329):** "a lawyer," including people acting at the lawyer's direction or on the lawyer's behalf (investigators, paralegals; MR 8.4(a), 5.3). It applies even if the represented person starts the conversation or consents (cmt [3]); only the lawyer can consent.

**Who is protected (CB 331–336):** a person who has retained counsel in the matter, and, when an organization is represented in the matter, three categories of constituents (MR 4.2 cmt [7]; any one suffices): (1) a constituent who supervises, directs, or regularly consults with the organization's lawyer about the matter ("Upjohn management"); (2) one who has authority to obligate the organization about the matter; or (3) one whose act or omission in the matter may be imputed to the organization for civil or criminal liability. Former constituents aren't protected, and a constituent with personal counsel needs only that counsel's consent. Older versions and state variations differ, so check your jurisdiction (CB 334).

**"In the matter":** an organization with an in-house legal department isn't necessarily "represented in the matter" you're investigating (Problem 11B; see Jorgenson v. Taco Bell). **United States v. Talao** (9th Cir. 2000): a protected employee who wants to talk without company counsel present, to report the employer's wrongdoing, presents a different case.

**Knowledge (CB 338):** actual knowledge, but willful blindness counts the same (Global-Tech Appliances v. SEB; cmt [8]). If you're unsure, ask; the better practice is to ask a pro se litigant who may be ghost-advised (ABA Op. 15-472). A witness who honestly says "no lawyers" when an in-house lawyer has secretly been involved doesn't put you in violation.

**Communication (CB 339):** investigation without communicating (watching in public, reading public posts) doesn't violate the Rule (Problems 11D-2, 11D-3). Getting behind privacy settings with a "friend" request, or through someone else's account, raises the communication question (see In re Robertelli, N.J. 2020).
**With opposing counsel's consent** (CB 341). Get it clearly, preferably in writing.
**Not about the subject of the representation:** chatting about the weather or an unrelated matter (CB 342).
**As a party:** a lawyer who is a party may talk to the other party, and parties may always talk to each other directly; the lawyer may advise the client about such talks (cmt [4]).
**With someone you also represent or are asked to represent,** e.g., a person seeking a second opinion (CB 343; cmt [4]).

**Authorized by law or court order** (CB 344): statutory pre-filing investigations by government lawyers (subject to the McDade Amendment), communications with represented government agencies or officials on policy issues, and court-approved notices in class actions.

**Discipline** (see In re Howes, N.M. 1997). **Information-protective remedies:** disqualification, exclusion of the improperly obtained evidence, and monetary sanctions. **Decision-protective remedies:** rescission of agreements and relief from judgments or orders obtained through the forbidden contact.

body: (1) You must not state or imply that you are disinterested. (2) When you know or reasonably should know the unrepresented person misunderstands your role, for whatever reason, you must make reasonable efforts to correct it. (3) If the person's interests are or have a reasonable possibility of being in conflict with your client's, you must not give legal advice other than the advice to secure counsel. (4) You must not ask a non-client to refrain from voluntarily giving relevant information to another party, unless the person is the client's relative, employee, or agent and you reasonably believe the person's interests won't be adversely affected (MR 3.4(f)).
blocks.title: MR 4.3 and 3.4(f) — four things you must or must not do (CB 355)

items: **What you may do:** answer factual questions, give information, negotiate, and advocate for your client, truthfully, as long as none of it is dressed up as advice to the unrepresented person (CB 363). The line between "legal advice" and a statement of fact or position often turns on context and word choice: "the law requires you to sign this" is advice; "my client won't settle unless you sign this" is position.
**"Reasonable possibility" of conflict** and "knows or reasonably should know" set a low threshold (CB 598–599); when in doubt, assume the interests conflict.

**Organizational constituents:** company counsel must remind constituents that counsel represents only the company whenever counsel knows the company's interests are adverse to theirs (MR 1.13(f); Upjohn warning, Part IX).

**Consequences (CB 365):** discipline, and the same civil remedies as for no-contact violations: disqualification, evidentiary and monetary sanctions, rescission of agreements unfairly induced, and FRCP 60(b) relief.

body: A lawyer shall not counsel a client to engage, or assist a client, in conduct the lawyer **knows** is criminal or fraudulent, but may discuss the legal consequences of any proposed course of conduct and may counsel or assist a client to make a good-faith effort to determine the validity, scope, meaning, or application of the law.
blocks.title: MR 1.2(d)

items: **Knowledge (CB 372):** actual knowledge, which may be inferred from circumstances, including **willful blindness** (conscious avoidance): failing to learn what you consciously suspected and could have discovered with reasonable effort.

**Compliance advice vs. evasion advice:** advising how close a client can get to a legal line without crossing it is proper; advising how not to get caught, or how likely enforcement is, is counseling the client to break the law.

**Testing the law (CB 374):** advice about testing a statute or regulation by disobeying it can be proper (MR 1.2 cmt [12]). **Never counsel disobeying a court order**, even one you think is unconstitutional: that isn't a defense to contempt (Walker v. City of Birmingham).

blocks.title: A client proposes, persists in, or may be doing something unlawful (CB 374–379)

header: What you must, may, and should do
rows: **Must not** counsel or assist; **may**, should, and likely must explain the consequences (MR 1.2(d), 1.4(a)(5)); **may** give extra-legal advice about whether it's wise (MR 2.1). Never keep the client "happy" by blessing unlawful conduct.
Client persists without telling you, or despite your advice

Silence doesn't absolve you: the Comments suggest you **must** speak up. If the client keeps using your services in the unlawful conduct after the MR 1.4(a)(5) talk, you **must** decline or withdraw (MR 1.16(a)(4), 2023).
Client persists but isn't using your services
You **may**, and generally should, withdraw (MR 1.16(b)(1), (4), cmt [7]), subject to tribunal permission.
Client used your services in past unlawful conduct

You **may**, and generally should, withdraw (MR 1.16(b)(2)–(3)); you **must** if the client intends to keep using your services or your work implicates you (MR 1.16(a)(1), (4); MR 1.2 cmt [10]). Consider a noisy withdrawal (Part II).

The 2023 MR 1.16(a) amendment creates a duty to inquire into and assess the facts before and during every representation, scaled to the circumstances (not yet adopted anywhere as of the casebook). Whether or not required, you should investigate to confirm or allay suspicions and manage your own risk.

items: **Vicarious liability (CB 380):** willful blindness or assistance can make you criminally liable as an aider and abettor (18 U.S.C. § 2) or conspirator (MPC § 5.03), and civilly liable to third parties under standards that vary state to state.

blocks.title: Abusive Tactics, Threats, and Reporting Misconduct (MR 4.4(a), 8.3)
Embarrassing, delaying, or burdening others: MR 4.4(a) (Ch. 14; CB 393)

body: In representing a client, a lawyer shall not use means that have **no substantial purpose other than** to embarrass, delay, or burden a third person, or use methods of obtaining evidence that violate the legal rights of such a person.
blocks.title: MR 4.4(a)

items: **The elements (all required):** (1) "in representing a client" (not grocery shopping); (2) a "third person," meaning anyone but your client (fiduciary duties already require better behavior toward clients); (3) "means," actual speech or conduct, which violate the Rule when undertaken with the bad purpose, even if they don't succeed; and (4) "no substantial purpose other than" to embarrass, delay, or burden. Some embarrassment and burden are unavoidable; the Rule reaches only what isn't reasonably necessary.
**Contrast MR 8.4(g)**, which reaches harassment or discrimination on a protected basis in any conduct related to the practice of law, whether or not you're representing a client (Part XII).
**Overlap (CB 396):** most conduct violating MR 4.4(a) violates other Rules too, and supports court sanctions (FRCP 11, 37; § 1927) and sometimes tort liability.

**The First Amendment (CB 396):** no formal consequences may rest on protected speech, but the case law is confused and courts read lawyers' speech rights narrowly (Gentile; Part VIII). [[Example: United States v. Wunsch (9th Cir. 1996) held a local rule against "offensive personality" too vague to punish a lawyer's sexist letter to a prosecutor.]]

**The old Model Code rule** (DR 7-105(A)), still followed in a significant minority of states, barred threatening criminal charges solely to gain advantage in a civil matter. The Model Rules dropped it as redundant of more general prohibitions.

**ABA Op. 92-363 (CB 417):** under the Model Rules, a lawyer may threaten to bring, or agree not to bring, criminal or quasi-criminal charges to gain advantage in a civil dispute if (all required): (1) the charge is **related** to the civil claim; (2) the lawyer has a **well-founded belief** that both the civil claim and the criminal charges are warranted by law and fact; and (3) the lawyer doesn't attempt to exert or suggest **improper influence** over the criminal process.

**Never okay, anywhere (CB 418; any one is extortionate):** threats (1) to make charges unrelated to, or to disclose embarrassing facts not genuinely relevant to, the civil dispute; (2) to make charges with no substantial basis in fact or law (MR 3.1, 8.4(d)); (3) to engage in lawful conduct you don't actually intend to pursue (MR 4.1(a)); (4) based on improperly influencing officials, or suggesting you can (MR 8.4(e)); or (5) to commit violence or other illegal acts. These are torts and potentially crimes even when the threatened disclosures are true, and violate MR 4.4(a) and often 8.4(b).
**FRE 408 is no shield:** an extortionate threat couched as a settlement demand is admissible to prove the threat itself (FRE 408(b)), and the victim can always report it.

**Practical tiers (CB 419):** (1) threatening civil claims your client colorably has is the essence of a demand letter; (2) threatening to report opposing counsel's ethics violation to gain an advantage: don't, since in MR 8.3 states you must report it anyway, so it can't be a bargaining chip; and (3) anything else, think twice: the line between a proper threat and extortion can be razor-thin.
**Presenting charges without threatening first (CB 420):** under the majority view, you may present a charge you could properly threaten, but not one you couldn't.

blocks.name: Flatley v. Mauro, 39 Cal. 4th 299
blocks.topic: extortion dressed as a settlement demand
blocks.facts: A lawyer demanded a seven-figure "settlement" from Michael Flatley (of Riverdance) to resolve a sexual assault claim, warning that otherwise an investigation would expose immigration, Social Security, and tax matters to "any and all appropriate authorities," and that press releases would go to media worldwide.
blocks.held: The demand was criminal extortion as a matter of law. Flatley sued for civil extortion and defamation; Mauro was suspended for a year in Illinois and paid Flatley $400,000.
blocks.why: The model of a forbidden threat: unrelated charges and disclosures used as leverage (CB 415, 421).

blocks.title: Reporting another lawyer's misconduct: MR 8.3 (Ch. 16.D; CB 422)

items: **The elements (all required for the duty):** (1) you **know** (actual knowledge or willful blindness); (2) **another lawyer** (any other lawyer, including opposing counsel); (3) committed a violation of the Rules that raises a **substantial question** as to that lawyer's honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness as a lawyer in other respects; then (4) you shall inform the **appropriate professional authority** (the disciplinary agency, not the lawyer's boss).

**Exceptions (any one suffices):** (1) information protected by MR 1.6 (confidentiality trumps reporting unless an exception or consent applies); or (2) information gained while participating in an approved lawyers assistance program.
**MR 8.3(b)** imposes the same duty for judges' serious violations of the judicial conduct rules.

**Chapter 16 review Q3–Q4:** the client's no-objection removes the confidentiality bar, so knowing of opposing counsel's extortionate threat that raises a substantial question about his honesty and doing nothing violates MR 8.3. **In re Riehlmann** (La. 2005): a lawyer who waited years to report a friend's confession that, as a prosecutor, he had suppressed exculpatory evidence was disciplined.

blocks.text: Ch. 17 (MR 5.6 was assigned in Week 12).

body: A lawyer shall not participate in offering or making (either is barred): (a) a partnership, shareholders, operating, employment, or other similar agreement that restricts a lawyer's right to practice after the relationship ends, except an agreement concerning benefits upon retirement; or (b) an agreement in which a restriction on the lawyer's right to practice is part of the settlement of a client controversy.
blocks.title: MR 5.6

items: **Elements:** (1) "shall not" (mandatory); (2) "participate in offering or making," so defense counsel who proposes it and plaintiff's counsel who accepts it both violate; (3) an agreement that is part of the settlement of a client controversy; (4) containing a restriction on the lawyer's right to practice (e.g., "plaintiff's counsel will never sue H2Whoa again," or won't use what was learned in discovery against it in future cases).

**Why it's forbidden (CB 705):** it pits the lawyer's interests against the client's (a premium for the lawyer's promise), deprives future clients of the most knowledgeable counsel, and lets defendants buy off the lawyers who know where the bodies are. Frank and Happy's H2Whoa contamination case (Ch. 17 intro) is the setup.

**Consequences (CB 708):** discipline; breach of fiduciary duty and restitution of the lawyer's ill-gotten gains to the client; and the restriction is usually unenforceable as against public policy. Confidentiality terms that don't restrict practice are generally allowed, though increasingly controversial.

blocks.title: Employment and partnership restrictions: MR 5.6(a) (Ch. 17.B; CB 710–713)

items: Bars covenants not to compete for clients after leaving a firm, often limited by time, place, or practice area, because clients must be free to choose counsel (cmt [1]).
**Exceptions (any one suffices):** (1) restrictions tied to retirement benefits; and (2) restrictions in the sale of a law practice under MR 1.17 (MR 5.6 cmt [3]).

**Consequences:** discipline, and the restriction is voidable as against public policy, with amounts paid or withheld recoverable as unjust enrichment. Courts split on financial disincentives: compare Howard v. Babcock (Cal. 1993) (a reasonable cost imposed on departing partners who compete may be enforced) with Moskowitz v. Jacobson Holman (E.D. Va. 2015). Clawbacks of bar-exam or moving expenses from short-tenure hires are a different, rarer issue.

blocks.name: Howard v. Babcock, 6 Cal. 4th 409
blocks.topic: a reasonable toll on departing partners
blocks.facts: A law firm partnership agreement reduced the withdrawal benefits of partners who left and competed with the firm in the same area.
blocks.held: The California Supreme Court held that an agreement imposing a reasonable cost on departing partners who compete is not void per se and may be enforced.
blocks.why: The minority view on MR 5.6(a). [[Most courts, e.g., Cohen v. Lord, Day & Lord (N.Y. 1989), treat financial penalties for competing as unenforceable restrictions on practice.]]

items: **Bates v. State Bar of Arizona (1977):** truthful lawyer advertising is commercial speech protected by the First Amendment. Regulation gets **intermediate scrutiny**: the state must prove the rule (all required) (1) serves a **substantial** state interest; (2) **directly advances** it; and (3) is **no more extensive than necessary** (Central Hudson).
**Antitrust** may also limit a self-regulating bar's anticompetitive rules (North Carolina State Board of Dental Examiners v. FTC; Goldfarb, Part V).

**States still regulate aggressively**, and some rules are unconstitutional in part. Florida disciplined Sylvia Ibanez for truthfully listing her CPA and CFP credentials until the Supreme Court reversed (Ibanez). Know your state's rules before you post anything, including a website, and decide whether a fight over an overbroad rule is worth it. Florida found a pit bull and "1-800-PIT-BULL" misleading (Florida Bar v. Pape).

blocks.name: Bates v. State Bar of Arizona, 433 U.S. 350
blocks.facts: Two lawyers running a low-cost "legal clinic" advertised routine services, such as uncontested divorces and simple bankruptcies, at stated fees, in violation of Arizona's ban on lawyer advertising.
blocks.held: A blanket ban on truthful advertising of routine legal services and prices violates the First Amendment; states may still regulate false, deceptive, or misleading advertising and in-person solicitation.
blocks.why: The start of the modern regime: MR 7.1 targets only false or misleading communications.

blocks.name: Zauderer v. Office of Disciplinary Counsel, 471 U.S. 626
blocks.topic: illustrated ads, legal advice in ads, and required disclosures
blocks.source: assigned reading, Week 14 syllabus; casebook Ch. 18.B (CB 455 n.13, 458).
blocks.facts: An Ohio lawyer ran a newspaper ad aimed at women injured by the Dalkon Shield IUD. It included a drawing of the device, said the lawyer was handling such cases, and stated that cases were taken on a contingent-fee basis and "if there is no recovery, no legal fees are owed by our clients." Ohio disciplined him for soliciting through the ad, giving legal advice in it, using an illustration, and omitting that clients might owe costs.
blocks.held: (1) A state may not discipline a lawyer for truthful, nondeceptive printed advertising giving accurate information about potential clients' legal rights. (2) The ban on illustrations (Ohio's "dignity" rule) was unconstitutional: an accurate drawing isn't misleading and the state showed no substantial interest it advanced. (3) But the state may require disclosure that clients may be liable for significant litigation costs even if they lose; a disclosure requirement is valid if reasonably related to preventing deception and not unjustified or unduly burdensome, so the "no legal fees" ad without that disclosure was misleading.
blocks.why: The line between protected targeted advertising and regulable deception, and the deferential standard for compelled factual disclosures. It's why "no fee unless we win" ads must disclose costs (MR 7.1; Part V).

blocks.title: False or misleading communications: MR 7.1 (Ch. 18.B; CB 450–457)

body: A lawyer shall not make a false or misleading communication about the lawyer or the lawyer's services. A communication is false or misleading if it (any one suffices): (1) contains a material misrepresentation of fact or law; or (2) omits a fact necessary to make the statement considered as a whole not materially misleading.
blocks.title: MR 7.1

items: **Every communication counts** (CB 450): ads, websites, social media, business cards, letterhead, and firm names, made by or for the lawyer.

**Categories states condemn, rightly or not (MR 7.1 cmt [3]; CB 733–737):** (1) truthful reports of past results or testimonials that create **unjustified expectations** of similar results without reference to each case's facts ("he got me ONE MILLION DOLLARS, and he can do that for you, too!"); (2) **unsubstantiated comparisons** with other lawyers' services or fees, if specific enough to suggest they can be substantiated ("the lowest cost for a will in Yoknapatawpha County"), as opposed to puffery ("don't settle for less than the best"); and (3) claims of expertise or specialization (MR 7.2(c)). Some states ban testimonials, dramatizations, or superlatives outright; such categorical bans are constitutionally vulnerable. Paid spokespersons usually need a visible disclaimer (CB 466).
**Misleading by implication:** a firm name implying a partnership that doesn't exist, or ads implying you can achieve results by means that violate the law (MR 8.4(e)).
**MR 7.2(a):** a lawyer may communicate information about the lawyer's services through any media.

**MR 7.2(b)** forbids giving anything of value for recommending the lawyer's services, with the five exceptions in Part V (advertising costs; legal service plans and not-for-profit or qualified referral services; buying a practice; non-exclusive, disclosed reciprocal referral agreements; nominal thank-you gifts). It bars **"capping" and "running":** paying EMTs, hospital staff, tow-truck drivers, funeral directors, or anyone else to steer clients, whether by cash, kickbacks per client, or payments to hand out cards.

**MR 7.2(c) specialists:** don't state or imply certification as a specialist unless (all required) (1) the lawyer is certified by an organization approved by a state authority or accredited by the ABA; and (2) the certifying organization is clearly named. Saying you "concentrate in" or "focus on" an area is fine if true.

**MR 7.2(d):** every communication must include the name and contact information of at least one lawyer or firm responsible for its content. Many states add filing, labeling, and record-keeping requirements.

body: **(a)** "Solicitation" is a communication initiated by or for a lawyer, directed to a specific person the lawyer knows or reasonably should know needs legal services in a particular matter, that offers, or reasonably can be understood as offering, to provide legal services for that matter. **(b)** A lawyer shall not solicit professional employment by **live person-to-person contact** when a significant motive is the lawyer's or firm's pecuniary gain, unless the contact is with (any one suffices): (1) a lawyer; (2) a person with a family, close personal, or prior business or professional relationship with the lawyer or firm; or (3) a person who routinely uses for business purposes the type of legal services offered. **(c)** Even when (b) doesn't bar it, a lawyer shall not solicit if (any one bars it): (1) the target has made known a desire not to be solicited; or (2) the solicitation involves coercion, duress, or harassment. **(d)** The Rule doesn't prohibit communications authorized by law or ordered by a court. **(e)** A lawyer may participate in a prepaid or group legal service plan, operated by an organization the lawyer doesn't own or direct, that uses live contact to enroll members who aren't known to need legal services in a particular matter.
blocks.title: MR 7.3

items: **Why live contact is different (CB 461):** a person who just learned of a criminal charge or a loved one's death or injury is distressed and vulnerable, less able to exercise independent judgment, and more subject to a trained advocate's undue influence. Live person-to-person means in person, face-to-face, live telephone, and real-time visual or auditory contact; not letters, email, texts, or chat-room messages the recipient can ignore (MR 7.3 cmt [2]).

**Targeted letters and emails are generally allowed** under MR 7.3, but remain subject to MR 7.1 and to MR 7.3(c). [[The Supreme Court protected targeted letters (Shapero v. Kentucky Bar Ass'n, 1988) but upheld a 30-day ban on letters to accident victims (Florida Bar v. Went For It, 1995); it upheld discipline for in-person solicitation for profit (Ohralik v. Ohio State Bar, 1978) but protected nonprofit civil-rights solicitation (In re Primus, 1978).]]
**No pecuniary motive, no (b) problem:** pro bono or nonprofit outreach isn't barred by MR 7.3(b), though (c) still applies.
**A permissible solicitation can still be false or misleading** (MR 7.1; CB 464).
**Consequences (CB 464):** discipline, and in some states unenforceable fee agreements, fee forfeiture, or criminal "barratry" or "runner" statutes.

body: A lawyer or law firm shall not accept a government legal engagement or an appointment by a judge if the lawyer or firm makes a political contribution, or solicits political contributions, for the purpose of obtaining or being considered for that type of engagement or appointment.
blocks.title: MR 7.6 — political contributions to obtain government work ("pay to play")

items: Lawyers may participate fully in politics (cmt [1]). The Rule reaches only contributions made for the purpose of getting the work: contributions that wouldn't have been made but for the desire to be considered (cmt [5]). "Government legal engagement" means work a public official can award; "appointment by a judge" includes referees, special masters, receivers, guardians, and similar posts, but not substantially uncompensated services, engagements made on the merits after a request for proposals or other process free of political influence, or appointments made on a rotational basis from a list compiled without regard to contributions (cmt [3]). The ban covers PACs and entities the lawyer or firm controls (cmt [4]).

blocks.text: Reading: MR 8.4(g); Ch. 15. Taught during the make-up week (Nov. 30–Dec. 3).

items: **Why the Rule exists (CB 404):** good intentions get us only part of the way; people believe they are free of bias when they aren't. The ABA adopted MR 8.4(g) in 2016 to educate the bar and act against the invidious discrimination some colleagues still face. Goal B of the syllabus: a justice system that provides equal access and eliminates harassment, bias, discrimination, and racism in the law.

body: It is professional misconduct to engage in conduct that the lawyer **knows or reasonably should know** is **harassment or discrimination on the basis of** race, sex, religion, national origin, ethnicity, disability, age, sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status, or socioeconomic status **in conduct related to the practice of law**. This paragraph does not limit the ability of a lawyer to accept, decline, or withdraw from a representation in accordance with MR 1.16. This paragraph does not preclude legitimate advice or advocacy consistent with these Rules.
blocks.title: MR 8.4(g)

items: **Harassment or discrimination** (CB 405): defined by general anti-discrimination law, and by MR 8.4 cmt [3]: discrimination includes harmful verbal or physical conduct that manifests bias or prejudice; harassment includes sexual harassment and derogatory or demeaning verbal or physical conduct; sexual harassment includes unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favors, and other unwelcome verbal or physical conduct of a sexual nature.
**On the basis of a protected category** (CB 405): only the eleven listed categories. Harassment that isn't based on one (pure rudeness) may still violate MR 4.4(a) or 8.4(d), but not (g).
**Knows or reasonably should know** (CB 406): an objective standard, not just actual knowledge. Not knowing your joke was demeaning is no defense if a reasonable lawyer would have known.

**In conduct related to the practice of law** (CB 406; cmt [4]): much wider than client work: representing clients; interacting with witnesses, coworkers, court personnel, lawyers, and others while engaged in the practice of law; operating or managing a firm; and participating in bar association, business, or social activities connected with the practice of law.
**(1) Accepting, declining, or withdrawing** under MR 1.16 isn't limited: if MR 1.16 allows it, MR 8.4(g) probably doesn't forbid it (but other anti-discrimination law may; see Stropnicky).
**(2) Legitimate advice or advocacy** consistent with the Rules and the First Amendment rights of expression and petition is protected, even if others find the ideas discriminatory or hateful.
**(3) Promoting diversity and inclusion:** conduct to promote diversity, equity, and inclusion in the workplace or the bar, permitted by other law, doesn't violate the Rule.

**(4) Other carve-outs:** a trial judge's finding that peremptory challenges were exercised on a discriminatory basis (a Batson violation) doesn't alone establish a violation, though it has other consequences; limiting your practice by subject matter or to underserved populations is allowed; and charging reasonable, lawful fees isn't discrimination.

**Adoption is thin:** only a few states adopted it verbatim, though about half have some prohibition on discriminatory conduct, usually from a Comment treating discrimination as conduct "prejudicial to the administration of justice" (MR 8.4(d)). Delaware's MR 8.4 has no paragraph (g) (Part I). Virtually every jurisdiction has general anti-discrimination and anti-harassment laws that also reach lawyers.

**Free speech and vagueness challenges:** a federal court enjoined Pennsylvania's version as vague and overbroad (Greenberg v. Haggerty, E.D. Pa. 2020), but the Third Circuit reversed for lack of standing without reaching the merits (Greenberg v. Lehocky, 3d Cir. 2023).

**Other law already applies:** Title VII covers professional partnerships (Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins), and a firm and its partner paid compensatory and punitive damages for the partner's serial harassment of subordinates (Weeks v. Baker & McKenzie, Cal. Ct. App. 1998). The Supreme Court's limits on race-conscious admissions (Students for Fair Admissions, 2023) bear on what "permitted by other law" means for diversity programs.

blocks.name: Stropnicky v. Nathanson
blocks.facts: A divorce lawyer who represented only wives, as a matter of principle, refused to take a husband as a client.
blocks.held: The Massachusetts Commission Against Discrimination found that refusing him because of his sex violated the state public-accommodations law.
blocks.why: MR 8.4(g) doesn't limit declining under MR 1.16, but general anti-discrimination law may still forbid refusing clients because of a protected trait. Contrast limiting a practice to underserved populations or a subject matter, which cmt [5] allows (the basis for a Ch. 15 problem).

body: MR 4.4(a) needs a client representation and a "no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, delay, or burden" means, aimed at a third person. MR 8.4(g) needs a protected basis but reaches any conduct related to the practice of law (a firm party, a bar dinner, how you treat staff), and requires only that you reasonably should have known the conduct was harassment or discrimination.

Former government lawyer (MR 1.11(a)(2)); current government lawyer's prior private matter (MR 1.11(d)(2)(i))

items: **Discipline needs a Rule; disqualification doesn't.** Hot-potato violations, conflicts with non-clients owed confidentiality, and playbook disputes are fought through disqualification, not discipline.
**"May" isn't "must."** Every MR 1.6(b) exception is permissive, but MR 4.1(b), 3.3(c), and court orders can make disclosure mandatory.
**Consent form matters.** Confirmed in writing, signed by the client, and independently represented are different requirements (Part V ladder).
**Prosecutors are lawyers first.** MR 3.8 adds to, never subtracts from, MR 3.3, 3.4, 3.6, 4.1, and 4.2.
**Delaware differs:** no MR 8.4(g); its own MR 1.15 details. The MPRE and the final test the ABA text unless a question says otherwise.
